A complete, hands-on guide to reactive programming with Spring — from the Reactive Streams specification to production microservices — built on Java 21+ and Spring Boot 4.1.2 (Spring Framework 7, Project Reactor 3.8, Reactor Netty 1.3).

Every example is real code

The Reactor and WebFlux examples in this playbook are not pasted text: they live in the playbook-examples module as 97 passing JUnit tests and are embedded into these pages at build time. If an example breaks, the docs build breaks.

  • Career Roadmap: 0 → 15+ years

    Five levels from Foundation to Architect, each with topics, exercises and a checkpoint.

    Find your level

  • Interview Questions

    110 questions with detailed answers by experience band, plus tested coding exercises, "what does this print?" puzzles and system-design scenarios.

    Practise

  • Fundamentals

    Why reactive exists, the Reactive Manifesto, the Reactive Streams contract, backpressure, and an honest comparison with virtual threads.

    Start here

  • Project Reactor

    Mono and Flux, 80+ operators grouped by intent, schedulers, hot vs cold, Sinks, Context, debugging — each with a tested example.

    Learn Reactor

  • Spring WebFlux

    Netty and the event loop, annotated and functional endpoints, WebClient, HTTP interface clients, SSE, WebSocket, error handling with RFC 9457.

    Build APIs

  • Data, Security, Messaging

    R2DBC, reactive MongoDB and Redis, reactive transactions, Spring Security for WebFlux, OAuth2/JWT, Kafka, RSocket and Spring Cloud Gateway.

    Go deeper

  • Resilience, Testing, Production

    Timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, observability, StepVerifier, WebTestClient, Testcontainers, BlockHound, tuning and anti-patterns.

    Ship it

  • Capstone: Food Delivery App

    Six reactive microservices — gateway, restaurants, orders, payments, delivery tracking and live notifications — wired with Kafka, R2DBC, MongoDB, SSE and WebSocket.

    See it all together

docs.title: Spring Reactive Playbook
docs.text:
Reactive programming with Project Reactor, Spring WebFlux and Spring Boot 4, from the Reactive Streams spec to a production food-delivery microservice. Every example is real, tested code.

Start with the roadmap Project Reactor Food Delivery App

docs.title: How this playbook is organised
docs.text:
flowchart LR R([Roadmap: pick your level]) --> A A[Fundamentals] --> B[Project Reactor] B --> C[Spring WebFlux] C --> D[Reactive Data] C --> E[Security] C --> F[Messaging] D & E & F --> G[Resilience & Observability] G --> H[Testing] H --> I[Production] I --> Q[Interview Questions] Q --> J[[Food Delivery App]]

The Roadmap tab maps every page to an experience level (0–2, 2–5, 5–8, 8–12, 12–15+ years) and the Interview tab tests each level. Every topic tab uses small, generic examples (numbers, users, products, price tickers) so each concept is seen in isolation. The final Food Delivery App tab composes all of them into one event-driven system you can run with Docker Compose.

docs.title: Learning Path
docs.text: A compact reading order with a checkpoint per stage. For the full beginner → 15+ years plan with exercises per level, see the Career Roadmap.

docs.title: Stage 1 — Think in streams (1–2 days)
docs.text:
• Why reactive? — explain thread-per-request vs event loop
  • Reactive Streams — name the 4 interfaces and the signals
  • Backpressure — explain request(n) in your own words
  • Reactive vs virtual threads

Checkpoint: you can say why a Flux does nothing until subscribed.

docs.title: Stage 2 — Reactor fluency (3–5 days)
docs.text:
• Mono & Flux, Creating
  • Transforming — map vs flatMap vs concatMap vs switchMap
  • Filtering, Combining
  • Error handling — retries with backoff, timeouts
  • Schedulers — publishOn vs subscribeOn, wrapping blocking calls
  • Hot vs cold & Sinks, Context
  • Testing with StepVerifier

Checkpoint: run ./gradlew :playbook-examples:test, then change an expectation and watch it fail.

docs.title: Stage 3 — Build reactive services (1 week)
docs.text:
• WebFlux architecture and setup
  • Annotated and functional endpoints
  • WebClient, HTTP interface clients
  • SSE, WebSocket
  • R2DBC, MongoDB, transactions
  • Security, JWT

docs.title: Stage 4 — Distributed and production-ready (1 week)
docs.text:
• Kafka, Gateway
  • Resilience, Observability
  • Integration tests, BlockHound
  • Performance, Anti-patterns

docs.title: Stage 5 — Capstone
docs.text:
• Run the Food Delivery App and trace one order end to end
  • Add a feature: e.g. order cancellation that cancels the courier simulation (Disposable)

docs.title: Master Prompt — Spring Reactive Playbook + Food Delivery Capstone
docs.text:
Copy everything inside the box below into an AI coding assistant (Claude Code, etc.) to regenerate or extend this project. It encodes every decision taken while building it.

ROLE
You are a senior Java/Spring engineer and technical writer. Build "spring-reactive-webapp": a complete,
self-contained learning playbook for reactive programming with Spring, published as an MkDocs site,
plus runnable, tested code behind every example.

STACK (pin exact versions; verify each one resolves on Maven Central before using it)
- Java 21 baseline (must also build and run unchanged on Java 25 LTS)
- Latest GA Spring Boot (4.1.x at time of writing → Spring Framework 7, Reactor 2025.x / reactor-core 3.8,
  Reactor Netty 1.3, Spring Security 7, Spring Data 2026.0, Spring Kafka 4, Jackson 3)
- Spring Cloud release train compatible with that Boot line (Gateway server-webflux, reactive
  Resilience4j circuit breaker)
- Gradle 9 Kotlin DSL multi-project build with a version catalog (gradle/libs.versions.toml)
- Docs: MkDocs + Material for MkDocs (navigation.tabs, sticky tabs, instant navigation, search
  suggest/highlight, code copy + annotations, light/dark/auto palette toggle, admonitions, content tabs,
  Mermaid diagrams via superfences, pymdownx.snippets with check_paths: true)

STRUCTURE — TWO PARTS, IN THIS ORDER
PART 1 — THE PLAYBOOK (all tabs except the last)
  Cover EVERY topic and subtopic below. Every example in Part 1 uses GENERIC domains (numbers, strings,
  users, products, prices, stock tickers, orders-as-abstract-ids…). DO NOT use the food delivery
  domain anywhere in Part 1.
  Each page: concept explanation → marble/sequence diagram (Mermaid) where it helps → runnable example
  → "when to use / pitfalls" admonitions → key takeaways.
  Examples for Reactor and WebFlux MUST live as passing JUnit 5 tests in a `playbook-examples` module
  so the docs can never drift from working code. Use StepVerifier.withVirtualTime for anything
  time-based (no Thread.sleep, no flaky timing).

  Tab "Home": overview, getting started (build, test, serve docs), this master prompt, quick learning path.
  Tab "Roadmap": a 0 → 15+ years career roadmap in five levels — Foundation (0–2), Practitioner (2–5),
      Senior (5–8), Lead (8–12), Architect (12–15+). Per level: topics to master (linked to pages),
      hands-on exercises, a checkpoint, typical mistakes, and the matching interview set.
  Tab "Fundamentals": why reactive (thread-per-request limits, I/O-bound workloads), Reactive Manifesto,
      Reactive Streams spec (Publisher/Subscriber/Subscription/Processor, signals, rules), backpressure,
      reactive vs virtual threads (Loom) — honest decision guide.
  Tab "Project Reactor": Mono & Flux, assembly vs subscription time, cold by default; creating
      sequences (just/empty/error/defer/fromCallable/fromIterable/range/interval/generate/create);
      transforming (map/flatMap/concatMap/flatMapSequential/switchMap/handle/expand/transform,
      collect/reduce/scan); filtering (filter/filterWhen/distinct/take/skip/next/defaultIfEmpty/
      switchIfEmpty); combining (zip/merge/concat/combineLatest/firstWithValue/then/when/startWith);
      error handling (onErrorReturn/Resume/Map/Complete, per-element recovery, retry/retryWhen backoff,
      timeout, Exceptions.propagate, doOn* hooks); schedulers (publishOn vs subscribeOn,
      boundedElastic for blocking, parallel/ParallelFlux, virtual-thread scheduler); hot vs cold
      (share, publish/autoConnect, cache, replay) and Sinks (one, many unicast/multicast/replay,
      EmitResult, emit failure handlers); backpressure strategies (request(n), limitRate,
      onBackpressureDrop/Latest/Buffer + overflow strategies) and batching (buffer, bufferTimeout,
      window, groupBy); Context (contextWrite, deferContextual, propagation direction); resources &
      cancellation (using/usingWhen, Disposable, doFinally); time operators (delayElements,
      delaySubscription, sample/sampleFirst/sampleTimeout, elapsed/timed, repeat/repeatWhen polling,
      time windows); debugging (log, checkpoint, Hooks, ReactorDebugAgent); operator cheat sheet;
      advanced internals (assembly/subscription/execution, operator fusion, prefetch/queues, Scannable,
      custom operators via transform/transformDeferred, JDK Flow + RxJava/Mutiny/coroutines interop,
      ReactiveAdapterRegistry, reactor-pool/extra/tools).
  Tab "Spring WebFlux": architecture (Netty event loop, HttpHandler, DispatcherHandler, request
      lifecycle); project setup; annotated controllers; functional endpoints (RouterFunction,
      HandlerFunction, HandlerFilterFunction); error handling (ProblemDetail/RFC 9457,
      @RestControllerAdvice, WebExceptionHandler); WebFilter; WebClient (retrieve vs exchange,
      onStatus, timeouts, retries, connection pool, filters); HTTP interface clients (@HttpExchange);
      streaming (SSE, NDJSON); WebSocket; codecs, CORS, multipart, server configuration; files and
      DataBuffers (zero-copy downloads, streaming uploads, buffer release); GraphQL (Spring for GraphQL,
      @BatchMapping, subscriptions); Reactor Netty used directly (HttpClient/TcpServer, pools, wiretap).
  Tab "Reactive Data": R2DBC (repositories, DatabaseClient, R2dbcEntityTemplate, pooling, schema
      management), reactive MongoDB (repositories, template, tailable cursors, change streams),
      reactive Redis (templates, caching, pub/sub), reactive transactions (@Transactional,
      TransactionalOperator); other stores (Cassandra, Elasticsearch, Neo4j), reactive @Cacheable with
      Caffeine async mode, reactive sessions (WebSession + Spring Session).
  Tab "Security": SecurityWebFilterChain, ReactiveUserDetailsService, ReactiveSecurityContextHolder,
      OAuth2 resource server with JWT, OAuth2 client + WebClient token relay, @EnableReactiveMethodSecurity.
  Tab "Messaging": Kafka in reactive apps (KafkaTemplate → Mono.fromFuture, async @KafkaListener
      returning Mono, ordering, idempotency, outbox; note reactor-kafka status), RSocket (4 interaction
      models), Spring Cloud Gateway (routes, predicates, filters, global filters), Spring Cloud Stream
      reactive functions, streaming LLM responses with Spring AI ChatClient.stream() over SSE.
  Tab "Resilience & Observability": timeouts, retries with jitter, circuit breaker, bulkhead,
      rate limiting, fallbacks; Micrometer observation, tracing & automatic context propagation,
      logging/MDC in reactive code, Actuator.
  Tab "Testing": StepVerifier (expectations, virtual time, context, TestPublisher, PublisherProbe),
      WebTestClient (bindToController/RouterFunction/server), Boot test slices and Testcontainers ITs,
      BlockHound.
  Tab "Production": performance tuning (event loops, pools, memory, codecs limits), best practices &
      anti-patterns (block(), subscribe() inside operators, ThreadLocal, unbounded flatMap, etc.),
      migrating from Spring MVC, Kotlin coroutines interop, reactive @Scheduled and background-stream
      lifecycle, graceful shutdown, containers/Kubernetes sizing for Netty, GraalVM native images.
  Tab "Interview": 110+ questions with detailed model answers split by experience band (Beginner 0–2,
      Intermediate 2–5, Senior 5–8, Lead 8–12, Architect 12–15+), each as a collapsible Q&A with
      follow-ups; 10 coding exercises and 10 "what does this print?" puzzles whose solutions are
      passing tests; system-design scenarios (live tracking at scale, aggregating BFF, exactly-once
      payments, streaming exports, real-time notifications, rate-limited partner APIs).

PART 2 — THE CAPSTONE (exactly ONE final tab, AFTER all other tabs: "Food Delivery App")
  Only here, build a microservice food delivery platform that applies the topics from Part 1, with a
  page per service plus overview/architecture, run instructions, end-to-end flow (Mermaid sequence
  diagram), testing and production hardening. Services (each a Spring Boot WebFlux app):
  - api-gateway (8080): Spring Cloud Gateway, JWT resource server (dev HS256 token endpoint),
    X-User-Id relay from the security context, correlation-id GlobalFilter, retry on idempotent GETs,
    serves a small static UI (vanilla JS) that orders and tracks live via SSE + WebSocket.
  - restaurant-service (8081): functional endpoints, R2DBC PostgreSQL, programmatic validation,
    ProblemDetail errors, batch menu-item lookup.
  - order-service (8082): annotated controllers, hexagonal ports, R2DBC with a reactive transaction
    over two tables, Idempotency-Key, HTTP interface client to restaurant-service, WebClient +
    Resilience4j circuit breaker + retry/backoff to payment-service, publishes OrderPlaced to Kafka,
    consumes delivery status with an async listener, order state machine, SSE status stream (Sinks).
  - payment-service (8085): simulated latency (Mono.delay), configurable failure rate, idempotent
    replays via Mono.cache().
  - delivery-service (8083): reactive MongoDB, consumes OrderPlaced, assigns a courier, simulates the
    trip with Flux.interval + concatMap, publishes status events, SSE tracking.
  - notification-service (8084): consumes all events, fans out through a replaying Sink to WebSocket
    clients (with SSE fallback).
  - common-events: framework-free event records + topic names (food.<context>.<aggregate>.<event>.v1).
  Money is long minor units (paise), never floating point. Timestamps are Instant/TIMESTAMPTZ UTC.
  Provide docker-compose (Postgres 17, MongoDB 8, Kafka KRaft; apps behind a profile) and a
  multi-stage Dockerfile. Unit/slice tests must run without Docker.

QUALITY BAR
- Constructor injection, records, jakarta.* imports, no field injection, no block() in request paths.
- `./gradlew build` is green; `mkdocs build --strict` is green.
- Verify the capstone end to end (place order → payment → Kafka → courier simulation → SSE/WebSocket
  updates until DELIVERED) before calling it done.
- README with quick start; this prompt saved as MASTER_PROMPT.md and rendered as a docs page.

docs.title: Why the prompt is shaped this way
docs.text:
• Generic first, capstone last. Topic pages stay focused on one concept each; the food delivery app is where they are composed, so a reader meets each idea in isolation before seeing it under load.
  • Examples are tests. Snippet markers + check_paths: true mean a renamed method or a broken example breaks the docs build, not the reader's trust.
  • Versions are verified, not remembered. Reactive Spring changes fast (Boot 4 split auto-configuration into modules, Jackson 3 moved to tools.jackson, Gateway moved properties under spring.cloud.gateway.server.webflux), so the prompt insists on checking Maven Central.

docs.title: Coding Interview: 12 Reactor & WebFlux Problems, Solved & Tested
docs.text:
Reactive coding rounds test whether you can pick the right operator under pressure: zip vs flatMap, switchMap vs concatMap, where subscribeOn goes, what happens to an error inside flatMap, why Mono.just blocks. They also test whether you can prove it with StepVerifier. These 12 problems are different from the ten in Coding Exercises and lean more on WebFlux: functional endpoints, WebClient fan-out, SSE-style hot feeds, Context, sagas and a hand-written circuit breaker.

Every solution lives in playbook-examples/.../codinginterview with a test class per problem (39 tests, using virtual time wherever time matters, so they run in milliseconds). CI runs them as part of ./gradlew build, and each page shows that problem's real test report.

One trap was hit for real while writing the tests, and it's kept as a lesson: StepVerifier sends a leading thenRequest() inside onSubscribe, before a Flux.create producer starts emitting, so the backpressure overflow never happened (problem 4).

Each page follows the same structure:

  1. Problem: the statement as an interviewer would give it.
  2. Key idea: the shape of the solution before any code, with a diagram.
  3. Solution: the complete, runnable code (included from the repository, so it is exactly what CI ran).
  4. Walkthrough: the important lines and why they are written that way.
  5. Complexity: time and space for each approach.
  6. Run it: the command and its real output.
  7. Common mistakes and follow-up questions with answers.

docs.title: How to answer a coding round
docs.text:
1. Draw the marble diagram first: what goes in, when, and what comes out. Most bugs are visible on the diagram.
  2. Choose the flattening operator deliberately: flatMap (concurrent, unordered), flatMapSequential (concurrent, ordered), concatMap (one at a time), switchMap (latest wins).
  3. Keep blocking out of the chain, or isolate it on a bounded scheduler, and say so explicitly.
  4. Test with StepVerifier, using withVirtualTime for anything with delays, timeouts or retries, and assert on the side effects (calls made, cancellations).
  5. Name the failure semantics: what errors do to the stream, what cancellation does to in-flight work, and where backpressure applies.

docs.text:

coding-interview/run-tests.sh --check  # fails on any failing test or changed report (CI checks the reports after ./gradlew build)

docs.title: 1. Functional Endpoints: CRUD with Validation
docs.text: L1 ★★☆ · RouterFunction, ServerRequest/ServerResponse, manual validation, ProblemDetail

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Implement POST /products, GET /products/{id} and DELETE /products/{id} with functional endpoints (no @RestController). Validate the body and return 201 + Location, 404 and 400, each as a ProblemDetail that lists every violation.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
A RouterFunction maps requests to handler functions (ServerRequest -> Mono<ServerResponse>). Nothing is implicit: you decode the body with bodyToMono, call the validator yourself, and build responses explicitly. Use switchIfEmpty(Mono.defer(...)) for 404 so the error response is only built when it's needed.

flowchart LR R["POST /products"] --> RF{RouterFunction} RF --> H["create(ServerRequest)"] H --> B["bodyToMono(CreateProduct)"] --> V{validate} V -->|violations| E400["400 ProblemDetail"] V -->|ok| S["store → 201 + Location"]

docs.title: Solution
Walkthrough
docs.text: Code Why route().path("/products", b -> b.GET("/{id}", this::get).POST("", this::create).DELETE(...)).build() Nested routes keep one prefix and read like a routing table, so you can test them without a Spring context (WebTestClient.bindToRouterFunction). .switchIfEmpty(Mono.error(new IllegalArgumentException("request body is required"))) An empty body is a client error, not a silently empty Mono that completes with no response. .flatMap(this::validate) Functional endpoints have no @Valid, so validation is an explicit step that returns either the value or an error. .switchIfEmpty(Mono.defer(() -> problem(NOT_FOUND, ...))) defer builds the 404 response lazily. Without it, the response Mono is assembled on every call, found or not. .onErrorResume(IllegalArgumentException.class, e -> problem(BAD_REQUEST, e.getMessage())) Map the domain error to HTTP in the handler. A WebExceptionHandler would centralise this across routes.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space per request O(1) map ops + validation O(products)

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
./gradlew :playbook-examples:test --tests '*P01ProductRouterTest'

P01ProductRouterTest: 4 tests, 0 failures
  ✔ create · returns201 · with location
  ✔ invalid body · returns400 · with every violation
  ✔ missing product · returns404 · problem detail
  ✔ round trip · create get delete

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Forgetting that bodyToMono on an empty body completes empty, so the chain does nothing and returns an empty response.
  • Calling .block() in a handler to get the body. That blocks the event loop.
  • Using switchIfEmpty(problem(...)) without defer. It works, but the response is assembled eagerly every time.

docs.title: Follow-up questions
docs.text:
Annotated controllers vs functional endpoints: when would you choose each?

Annotated controllers are familiar, with declarative validation and less code. Functional endpoints give explicit, composable routing (routes are values you can build in code, filter and test without a context), suit lightweight apps, and keep request handling free of reflection. Both run on the same WebFlux engine.

How do you add a cross-cutting filter to a router?

routes().filter((req, next) -> ...) for per-router filters (auth checks, timing), or a WebFilter bean for the whole application.

docs.title: 2. WebClient Fan-Out with Partial Fallbacks
docs.text: L2 ★★☆ · Mono.zip, per-call timeout, onErrorResume, required vs optional

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: A profile page needs the user (required), recent orders and loyalty points (optional). Call the three services in parallel. A slow or failing optional service gives a fallback and a "degraded" note, while a failing required call fails the whole response. Test it without a network.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
Mono.zip subscribes to all its sources at once, so latency is that of the slowest call. Each optional call gets its own timeout and onErrorResume, which turn failure into a value. Here that value is a small Result carrying the fallback and the reason, so zip never sees an error from it. The test plugs a stub ExchangeFunction into the real WebClient, which keeps the actual encoding and decoding but needs no server.

sequenceDiagram participant A as aggregator participant U as /users participant O as /orders (5 s) participant L as /loyalty (503) par zip subscribes to all A->>U: GET A->>O: GET (timeout 200 ms) A->>L: GET end U-->>A: user L-->>A: 503 → fallback 0, "loyalty: 503" Note over A,O: 200 ms → fallback [], "orders: timeout" A-->>A: Profile(user, [], 0, degraded)

docs.title: Solution
Walkthrough
docs.text: Code Why Mono.zip(user, orders, points) Parallel by construction. The first test asserts that three 100 ms calls finish in well under 300 ms. .timeout(optionalTimeout).map(Result::ok).onErrorResume(e -> Mono.just(Result.fallback(...))) The order matters: the timeout must sit before onErrorResume, so the timeout error is what gets converted into the fallback. bodyToFlux(Order.class).take(3).collectList() take(3) cancels the upstream after three items, so a long list isn't downloaded. WebClient.builder().exchangeFunction(req -> ...) A test seam built into WebClient. Responses are created with ClientResponse.create(status).body(json). expectError(WebClientResponseException.NotFound.class) The required call has no fallback, so retrieve() turns the 404 into an exception that fails the zip.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space latency max(call latencies, bounded by timeouts) O(response sizes)

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
./gradlew :playbook-examples:test --tests '*P02ProfileAggregatorTest'

P02ProfileAggregatorTest: 3 tests, 0 failures

  ✔ required service failure · fails the whole profile
  ✔ slow and failing optional services · degrade gracefully

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Using flatMap chains (user.flatMap(u -> orders...)), which makes the calls sequential: latency is the sum.
  • onErrorResume before timeout, so the timeout fires after the fallback point and fails the zip.
  • Letting an optional source complete empty. zip then completes empty and the whole profile disappears. Always map to a value.

docs.title: Follow-up questions
docs.text:
zip vs zipWhen vs Mono.when?

zip combines independent sources in parallel. zipWhen runs the second source after the first, with the first's value (dependent calls). when waits for completion and ignores values, which suits fire-and-forget side effects.

How do you add retries and circuit breaking?

Add retryWhen(Retry.backoff(2, 100ms).filter(transient)) per call, inside the timeout budget, and Resilience4j's transformDeferred(CircuitBreakerOperator.of(cb)), or Spring Cloud Circuit Breaker's ReactiveCircuitBreaker. Problem 12 builds one by hand.

docs.title: 3. Calling Blocking Code from WebFlux
docs.text: L2 ★★☆ · Mono.fromCallable, subscribeOn, dedicated bounded scheduler, Mono.just trap

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: A legacy CRM SDK is blocking (50 ms per call). Call it from a WebFlux service without blocking the event loop, make it lazy, give it a timeout, and stop a slow CRM from exhausting the threads that other blocking work needs.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
Wrap the call in Mono.fromCallable, which is lazy and runs once per subscription, and move execution with subscribeOn to a dedicated, bounded scheduler (Schedulers.newBoundedElastic(10, 100, "legacy-crm")). The tests prove which thread did the work, that nothing runs before subscription, and that Mono.just(blockingCall()) runs at assembly time on the caller's thread.

flowchart LR EL["event loop (reactor-http-nio)"] -->|"subscribe"| FC["Mono.fromCallable(legacy::load)"] FC -->|"subscribeOn"| BP["legacy-crm pool (max 10 threads, queue 100)"] BP -->|"result"| EL2["continue the chain"] X["Mono.just(legacy.load())"] -.->|"runs NOW, on the caller"| EL

docs.title: Solution
Walkthrough
docs.text: Code Why Mono.fromCallable(() -> legacy.loadCustomer(id)) Lazy: the callable runs when someone subscribes, once per subscription, as the second test proves. .subscribeOn(blockingPool) Moves the subscription (and so the callable) onto the pool. Its position in the chain doesn't matter for the source. Schedulers.newBoundedElastic(10, 100, "legacy-crm") A bulkhead: at most 10 threads and 100 queued tasks for this dependency. The shared boundedElastic() is used by everything else. Mono.just(legacy.loadCustomer(id)) The classic trap: the argument is evaluated immediately, before any subscriber exists, on whatever thread built the pipeline. That's often the event loop. flatMap over 10 ids → < 400 ms Ten 50 ms calls run in parallel on the pool rather than one after another.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space per call blocking time, on a pool thread 1 pool thread while running

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
./gradlew :playbook-examples:test --tests '*P03BlockingBridgeTest'

P03BlockingBridgeTest: 4 tests, 0 failures
  ✔ blocking call · runs on the dedicated pool · not the caller
  ✔ from callable · is lazy · nothing runs until subscribe
  ✔ many concurrent calls · do not serialise
  ✔ mono just · blocks the caller at assembly time

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Mono.just(blocking()) or Mono.fromCallable(...) without subscribeOn: both block the event loop.
  • Using publishOn to fix a blocking source. publishOn only moves the operators after it.
  • Using Schedulers.parallel() for blocking I/O. It has one thread per core, and blocking them starves all CPU work.
  • Running a blocking JDBC repository inside WebFlux at high load. Prefer R2DBC, or use Spring MVC on virtual threads.

docs.title: Follow-up questions
docs.text:
How do you detect accidental blocking calls?

Use BlockHound (BlockHound.install() in tests): it throws when a blocking call such as Thread.sleep, socket reads or FileInputStream.read happens on a non-blocking thread. Reactor-tools' ReactorDebugAgent helps trace where it came from.

With virtual threads, is WebFlux still worth it?

For request/response services over blocking libraries, Spring MVC on virtual threads is simpler and often just as scalable. WebFlux still shines for streaming (SSE, WebSockets), backpressure, and composing many async sources.

docs.title: 4. Backpressure: Buffer, Drop or Keep Latest
docs.text: L3 ★★★ · onBackpressureBuffer + DROP_OLDEST, onBackpressureDrop, onBackpressureLatest, limitRate

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: A producer pushes 100 events and ignores demand (UI events, a sensor, a hot feed). The consumer is slow. Implement and test three policies: bounded buffer keeping the newest, drop while busy, and keep only the latest. Also show a cold source consumed in batches of 10.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
Backpressure operators sit between a producer that can't slow down and a consumer that requests at its own pace. They decide what to lose when demand is zero: the oldest (DROP_OLDEST), new arrivals (onBackpressureDrop), or everything but the latest. For sources that can slow down, limitRate(n) turns unbounded demand into batches.

flowchart LR P["producer: 1..100 (ignores demand)"] --> B{"consumer demand = 0"} B -->|"buffer(10, DROP_OLDEST)"| R1["keeps 91..100, drops 1..90"] B -->|"onBackpressureDrop"| R2["delivers what was requested, drops the rest"] B -->|"onBackpressureLatest"| R3["keeps only 100"] C["cold Flux.range"] -->|"limitRate(10)"| R4["request(10), then replenish ≤ 10"]

docs.title: Solution
Walkthrough
docs.text: Code Why Flux.create(sink -> ..., FluxSink.OverflowStrategy.IGNORE) Simulates a producer that pushes regardless of demand, so the downstream operator is what has to cope. hot.onBackpressureBuffer(size, dropped::add, BufferOverflowStrategy.DROP_OLDEST) Bounded memory. The overflow callback lets you count or log losses. Always measure what you drop. class LateSubscriber ... hookOnSubscribe(s) { /* request nothing yet */ } A trap hit for real: StepVerifier runs a leading thenRequest() inside onSubscribe, but Flux.create emits only after onSubscribe returns. Demand therefore arrived first and nothing overflowed. A subscriber that requests later reproduces a genuinely slow consumer. requests.get(0) == 10 && all <= 10 limitRate(10) asks the source for 10, then replenishes in smaller batches (75% by default), never Long.MAX_VALUE.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space buffer O(1) per element O(buffer size) drop / latest O(1) O(1)

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
./gradlew :playbook-examples:test --tests '*P04BackpressureTest'

P04BackpressureTest: 4 tests, 0 failures
  ✔ bounded buffer · keeps newest10 · drops oldest
  ✔ drop · delivers only what was requested
  ✔ latest · keeps only the most recent value
  ✔ limit rate · requests in batches · never unbounded

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Using onBackpressureBuffer() with no size limit: an unbounded buffer is an out-of-memory error waiting to happen.
  • Dropping silently. Count drops (a metric) so lossy behaviour shows up in dashboards.
  • Applying limitRate to a hot source that ignores demand. It only helps sources that honour request(n).
  • Testing backpressure with a StepVerifier that already requested, which tests nothing (see the walkthrough).

docs.title: Follow-up questions
docs.text:
How does backpressure work across the network in WebFlux?

Reactor Netty translates demand into TCP flow control: when the subscriber stops requesting, Netty stops reading from the socket, the receive window fills, and the sender slows down. For SSE or WebSockets to browsers you usually also need application-level policies (drop, sample or latest), because clients vary wildly in speed.

sample vs onBackpressureLatest?

sample(Duration) emits the latest value on a fixed timer, regardless of demand. onBackpressureLatest keeps the latest value until the consumer asks. Use sample for UI refresh rates and latest for "as fast as the consumer can go".

docs.title: 5. Batch Writes by Size or Time
docs.text: L2 ★★☆ · bufferTimeout, concatMap, virtual time

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Events arrive in bursts and trickles. Write them to the database in batches of up to 10, or after 1 second, whichever comes first, with one batch in flight at a time so the DB isn't overloaded and order is preserved. Test it without waiting in real time.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
bufferTimeout(maxSize, maxWait) emits a batch when it's full or when the timer started by its first element fires. That gives low latency for trickles and efficiency for bursts. concatMap(bulkInsert) runs one write at a time, in order. StepVerifier.withVirtualTime replaces the clock, so 15 seconds of traffic run in milliseconds.

flowchart LR E["burst: 25 events at t=0, then 1 event every 5 s"] --> BT{"bufferTimeout(10, 1 s)"} BT -->|"full"| B1["[10] [10] at t=0"] BT -->|"timer"| B2["[5] at t=1 s"] BT -->|"timer"| B3["[1] [1] [1]"] B1 & B2 & B3 --> CM["concatMap(bulkInsert): one at a time"]

docs.title: Solution
Walkthrough
docs.text: Code Why .bufferTimeout(maxSize, maxWait) Size or time. buffer(10) alone would hold the last 5 events until 5 more arrived, possibly forever. .concatMap(bulkInsert) concatMap subscribes to the next insert only after the previous one completes: ordered, with one batch in flight. flatMap would run them concurrently and out of order. StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> ...) The pipeline must be built inside the supplier so that Flux.interval and the buffer timers use the virtual scheduler. .expectNext(10, 10).thenAwait(Duration.ofSeconds(1)).expectNext(5) Proves both triggers: size-triggered batches immediately, then a time-triggered remainder. maxInFlight == 1, firstIds == [1, 11, 21] The second test checks that there's no overlap between inserts and that the order is kept.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space per event O(1) O(batch size)

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
./gradlew :playbook-examples:test --tests '*P05BatcherTest'

P05BatcherTest: 2 tests, 0 failures
  ✔ burst flushes by size · trickle flushes by time
  ✔ one batch in flight at atime · preserves order

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• buffer(n) without a timeout. Low-traffic periods never flush.
  • Creating the pipeline outside the withVirtualTime supplier, so the real clock is used and the test hangs or flakes.
  • flatMap for writes, which gives unbounded parallel inserts and lost ordering.
  • Forgetting that bufferTimeout with slow downstream demand can back up. Newer Reactor versions offer a fairBackpressure variant.

docs.title: Follow-up questions
docs.text:
How would you make the writes idempotent if a batch is retried?

Give events ids and use INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (id) DO NOTHING (or a unique constraint plus ignoring duplicates), so retrying a partially applied batch is safe. Retry with retryWhen inside concatMap.

window vs buffer?

buffer collects elements into a List (memory for the whole batch). window emits a Flux per window, so you can stream into the sink without holding the batch, which is useful for large batches or streaming uploads.

docs.title: 6. Hot Price Feed with Replay for Late Subscribers
docs.text: L2 ★★☆ · Sinks.many().replay().limit(n), hot vs cold, asFlux, subscriber count

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: One live price feed must serve many subscribers (browser tabs over SSE). A subscriber that joins late should immediately get the last 3 prices, then live ones. Cancelling one subscriber must not affect the others, and completion must reach everyone.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
A sink is a programmatic, hot publisher. Sinks.many().replay().limit(3) multicasts to all subscribers and replays the last three values to each new one. Expose it as a Flux (asFlux()) so callers can't emit. Producers use emitNext with an explicit failure handler, so concurrent-emission bugs surface instead of being silently dropped.

sequenceDiagram participant P as producer participant S as replay(limit 3) sink participant A as subscriber A (early) participant B as subscriber B (late) P->>S: 100 .. 105 S->>A: 100 .. 105 (live) B->>S: subscribe S-->>B: replay 103, 104, 105 P->>S: 106, 107 S->>A: 106, 107 S->>B: 106, 107

docs.title: Solution
Walkthrough
docs.text: Code Why Sinks.many().replay().limit(replayLast) Hot plus bounded history. multicast().onBackpressureBuffer() has no history; replay().all() keeps everything, which is a memory leak for an endless feed. sink.emitNext(t, Sinks.EmitFailureHandler.FAIL_FAST) Sinks are not safe for concurrent emitNext. FAIL_FAST throws instead of silently dropping. For multiple producer threads, use busyLooping(Duration) or serialise the emitters. public Flux<Tick> ticks() { return sink.asFlux(); } Read-only view. Consumers can't call emitNext or complete the feed. subscriberCount() 2 → 1 after dispose Cancelling one subscriber leaves the source and the other subscribers running, unlike a cold Flux, where each subscriber has its own source.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space emit O(subscribers) O(replay size)

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
./gradlew :playbook-examples:test --tests '*P06PriceFeedTest'

P06PriceFeedTest: 3 tests, 0 failures
  ✔ filter per symbol · and completion reaches subscribers
  ✔ late subscriber · gets last three · then live ticks
  ✔ many subscribers · share one upstream · and receive the same ticks

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Using replay().all() for an infinite feed, which is unbounded memory.
  • Calling emitNext from several threads with the default handling, which causes FAIL_NON_SERIALIZED drops.
  • Returning the Sinks.Many itself from an API, which lets any caller emit or complete it.
  • Expecting a cold Flux to behave like this. Each subscriber would restart the source, for example re-opening the upstream connection per browser tab.

docs.title: Follow-up questions
docs.text:
How do you turn a cold source (one upstream connection) into a shared hot one?

coldFlux.share() (multicast while subscribers exist), publish().refCount(n) or autoConnect(n) (start after n subscribers), or replay(3).refCount() for history. This way 100 browser tabs share one upstream connection.

How would you expose this over SSE?

@GetMapping(produces = TEXT_EVENT_STREAM_VALUE) Flux<ServerSentEvent<Tick>> stream() { return feed.ticks().map(t -> ServerSentEvent.builder(t).id(...).build()); }. Add a heartbeat (Flux.interval merged in) so proxies don't close idle connections.

docs.title: 7. Propagating Tenant Id with Reactor Context
docs.text: L3 ★★★ · contextWrite, deferContextual, upstream propagation, thread hops

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Every query and downstream call must carry the caller's tenant id. In reactive code a ThreadLocal doesn't work, because operators hop threads. Pass the tenant through Reactor Context, show it surviving thread changes, and show why where you write it matters.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
Context is attached to the subscriber and flows upstream, from the subscriber towards the source. Write it once at the edge (contextWrite, typically in a WebFilter) and read it anywhere above that point (Mono.deferContextual). An inner contextWrite overrides the value for its own subtree only.

flowchart BT SUB["subscriber"] --> CW["contextWrite(tenant=acme)"] CW --> FM["flatMap(loadInvoices) reads ctx: sees acme ✓"] FM --> PO["publishOn(parallel): thread hop, context intact"] PO --> SRC["Mono.just(c-42)"] W["contextWrite ABOVE a reader"] -.->|"reader below can't see it"| X["UNKNOWN"]

docs.title: Solution
Walkthrough
docs.text: Code Why Mono.deferContextual(ctx -> ... ctx.getOrDefault(TENANT, "UNKNOWN")) Reads the Context at subscription time. getOrDefault makes a missing tenant visible instead of throwing deep inside a query. pipeline.contextWrite(Context.of(TENANT, tenant)) Write at the end of the chain, as the outermost operator. It applies to everything above it. .publishOn(Schedulers.parallel()) The test hops threads before reading, which is exactly where a ThreadLocal would lose the value. placementMatters_contextOnlyFlowsUpstream contextWrite placed above the reader has no effect on it, and the test gets UNKNOWN. This is the most common Context bug. innerWriteOverridesOuter_forItsSubtreeOnly Nested writes shadow outer values for the part of the chain above them, which is handy for impersonation or per-call overrides.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space read / write O(1) O(entries), immutable

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
./gradlew :playbook-examples:test --tests '*P07TenantContextTest'

P07TenantContextTest: 4 tests, 0 failures
  ✔ context reaches deep operators · even across thread hops
  ✔ downstream call · receives tenant header
  ✔ inner write overrides outer · for its subtree only
  ✔ placement matters · context only flows upstream

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Using ThreadLocal or MDC directly. The values vanish after publishOn, flatMap on another scheduler, or a WebClient call.
  • Putting contextWrite in the middle of a chain and expecting operators below it to see the value.
  • Storing large or mutable objects in Context. It's meant for small, immutable request metadata.

docs.title: Follow-up questions
docs.text:
How do you get the tenant into log lines (MDC)?

Turn on automatic context propagation: Hooks.enableAutomaticContextPropagation() with Micrometer's context-propagation and registered ThreadLocalAccessors. In Boot, spring.reactor.context-propagation=auto. Reactor then restores ThreadLocals such as MDC from Context around each operator.

How does a WebFilter set it for every request?

(exchange, chain) -> chain.filter(exchange).contextWrite(Context.of(TENANT, exchange.getRequest().getHeaders().getFirst("X-Tenant"))). Validate the header against the authenticated principal; never trust it blindly.

docs.title: 8. Poll a Job Until Done (Backoff + Deadline)
docs.text: L2 ★★☆ · retryWhen(Retry.backoff) with filter, timeout, Mono.defer

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Starting a report export returns immediately. Poll its status with exponential backoff until it's DONE (then fetch the result) or FAILED (stop at once). Give up after an overall deadline. Test minutes of polling in milliseconds.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
Model "still running" as a retryable signal: map RUNNING to a lightweight exception and retryWhen(Retry.backoff(...).filter(isStillRunning)). Mono.defer re-runs the status call on each retry. FAILED maps to a different exception, which isn't retried. An outer timeout enforces the deadline over the whole retry loop.

stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> Poll Poll --> Wait: RUNNING → StillRunning (retry) Wait --> Poll: backoff 1s, 2s, 4s… (max 8s) Poll --> Fetch: DONE Poll --> Failed: FAILED → JobFailed (no retry) Wait --> Timeout: deadline exceeded Fetch --> [*]

docs.title: Solution
Walkthrough
docs.text: Code Why Mono.defer(statusCall) Retrying re-subscribes. Without defer, a Mono built once would replay the same cached call. case RUNNING -> Mono.error(new StillRunning()) A control-flow signal. StillRunning skips stack-trace capture (super(null, null, false, false)) because it's thrown often. Retry.backoff(Long.MAX_VALUE, firstDelay).maxBackoff(8s).filter(e -> e instanceof StillRunning) Unlimited attempts, bounded by the timeout instead. Jittered exponential delays, capped at 8 s, and FAILED isn't retried. .timeout(deadline) Placed after retryWhen, so it covers the whole polling loop, not a single attempt. polls between 3 and 12 in 30 s Proves it's backing off rather than polling in a tight loop.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space polls O(log(deadline / firstDelay)) before the cap O(1)

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
./gradlew :playbook-examples:test --tests '*P08JobPollerTest'

P08JobPollerTest: 3 tests, 0 failures
  ✔ job failure · stops polling immediately
  ✔ never finishes · times out at the deadline
  ✔ polls with backoff · until done · then fetches result

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Flux.interval(1s).flatMap(status) with no backoff, which hammers the status endpoint and keeps polling after DONE unless you add takeUntil.
  • timeout before retryWhen, which limits each attempt instead of the total wait.
  • Retrying on every error, including FAILED or a 404 for an unknown job id.

docs.title: Follow-up questions
docs.text:
Polling vs callbacks/webhooks vs SSE for long jobs?

Polling is simple and works through firewalls, but adds latency and load. Webhooks or callbacks are efficient but need a public endpoint and retries. SSE or WebSockets push status changes in real time. Many APIs offer polling with Retry-After hints plus an optional webhook.

How do you honour a server's Retry-After header?

Return the delay from the status call (for example a StillRunning(Duration)), and use retryWhen(Retry.from(signals -> signals.concatMap(s -> Mono.delay(((StillRunning) s.failure()).delay())))) for server-directed delays.

docs.title: 9. Partial Results: Don't Let One Bad Row Kill the Import
docs.text: L2 ★★☆ · Per-element onErrorResume, sealed outcomes, flatMapSequential

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Import 200 rows concurrently. Bad rows must be reported with reasons while good rows still succeed, results must stay in input order, and the job returns one summary. Show that the naive version fails completely on the first bad row.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
An error terminates a Reactive Streams sequence. Contain it inside the inner publisher of flatMap/flatMapSequential: process(id).map(Ok::new).onErrorResume(e -> Mono.just(new Failed(...))). Each element then becomes a value, either Ok or Failed, and the outer stream never sees an error. flatMapSequential keeps the concurrency but emits in input order.

flowchart LR IDS["a1, bad-2, a3, bad-4, a5"] --> FM{"flatMapSequential(…, 4)"} FM --> I1["a1 → Ok(A1)"] FM --> I2["bad-2 → error → onErrorResume → Failed"] FM --> I3["a3 → Ok(A3)"] I1 & I2 & I3 --> R["collect → Report(ok=[A1, A3, A5], failed=[bad-2, bad-4])"]

docs.title: Solution
Walkthrough
docs.text: Code Why .<Outcome>map(v -> new Ok(id, v)).onErrorResume(e -> Mono.just(new Failed(id, e.getMessage()))) The error is handled per element, inside the inner Mono. The explicit <Outcome> type witness lets both branches share the sealed type. flatMapSequential(..., concurrency) Runs up to N at a time but emits in source order. Plain flatMap would emit in completion order. withoutPerElementHandling_oneBadRowKillsEverything The naive ids.flatMap(process).collectList() errors on bad-2 and cancels all the other in-flight work. record Report(List<Ok> ok, List<Failed> failed) A summary that callers and operators can act on: retry the failed rows, alert, or write them to a dead-letter table.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space per row O(1) + processing O(rows) for the report

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
./gradlew :playbook-examples:test --tests '*P09PartialResultsTest'

P09PartialResultsTest: 3 tests, 0 failures
  ✔ bad rows are reported · good rows still succeed
  ✔ large import · keeps input order · with concurrency
  ✔ without per element handling · one bad row kills everything

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Using onErrorContinue. It depends on operator support, has surprising semantics, and can leak resources. Prefer explicit per-element onErrorResume.
  • Putting onErrorResume outside the flatMap. By then the stream has already terminated, and you just replace the whole result.
  • Catching errors and returning Mono.empty(), so failures disappear without a trace.

docs.title: Follow-up questions
docs.text:
When is failing fast the right behaviour?

When the batch must be atomic (a financial file in which all rows must apply or none), or when the error means the whole job is broken (database down). Then stop at once, perhaps after a retry, and roll back or compensate.

How do you retry only the failed rows?

Collect the Failed ids and re-run importAll(Flux.fromIterable(failedIds), ...) with a retry policy, or give the inner call retryWhen(...) before the onErrorResume, so transient failures are retried per row and only permanent ones are reported.

docs.title: 10. Reactive Saga with Compensation
docs.text: L3 ★★★ · Nested flatMap, onErrorResume compensations, reverse-order undo

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Placing an order reserves stock → charges the card → books a courier. If a step fails, undo the completed steps in reverse order (refund, then release) and surface the original error.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
Nest the steps so that each one has the previous results in scope. Attach onErrorResume to each step to run the compensations for the steps that came before it, then then(Mono.error(e)) to re-emit the original failure. Payment failure releases the stock. Courier failure refunds the charge, then releases the stock.

sequenceDiagram participant S as saga participant I as inventory participant P as payments participant C as courier S->>I: reserve → res-o3 S->>P: charge → ch-o3 S->>C: book → ✗ no riders S->>P: refund ch-o3 S->>I: release res-o3 S-->>S: error "no riders"

docs.title: Solution
Walkthrough
docs.text: Code Why inventory.reserve(order).flatMap(reservation -> payments.charge(order)... Nesting keeps reservation and charge in scope for the compensations. Flattening into separate flatMaps would lose them. .onErrorResume(e -> undo(payments.refund(charge), ...).then(undo(inventory.release(reservation), ...)).then(Mono.error(e))) Undo in reverse order, then re-throw the original error so the caller sees why the order failed. undo(action, label) → action.doOnSuccess(...) The compensations are recorded so the tests can assert exactly which ones ran, and in which order. paymentFails → ["release res-o2"] Only completed steps are compensated. Nothing is refunded if nothing was charged.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space per order 3 calls (+ up to 2 compensations) O(1)

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
./gradlew :playbook-examples:test --tests '*P10OrderSagaTest'

P10OrderSagaTest: 3 tests, 0 failures
  ✔ courier fails · refunds then releases · in reverse order
  ✔ happy path · no compensation
  ✔ payment fails · releases stock · and surfaces the original error

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Compensating steps that never completed, for example refunding when the charge itself failed.
  • Swallowing the original error after compensating, so the caller gets success or an empty result.
  • Assuming compensations always succeed. In production they need retries and idempotency, and a stuck saga needs an alert or manual queue.
  • Running the whole saga in memory. A crash mid-saga loses track of it. Durable sagas persist their state (an orchestrator table or a workflow engine).

docs.title: Follow-up questions
docs.text:
Orchestration vs choreography for sagas?

Orchestration: one coordinator (like this code, or Temporal, Camunda or Axon) calls each step and its compensation, which makes the flow explicit and easy to monitor. Choreography: services react to each other's events (OrderPlaced, PaymentFailed, ...), which is loosely coupled but harder to follow. Use orchestration for complex flows.

How do you make this crash-safe?

Persist the saga state after each step (an outbox row per transition), make every step and compensation idempotent (keyed by order id), and run a recovery job that resumes or compensates sagas stuck in intermediate states.

docs.title: 11. Search-as-You-Type with switchMap
docs.text: L2 ★★☆ · sampleTimeout debounce, distinctUntilChanged, switchMap cancellation

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Turn keystrokes into search requests. Debounce (wait 300 ms of quiet), ignore queries shorter than 2 characters, skip repeats, and when a new query starts, cancel the in-flight search so stale results never overwrite newer ones.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
sampleTimeout(q -> Mono.delay(quiet)) is Reactor's debounce: a value is emitted only if no newer value arrives within the window. distinctUntilChanged drops a repeated query. switchMap subscribes to the search for the newest query and cancels the previous one, which is the operator that fixes the classic out-of-order bug where results arrive late and overwrite newer ones.

sequenceDiagram participant K as keystrokes participant D as debounce 300 ms participant S as switchMap(search 600 ms) K->>D: j (0), ja (100), jav (200) D->>S: "jav" at 500 → search starts K->>D: java (700) D->>S: "java" at 1000 → CANCEL "jav", start "java" S-->>S: results for "java" at 1600 K->>D: "java " (1800) → strip → same → skipped

docs.title: Solution
Walkthrough
docs.text: Code Why .map(String::strip) Normalise before comparing, so "java " and "java" count as the same query. .sampleTimeout(q -> Mono.delay(quiet)) A value is emitted only if no newer keystroke arrives within quiet. Intermediate prefixes such as "j" and "ja" never reach the backend. .distinctUntilChanged() Compares with the previous emitted query only, so "jav", "java", "jav" still searches all three, but "java" twice in a row searches once. .switchMap(q -> search.apply(q)) The newest query wins. The test records that "jav" was started and then cancelled (doOnCancel), and only the "java" results are emitted. StepVerifier.withVirtualTime + Mono.delay keystrokes Exact timings (0, 100, 200, 700, 1800 ms) are replayed deterministically and instantly.

docs.text: Approach Time Space per keystroke O(1) O(1) (one in-flight search)

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:

  ✔ short queries · never hit the backend

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• flatMap(search): concurrent searches whose late responses for old queries overwrite newer results.
  • concatMap(search): searches queue up behind each other and the UI lags further and further.
  • Debouncing on the server only. Each keystroke still costs a request; debounce in the client too.

docs.title: Follow-up questions
docs.text:
Does cancellation actually stop the HTTP request?

With WebClient, yes: cancelling the subscription closes or releases the connection. Make sure the backend also stops work on client disconnect (WebFlux propagates cancellation to the handler's subscription).

switchMap vs exhaustMap-style behaviour?

switchMap: the newest wins and older work is cancelled (search, autocomplete). The opposite, ignoring new triggers while one is in flight (for example a "submit" button), has no direct Reactor operator. Use onBackpressureDrop with concatMap(..., 1), or a guard flag.

docs.title: 12. Write a Reactive Circuit Breaker Operator
docs.text: L3 ★★★ · transformDeferred, Mono.defer, state machine, injectable Clock

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Implement a circuit breaker that can wrap any Mono. After 3 consecutive failures it opens and fails fast without calling the dependency. After a 10 s cool-down it allows one half-open trial: success closes it, failure reopens it.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
Return a Function<Mono<T>, Mono<T>> and apply it with transformDeferred, which re-evaluates the function per subscription (transform runs once, at assembly). Inside, Mono.defer asks for permission at subscribe time. If the breaker is OPEN, it errors immediately and the source is never subscribed. Otherwise it subscribes and records the outcome with doOnSuccess/doOnError.

stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> CLOSED CLOSED --> OPEN: 3 consecutive failures OPEN --> HALF_OPEN: cool-down elapsed (checked on next call) HALF_OPEN --> CLOSED: trial succeeds HALF_OPEN --> OPEN: trial fails CLOSED --> CLOSED: success resets the count

docs.title: Solution
Walkthrough
docs.text: Code Why source -> Mono.defer(() -> { if (!tryAcquire()) return Mono.error(new CallNotPermitted()); ... }) The decision happens per subscription. When OPEN, the source Mono is never subscribed, which is what "fail fast" means (the test counts calls). .transformDeferred(breaker.protect()) Per-subscriber transformation. With transform, the function would run once when the pipeline is built, which is fine here thanks to defer, but transformDeferred makes the intent explicit. if (state == OPEN && !now.isBefore(openedAt + openFor)) state = HALF_OPEN A lazy transition: no timer thread. The next call after the cool-down becomes the trial. if (state == HALF_OPEN \|\| consecutiveFailures >= threshold) open() A failed trial reopens the circuit immediately and restarts the cool-down. synchronized methods + injectable Clock Simple and correct under concurrency. The test moves time forward instead of sleeping.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space per call O(1) O(1)

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
./gradlew :playbook-examples:test --tests '*P12CircuitBreakerTest'

P12CircuitBreakerTest: 4 tests, 0 failures
  ✔ half open trial · failure · reopens immediately
  ✔ half open trial · success · closes the circuit
  ✔ opens after threshold · and stops calling the dependency
  ✔ success resets the failure count

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Checking state at assembly time (outside defer), so a breaker that opens later never blocks already-built pipelines.
  • Letting many concurrent trial calls through in HALF_OPEN. Production breakers allow a bounded number of permitted calls.
  • Counting client errors (4xx, validation) as failures. Only count failures that say the dependency is unhealthy.
  • No fallback: callers get CallNotPermitted with nothing to show. Add onErrorResume(CallNotPermitted.class, ...) at the call site.

docs.title: Follow-up questions
docs.text:
How does Resilience4j's reactive breaker differ?

It uses a sliding window (count- or time-based) and a failure-rate threshold instead of consecutive failures, a slow-call rate, and a configurable number of half-open permits. It publishes events and metrics, and applies via transformDeferred(CircuitBreakerOperator.of(cb)), the same shape as here.

Where should the breaker sit relative to retry and timeout?

timeout sits innermost, so each attempt is bounded. Retry goes inside the breaker, so each attempt counts as an outcome, and an open breaker stops retries. Order: call.timeout(...).retryWhen(...).transformDeferred(breaker), plus a fallback outside.

docs.title: Reactive Data
docs.text:
A reactive web layer only pays off if the data layer is non-blocking too. One blocking JDBC call on an event loop undoes everything.

Store Reactive driver Spring module Page PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, Oracle, H2 R2DBC Spring Data R2DBC R2DBC MongoDB MongoDB Reactive Streams driver Spring Data MongoDB (reactive) MongoDB Redis Lettuce Spring Data Redis (reactive) Redis Cassandra DataStax driver Spring Data Cassandra (reactive) Other stores Elasticsearch / OpenSearch reactive clients Spring Data Elasticsearch Other stores

JPA/Hibernate is blocking

There is no reactive JPA in Spring Data. If you must use JPA or JDBC from WebFlux, wrap calls in Mono.fromCallable(...).subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) and size that pool deliberately — or reconsider Spring MVC + virtual threads.

Spring's @Cacheable supports Mono/Flux return types (Framework 6.1+) when the cache provider is asynchronous — e.g. Caffeine with AsyncCache mode:

docs.title: R2DBC
docs.text:
R2DBC (Reactive Relational Database Connectivity) is a non-blocking SPI for SQL databases. Spring Data R2DBC adds repositories, mapping and R2dbcEntityTemplate on top.

implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-data-r2dbc")
runtimeOnly("org.postgresql:r2dbc-postgresql")

spring:

    url: r2dbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/catalog
    username: app
    password: secret
    pool:
      initial-size: 5
      max-size: 20
      max-idle-time: 30m

docs.title: Entities are simple — records work
docs.text:
@Table("products")
public record ProductRow(@Id Long id, String name, String category, long priceMinor, Instant createdAt) { }

R2DBC is not an ORM: no lazy loading, no cascades, no @OneToMany. Model aggregates explicitly and load children with a second query (or a join via DatabaseClient).

docs.title: Repositories
docs.text:
public interface ProductRowRepository extends ReactiveCrudRepository<ProductRow, Long> {

    Flux<ProductRow> findByCategoryOrderByName(String category);          // derived query

    @Query("SELECT * FROM products WHERE price_minor BETWEEN :min AND :max")
    Flux<ProductRow> findInPriceRange(long min, long max);

    @Modifying
    @Query("UPDATE products SET price_minor = :price WHERE id = :id")
    Mono<Integer> updatePrice(Long id, long price);                      // rows affected
}

Insert vs update

save() inserts when the @Id is null and updates otherwise. If you assign ids (UUIDs), save() tries an UPDATE and affects 0 rows. Either let the database generate ids, implement Persistable with an isNew() flag, or call R2dbcEntityTemplate.insert(entity).

docs.title: R2dbcEntityTemplate — fluent, type-safe queries
docs.text:
Flux<ProductRow> cheap = template.select(ProductRow.class)
        .matching(query(where("category").is("books").and("price_minor").lessThan(1_000))
                .sort(by("name")).limit(20))

docs.title: DatabaseClient — raw SQL, full control
docs.text:
Flux<CategoryCount> counts = databaseClient.sql("""
            SELECT category, count(*) AS n FROM products GROUP BY category
            """)
        .map((row, meta) -> new CategoryCount(row.get("category", String.class), row.get("n", Long.class)))
        .all();

docs.title: Schema management
docs.text:
R2DBC has no schema tooling of its own. Options:

  • Flyway/Liquibase over JDBC at startup (add the JDBC driver; Boot runs migrations with a separate JDBC DataSource used only for migrations) — recommended for production.
  • spring.sql.init.mode=always with schema.sql/data.sql (demo/test only — the capstone uses this).

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Streaming large results is real streaming — keep the subscription short or the connection stays checked out of the pool.
  • Pool exhaustion shows up as latency, not errors: watch r2dbc.pool.* metrics.
  • Every query must be subscribed (returned) — a dropped Mono never executes.

docs.title: Read-through cache
docs.text:
Spring's @Cacheable does not cache the value of a Mono reliably across all providers. A simple, explicit pattern:

Mono<Product> cached(String id) {
    String key = "product:" + id;
    return productTemplate.opsForValue().get(key)
            .switchIfEmpty(Mono.defer(() -> repository.findById(id)
                    .flatMap(p -> productTemplate.opsForValue().set(key, p, Duration.ofMinutes(10)).thenReturn(p))));
}

Mono<Long> publish(PriceTick tick) {
    return redis.convertAndSend("prices", json(tick));
}

Flux<String> subscribe() {
    return redis.listenToChannel("prices").map(ReactiveSubscription.Message::getMessage);
}

docs.title: Reactive Transactions
docs.text: Spring's transaction abstraction works reactively through ReactiveTransactionManager (R2dbcTransactionManager, ReactiveMongoTransactionManager). The transaction is bound to the Reactor Context, not a thread.

docs.title: Declarative
docs.text:
@Service
class TransferService {

    @Transactional                          // works on methods returning Mono/Flux
    public Mono<Void> transfer(long from, long to, long amountMinor) {
        return accounts.debit(from, amountMinor)
                .then(accounts.credit(to, amountMinor))
                .then(ledger.record(from, to, amountMinor));
        // any onError → rollback; completion → commit; cancellation → rollback
    }
}

docs.title: Programmatic
docs.text:
TransactionalOperator tx = TransactionalOperator.create(transactionManager);

Mono<Void> work = accounts.debit(from, amount)
        .then(accounts.credit(to, amount))
        .as(tx::transactional);

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
1. The whole pipeline must be returned — a nested subscribe() runs outside the transaction.
  2. Everything inside must use the same reactive connection factory; a WebClient call inside a transaction is not part of it (and holds the DB connection while waiting — avoid remote calls inside transactions).
  3. @Transactional on a method returning Flux commits when the Flux completes — streaming a huge result keeps the transaction open.
  4. Self-invocation (this.method()) bypasses the proxy, exactly as in Spring MVC.

Database + message broker

A DB transaction cannot include a Kafka send. Use the transactional outbox: write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction and relay it asynchronously (Debezium CDC or a poller).

docs.title: Security chain
docs.text:
@Bean
SecurityWebFilterChain securityWebFilterChain(ServerHttpSecurity http) {
    // Browsers cannot set headers on EventSource/WebSocket, so also accept ?access_token=…
    var bearer = new ServerBearerTokenAuthenticationConverter();
    bearer.setAllowUriQueryParameter(true);

    return http
            .csrf(ServerHttpSecurity.CsrfSpec::disable)              // stateless bearer-token API
            .authorizeExchange(auth -> auth
                    .pathMatchers("/", "/index.html", "/favicon.ico", "/auth/token", "/actuator/health/**").permitAll()
                    .pathMatchers(org.springframework.http.HttpMethod.GET, "/api/restaurants/**").permitAll()
                    .anyExchange().authenticated())
            .oauth2ResourceServer(rs -> rs
                    .bearerTokenConverter(bearer)
                    .jwt(jwt -> { }))
            .build();
}

Restaurant browsing is public; everything else needs a JWT. Because EventSource and WebSocket cannot send headers, the token may also arrive as ?access_token=.

Dev-only token endpoint

POST /auth/token signs an HS256 token for any username so the demo runs with no identity provider. In production, delete TokenController and point spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri at Keycloak/Cognito/Auth0.

docs.text:
@Override
public Mono<Void> filter(ServerWebExchange exchange, GatewayFilterChain chain) {
    return ReactiveSecurityContextHolder.getContext()
            .map(ctx -> ctx.getAuthentication())
            .filter(JwtAuthenticationToken.class::isInstance)
            .map(auth -> ((JwtAuthenticationToken) auth).getToken().getSubject())
            .map(userId -> withUser(exchange, userId))
            .defaultIfEmpty(withUser(exchange, null))
            .flatMap(chain::filter);
}

Downstream services trust X-User-Id only because the gateway strips any client-supplied value first and the services are not exposed publicly.

docs.title: Delivery Service
docs.text: Role: assigns a courier when an order is paid and simulates the trip, publishing every move. Topics: Reactive MongoDB, Kafka, Resources & Cancellation, SSE.

docs.title: The trip is a pure, time-driven Flux
docs.text:
public static Flux<Waypoint> route(double fromLat, double fromLon, double toLat, double toLon,
                                   int steps, Duration tick) {
    return Flux.interval(tick)
            .take(steps + 1L)                       // tick 0 = pickup … tick N = drop-off
            .map(Long::intValue)
            .map(i -> {
                double f = (double) i / steps;      // linear interpolation along the route
                DeliveryStatus status = i == 0 ? DeliveryStatus.PICKED_UP
                        : i == steps ? DeliveryStatus.DELIVERED
                        : DeliveryStatus.IN_TRANSIT;
                return new Waypoint(status, fromLat + (toLat - fromLat) * f, fromLon + (toLon - fromLon) * f);
            });
}

docs.title: Running it: concatMap + a managed Disposable
docs.text:
private void startTrip(Delivery assigned) {
    ThreadLocalRandom rnd = ThreadLocalRandom.current();
    double toLat = HUB_LAT + rnd.nextDouble(-0.05, 0.05);
    double toLon = HUB_LON + rnd.nextDouble(-0.05, 0.05);

    Disposable trip = CourierSimulator.route(HUB_LAT, HUB_LON, toLat, toLon, sim.steps(), sim.tick())
            // concatMap: strictly one waypoint at a time — save, then publish, then the next one
            .concatMap(wp -> repository.findById(assigned.id())
                    .map(d -> d.moveTo(wp.status(), wp.latitude(), wp.longitude(), Instant.now()))
                    .flatMap(repository::save)
                    .flatMap(saved -> events.publish(toEvent(saved))))
            .subscribe(
                    ignored -> { },
                    error -> log.error("trip for order {} failed", assigned.orderId(), error),
                    () -> log.info("order {} delivered by {}", assigned.orderId(), assigned.courierId()));
    running.add(trip);
}
  • concatMap guarantees each waypoint is saved and published before the next one starts.
  • The trip outlives the Kafka message that started it, so it is a deliberate detached subscribe() — tracked in a Disposable.Composite and disposed on shutdown (@PreDestroy).

docs.title: WebSocket handler
docs.text:
@Override
public Mono<Void> handle(WebSocketSession session) {
    String orderId = queryParam(session.getHandshakeInfo().getUri(), "orderId");
    Mono<Void> outbound = session.send(hub.stream(orderId)
            .map(json::writeValueAsString)
            .map(session::textMessage));
    // drain inbound frames (client pings); when the client disconnects, receive() completes
    Mono<Void> inbound = session.receive().then();
    return Mono.firstWithSignal(outbound, inbound); // whichever side ends first closes the session
}

public Mono<Order> place(String idempotencyKey, PlaceOrder command) {

private Mono<Order> createAndPay(String idempotencyKey, PlaceOrder command) {
    return catalog.quotes(ids)                       // HTTP interface client → restaurant-service
            .collectList()
            .map(quotes -> Pricing.price(command.restaurantId(), command.items(), quotes))  // pure
            .map(priced -> new Order(... PENDING_PAYMENT ...))
            .flatMap(store::insert)                  // reactive transaction over 2 tables

docs.title: Payment call: timeout + retry + circuit breaker
docs.text:
@Override
public Mono<Receipt> charge(String idempotencyKey, String orderRef, String customerId, long amountPaise) {
    Mono<Receipt> call = paymentClient.post()
            .uri("/api/payments")
            .header("Idempotency-Key", idempotencyKey == null ? orderRef : idempotencyKey)
            .bodyValue(new ChargeBody(orderRef, customerId, amountPaise))
            .retrieve()
            .bodyToMono(PaymentResponse.class)
            .map(r -> new Receipt(r.paymentId(), Outcome.valueOf(r.status())))
            .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2))
            .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(2, Duration.ofMillis(200))
                    .filter(HttpPayments::isRetryable));
    return breaker.run(call, error -> Mono.error(new IllegalStateException("payment unavailable", error)));
}

/** Circuit breaker: opens at 50% failures over the last 10 calls, half-opens after 10s. */
@Bean
Customizer<ReactiveResilience4JCircuitBreakerFactory> paymentBreaker() {
    return factory -> factory.configure(builder -> builder
            .circuitBreakerConfig(CircuitBreakerConfig.custom()
                    .slidingWindowSize(10)
                    .minimumNumberOfCalls(5)
                    .failureRateThreshold(50)
                    .waitDurationInOpenState(Duration.ofSeconds(10))
                    .permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState(2)
                    .build())
            .timeLimiterConfig(TimeLimiterConfig.custom().timeoutDuration(Duration.ofSeconds(5)).build()),
            "payment");
}

Retrying a payment is only safe because the Idempotency-Key travels with every attempt and payment-service replays the first result.

docs.title: Live status over SSE
docs.text:
/** Server-Sent Events: the browser's EventSource keeps one HTTP connection open and receives pushes. */
@GetMapping(path = "/{id}/status-stream", produces = MediaType.TEXT_EVENT_STREAM_VALUE)
public Flux<ServerSentEvent<OrderStatusUpdate>> statusStream(@PathVariable long id) {
    Flux<ServerSentEvent<OrderStatusUpdate>> updates = orders.watch(id)
            .map(u -> ServerSentEvent.builder(u).event("status").id(u.status() + "-" + u.at()).build());
    // heartbeat comments keep proxies from closing an idle connection; stop them when updates complete
    Flux<ServerSentEvent<OrderStatusUpdate>> heartbeat = Flux.interval(Duration.ofSeconds(15))
            .map(t -> ServerSentEvent.<OrderStatusUpdate>builder().comment("keep-alive").build());
    return Flux.merge(updates, heartbeat.takeUntilOther(updates.ignoreElements().then(Mono.just(1))));
}

orders.watch(id) emits the current status, then live updates from a Sinks.many().multicast().directBestEffort() filtered by order id, and completes on a terminal status — which also stops the heartbeat.

docs.title: Idempotency with Mono.cache()
docs.text:
public Mono<Payment> charge(String idempotencyKey, ChargeRequest request) {
    return byIdempotencyKey.computeIfAbsent(idempotencyKey, key -> process(request)
            .doOnError(e -> byIdempotencyKey.remove(key))    // don't cache failures
            .cache());                                       // replay the first success to every retry
}

A cached Mono is hot after first subscription: the second request with the same key gets the same paymentId without re-charging. (In production this map would be a database table with a unique key.)

docs.title: Production Hardening
docs.text: The capstone favours clarity. Before running something like it for real:

docs.title: Reliability
docs.text:
• Transactional outbox in order-service so "order saved" and "event published" can't diverge.
  • Durable idempotency in payment-service (table with unique key) instead of an in-memory map.
  • Dead-letter topics and bounded retries for Kafka listeners (DefaultErrorHandler + DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer).
  • Cross-instance fan-out: SSE/WebSocket sinks are per instance — consume with a per-instance group id or use Redis pub/sub.
  • Persist courier simulations' progress (or replace with real courier pings) so restarts resume trips.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• Replace the dev token endpoint with a real IdP (Keycloak/Cognito) — issuer-uri + JWKS.
  • Make every service a resource server too (defence in depth) instead of trusting X-User-Id alone.
  • Restrict access_token query parameters to SSE/WS routes; scrub them from access logs.
  • Ownership checks: a customer may only read their own orders (@PreAuthorize).

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
• Flyway migrations instead of spring.sql.init.
  • Separate DB users per service; least privilege.

docs.title: Operations
docs.text:
• Rate limiting at the gateway (RequestRateLimiter + Redis).
  • Tracing (spring-boot-starter-opentelemetry), dashboards for RED metrics, consumer lag, breaker state.
  • Graceful shutdown (server.shutdown=graceful), readiness/liveness probes.
  • Helm charts / Kubernetes manifests with resource requests so Netty sizes event loops correctly.
