docs.title: Fundamentals
docs.text:
Before any operator or annotation, it pays to understand what problem reactive programming solves and what contract every reactive library implements.

Page You will learn Why Reactive? the cost of blocking threads and how an event loop avoids it Reactive Manifesto the four system properties reactive design aims for Reactive Streams Spec Publisher, Subscriber, Subscription, Processor and their rules Backpressure how a consumer controls the producer's speed Reactive vs Virtual Threads when to pick WebFlux, when Spring MVC + Loom is enough

docs.title: Backpressure
docs.text:
Backpressure is the ability of a consumer to tell a producer how much it can handle, so a fast producer cannot overwhelm a slow consumer (out-of-memory, unbounded queues, latency spikes).

In Reactive Streams it is built into the protocol: Subscription.request(n).

flowchart LR P[Producer<br/>10,000 msg/s] -- "onNext (≤ n)" --> C[Consumer<br/>1,000 msg/s] C -- "request(n)" --> P

docs.title: Pull, push, or both
docs.text:
• Pull (iterator): consumer asks for each item — safe but chatty.
  • Push (callbacks/events): producer sends whenever it likes — fast but can overflow.
  • Reactive Streams = dynamic push-pull: the consumer requests a batch (request(256)), the producer pushes up to that many, then waits for more demand.

docs.title: A subscriber controlling demand
docs.text:
List<Long> requests = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();
List<Integer> received = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();

Flux.range(1, 10)
        .doOnRequest(requests::add)                       // observe demand flowing upstream
        .subscribe(new BaseSubscriber<Integer>() {
            @Override
            protected void hookOnSubscribe(Subscription s) {
                request(2);                               // "I can handle 2 for now"
            }

            @Override
            protected void hookOnNext(Integer value) {
                received.add(value);
                if (received.size() % 2 == 0) {
                    request(2);                           // processed a batch → ask for more
                }
            }
        });

assertThat(received).hasSize(10);
assertThat(requests).containsOnly(2L);

docs.title: When the producer cannot slow down
docs.text: Some sources ignore demand: UI events, sensor feeds, a market ticker, messages pushed by a broker. Then you must decide what to do with the excess — drop, keep only the latest, buffer (bounded!), or error. Reactor's strategies are covered in Backpressure & Batching.

docs.title: Backpressure across the network
docs.text:
Transport Backpressure? Reactive Streams in-process ✅ request(n) HTTP/1.1 response body (WebFlux) ✅ via TCP flow control — Netty stops reading/writing when buffers fill SSE / WebSocket ⚠️ only TCP-level; the server must still choose a strategy for slow clients RSocket ✅ request(n) crosses the network as frames Kafka ✅ consumer pulls at its own pace (max.poll.records)

Takeaway

Every unbounded buffer is a latent OutOfMemoryError. In reactive code, demand flows upstream, data flows downstream — design both directions.

docs.title: The Reactive Manifesto
docs.text:
The Reactive Manifesto (2014) describes the system-level properties that reactive architecture aims for. Reactive programming (Reactor, WebFlux) is one tool to get there.

flowchart TB V[Value: <b>Responsive</b>] F[Form: <b>Elastic</b>] --> V R[Form: <b>Resilient</b>] --> V M[Means: <b>Message Driven</b>] --> F M --> R Property Meaning How Spring delivers it Responsive answers in a timely, consistent manner non-blocking I/O, timeout(), streaming partial results Resilient stays responsive in the face of failure retryWhen, circuit breakers, fallbacks, bulkheads, isolation per service Elastic stays responsive under varying load few threads handle many connections; stateless services scale horizontally Message driven asynchronous message passing, location transparency, backpressure Reactive Streams signals, Kafka, RSocket, SSE/WebSocket

docs.title: Reactive programming vs reactive systems
docs.text:
• Reactive programming — a code-level paradigm: asynchronous data streams + operators (Reactor's Mono/Flux). Scope: one process.
  • Reactive systems — an architecture: services that communicate asynchronously, isolate failures and scale elastically. Scope: the whole platform.

You can build a reactive system with imperative services that talk over Kafka, and you can write reactive code inside a monolith. The capstone in this playbook does both: reactive code in every service and asynchronous, event-driven communication between them.

Takeaway

Use the manifesto as a checklist for design reviews: what happens to latency when this dependency is slow? when it is down? when traffic triples?

docs.title: The Reactive Streams Specification
docs.text: Reactive Streams is a tiny standard (4 interfaces, ~40 rules) for asynchronous stream processing with non-blocking backpressure. Reactor, RxJava, Akka Streams, Mutiny and the JDK's java.util.concurrent.Flow all implement it, so they interoperate.

docs.title: The four interfaces
docs.text:
public interface Publisher<T> {
    void subscribe(Subscriber<? super T> s);
}

public interface Subscriber<T> {
    void onSubscribe(Subscription s);   // exactly once, first
    void onNext(T t);                   // 0..N times, never more than requested
    void onError(Throwable t);          // terminal
    void onComplete();                  // terminal
}

public interface Subscription {
    void request(long n);               // backpressure: "I can take n more"
    void cancel();                      // stop, release resources
}

public interface Processor<T, R> extends Subscriber<T>, Publisher<R> { }

docs.title: The protocol
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram participant S as Subscriber participant P as Publisher S->>P: subscribe(subscriber) P-->>S: onSubscribe(subscription) S->>P: request(2) P-->>S: onNext(a) P-->>S: onNext(b) S->>P: request(1) P-->>S: onNext(c) P-->>S: onComplete()

The signal grammar is: onSubscribe onNext* (onError | onComplete)?

docs.title: Rules worth memorising
docs.text:
1. Nothing happens until subscribe — and nothing is emitted until request(n).
  2. A publisher must not emit more onNext than requested — this is backpressure.
  3. Signals are serial: never two onNext calls concurrently on the same subscriber.
  4. onError and onComplete are terminal: no signal may follow them.
  5. null elements are forbidden.
  6. cancel() must eventually stop emissions and release resources.

You almost never implement these interfaces yourself

Writing a spec-compliant Publisher is notoriously hard (concurrency, re-entrancy, demand accounting). Use Reactor's factories (Flux.create, Flux.generate, Sinks) instead — see Creating Sequences.

docs.title: Reactor's view of the spec
Reactive vs Virtual Threads
docs.text: Java 21 introduced virtual threads (Project Loom): threads so cheap that blocking is no longer expensive. Does that make reactive programming obsolete? Not entirely — but it narrows where it is the best choice.

docs.title: Side by side
Decision guide
The thread-per-request model
docs.text:
A classic servlet application (Spring MVC on Tomcat) gives each request its own thread. While that thread waits for a database or an HTTP call, it is parked — holding ~1 MB of stack and doing nothing.

sequenceDiagram participant C as Client participant T as Worker thread participant DB as Database C->>T: GET /users/42 T->>DB: SELECT ... (thread blocks) Note over T: idle, but occupied<br/>for the whole DB round-trip DB-->>T: row T-->>C: 200 OK

With 200 threads and calls that take 100 ms each, the server tops out around 2,000 requests/second — regardless of how idle the CPU is. Raising the pool size costs memory and context-switching.

docs.title: The event-loop model
docs.text:
A reactive server (Netty) runs a small, fixed number of event-loop threads (≈ CPU cores). Nothing ever blocks: when a request needs I/O, the code registers what to do when the result arrives and the thread immediately moves on to other work.

sequenceDiagram participant C1 as Client A participant C2 as Client B participant L as Event loop (1 thread) participant DB as Database C1->>L: GET /users/42 L->>DB: query A (non-blocking) C2->>L: GET /users/7 L->>DB: query B (non-blocking) DB-->>L: result A L-->>C1: 200 OK DB-->>L: result B L-->>C2: 200 OK

docs.title: What "reactive programming" means in code
docs.text:
You describe a pipeline of transformations over values that will arrive later:

Mono<UserView> view = userRepository.findById(id)        // Mono<User> — 0 or 1 value, later
        .flatMap(user -> ordersClient.recentOrders(user.id())   // async call, no blocking
                .collectList()
                .map(orders -> new UserView(user, orders)))
        .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2));                  // declarative time limit

Nothing executes on that line. The pipeline runs when the framework subscribes (in WebFlux, when the HTTP response is written).

docs.title: When reactive pays off
docs.text:
Good fit Poor fit Many concurrent, I/O-bound requests (gateways, BFFs, aggregators) CPU-bound batch computation Streaming: SSE, WebSocket, Kafka → client fan-out Simple CRUD with low concurrency Fan-out/fan-in to many downstream services Teams/libraries that are entirely blocking (JDBC, JPA) Backpressure-aware pipelines (producer faster than consumer) Code where debugging simplicity outweighs throughput

Rule of thumb

Reactive is a tool for I/O concurrency and streaming. If your bottleneck is CPU, reactive will not make it faster — and Java 21 virtual threads may give you most of the scalability benefit with plain imperative code. See Reactive vs Virtual Threads.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Blocking wastes threads; event loops multiplex many requests over few threads.
  • Reactive code is declarative and lazy: you build a pipeline, subscription executes it.
  • The benefit is scalability and streaming under I/O load, not raw speed per request.

• Candidates: answer aloud first, then expand the answer. If you can't explain a why, revisit the linked playbook page.
  • Interviewers: the "Follow-ups" lines are where good answers separate from memorised ones. Ask for trade-offs, failure modes and production stories.

What strong answers have in common

docs.title: Architect (12–15+ years)
docs.text:
1. Reactive programming vs reactive systems — how do you explain the difference to executives?

Reactive programming is a coding technique that makes individual services handle more concurrent work with fewer resources. Reactive systems are an architecture — asynchronous messaging, isolation, elasticity — that keeps the whole platform responsive when parts fail or load spikes. You can have either without the other; business value comes from the system properties (availability, latency, cost per request), so invest in messaging, isolation and observability before rewriting code styles.

2. When would you advise against adopting reactive?

When workloads are CPU-bound or low-concurrency CRUD; when key dependencies are blocking with no reactive alternative; when the team lacks experience and timelines are tight; when virtual threads give the needed scalability; when operational tooling (profilers, APM) isn't ready. The cost is cognitive load, debugging difficulty and hiring — it must buy measurable gains.

3. Design flow control end to end, from browser to database.

Browser: SSE/WebSocket with client-side throttling. Edge: rate limiting, connection limits, HTTP/2 flow control. Services: bounded concurrency (flatMap(n)), bounded queues, limitRate, timeouts and load shedding when pending work grows. Messaging: Kafka consumers pull at their pace; lag is the buffer, autoscaling on lag. Database: pool limits act as backpressure — monitor pending acquisitions. Across all: propagate deadlines, fail fast, degrade gracefully. Reactive Streams gives in-process backpressure; the architecture must provide it between processes.

4. How do you guarantee consistency across services without distributed transactions?

Local transactions + outbox/CDC for reliable event publication; idempotent consumers; sagas with compensations; read models (CQRS) updated from events with eventual consistency; idempotency keys at API boundaries; reconciliation jobs for drift; explicit consistency SLAs in product requirements. "Exactly once" is achieved as effectively-once via idempotency, not by the transport.

5. How would you run live tracking for 1M concurrent viewers across regions?

See System Design: regional SSE/WebSocket edge tiers (WebFlux, HTTP/2), positions partitioned by courier/order in Kafka per region, edge instances subscribe to the subset they need (consistent hashing of order ids to instances or a pub/sub fan-out tier), onBackpressureLatest per client, sampling (1 update/s), snapshot + delta, CDN-friendly fallback polling, global routing to nearest region, and capacity planning by connections per core.

6. How do you set platform standards without blocking team autonomy?

Golden paths (templates with security, observability, error contracts, ArchUnit rules, CI checks including BlockHound), paved-road libraries, ADR templates with a reactive-vs-imperative decision tree, and fitness functions in CI — teams can leave the path with a documented reason.

7. What does observability need to look like for async, reactive platforms?

Distributed tracing across HTTP and messaging (trace context in Kafka headers), consistent correlation ids, SLOs per user journey (not per service), metrics with bounded cardinality, exemplars linking metrics to traces, event-level audit trails for sagas, consumer lag dashboards, and logs that carry trace ids via context propagation. Sampling strategies (tail-based) for high-volume streams.

8. How do you evaluate cost efficiency of reactive vs imperative services?

Measure cost per request at target p99 under realistic load: CPU, memory (heap + direct), instance count, plus engineering cost (delivery speed, incident MTTR). Reactive often reduces memory and instance count for I/O-heavy services; native images reduce memory/startup further. Include opportunity cost of complexity.

9. Which failure modes are unique to reactive systems?

Event-loop starvation from a single blocking call; silent work loss from unsubscribed publishers or detached subscriptions; unbounded buffers in hot sources; retry storms amplified by high concurrency; context loss (security/tenant/tracing) across async boundaries; cancellation not releasing resources; hard-to-read stack traces slowing incident response.

10. How do you plan for long-lived connections (SSE/WebSocket) in capacity and deployments?

Size by concurrent connections and memory per connection; spread across instances with load balancers that support long-lived connections; connection draining on deploy (complete streams, clients reconnect with resume tokens); limit per-user connections; heartbeats; prefer HTTP/2; separate streaming tier from request/response tier for independent scaling.

11. How do you think about API design for streaming?

Choose transport by direction and audience (SSE for browser push, NDJSON for service streaming, WebSocket/RSocket for bidirectional), define resumption semantics (event ids/offsets), message schemas and versioning, backpressure expectations, and termination (complete vs infinite). Provide a non-streaming fallback for constrained clients.

12. What is your stance on reactive in the data layer (R2DBC) vs JDBC on virtual threads?

R2DBC fits fully reactive services with streaming reads and high concurrency; ecosystem gaps (no ORM, fewer tools) are real. JDBC on virtual threads keeps JPA/tooling and scales well for typical OLTP; pool size remains the true limit either way. Decide per service; never mix blocking JDBC on event loops.

13. How do you de-risk a platform-wide Spring Boot major upgrade?

Inventory services and dependency graph; upgrade shared libraries/BOM first; automated recipes (OpenRewrite); compatibility test matrix; canary services; feature flags for behaviour changes; observability baselines to compare; a time-boxed parallel-support window; communication plan.

14. How do you mentor senior engineers into architects in this domain?

Give them ownership of cross-service flows (sagas, streaming tiers), require written ADRs with measurements, rotate them through incident reviews, have them run design reviews using the reactive manifesto lens, and pair on capacity planning and cost analysis.

15. What will change the reactive landscape in the next few years, and how do you prepare?

Virtual threads and structured concurrency reducing the need for reactive in request/response services; reactive remaining strong for streaming, backpressure and event processing; AI token streaming increasing streaming endpoints; platform consolidation on fewer, well-paved models. Prepare by keeping domain logic framework-agnostic (ports & adapters), measuring rather than following fashion, and maintaining both golden paths.

docs.title: Beginner (0–2 years)
Coding Exercises (with tested solutions)
docs.text: Try each exercise before expanding the solution. Every solution is a passing test in playbook-examples/src/test/java/com/example/reactive/playbook/interview/CodingExercisesTest.java.

docs.title: 1. Concurrent dashboard (beginner)
docs.text:
Build a Dashboard from users.apply(id) (Mono<User>) and orders.apply(id) (Flux<Order>). The calls are independent — total latency must be the max, not the sum.

Solution 
/** Ex 1: build a dashboard from two independent async calls, concurrently. */
static Mono<Dashboard> dashboard(String userId,
                                 Function<String, Mono<User>> users,
                                 Function<String, Flux<Order>> orders) {
    return Mono.zip(users.apply(userId), orders.apply(userId).collectList())
            .map(t -> new Dashboard(t.getT1(), t.getT2(),
                    t.getT2().stream().mapToLong(Order::amountMinor).sum()));
}

docs.title: 2. Bounded, ordered enrichment (intermediate)
docs.text:
Call a slow API for 100 ids with at most 5 calls in flight, returning results in input order.

Solution 
/** Ex 2: call a slow API for 100 ids, at most 5 concurrently, preserving input order. */
static Flux<String> enrichAll(List<Integer> ids, Function<Integer, Mono<String>> api) {
    return Flux.fromIterable(ids).flatMapSequential(api, 5);
}

docs.title: 3. Selective retry (intermediate)
docs.text:
Retry only server-side failures (IllegalStateException, timeouts) 3 times with exponential backoff; client errors fail immediately; after exhaustion surface the original exception.

Solution 
/** Ex 3: retry only 5xx-like failures, 3 times, exponential backoff; give up with the original error. */
static <T> Mono<T> resilient(Mono<T> call) {
    return call.timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(1))
            .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(100))
                    .filter(e -> e instanceof IllegalStateException || e instanceof java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException)
                    .onRetryExhaustedThrow((spec, signal) -> signal.failure()));
}

docs.title: 4. Single-flight cache (senior)
docs.text:
Concurrent callers for the same key must share one load; failures must not be cached.

Solution 
/** Ex 4: an in-memory cache where concurrent callers for the same key share ONE load. */
static final class SingleFlightCache<K, V> {
    private final Map<K, Mono<V>> cache = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final Function<K, Mono<V>> loader;

    SingleFlightCache(Function<K, Mono<V>> loader) {
        this.loader = loader;
    }

    Mono<V> get(K key) {
        return cache.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> loader.apply(k)
                .doOnError(e -> cache.remove(k))      // don't cache failures
                .cache(Duration.ofMinutes(5)));       // share the in-flight/completed value
    }
}

docs.title: 5. Batch insert (intermediate)
docs.text:
Insert a stream in batches of 100 or every 500 ms, whichever comes first, with at most 2 batches in flight.

Solution 
/** Ex 5: batch-insert a stream: groups of 100 or every 500 ms, whichever first; max 2 batches in flight. */
static Flux<Integer> batchInsert(Flux<String> rows, Function<List<String>, Mono<Integer>> insertBatch) {
    return rows.bufferTimeout(100, Duration.ofMillis(500))
            .flatMap(insertBatch, 2);
}

docs.title: 6. Pagination as a stream (intermediate)
docs.text:
Turn a page-by-page API into one Flux<String> that stops at the first empty page.

Solution 
/** Ex 6: paginate an API until an empty page, as one continuous Flux. */
record Page(int number, List<String> items) { }

static Flux<String> allItems(Function<Integer, Mono<Page>> fetchPage) {
    return fetchPage.apply(0)
            .expand(page -> page.items().isEmpty() ? Mono.empty() : fetchPage.apply(page.number() + 1))
            .concatMapIterable(Page::items);
}

docs.title: 7. Per-key ordering (senior)
docs.text:
Process events in order per account but in parallel across accounts.

Solution 
/** Ex 7: per-key ordering with cross-key parallelism (e.g. events for many accounts). */
record Event(String account, int seq) { }

static Flux<Event> processInOrderPerKey(Flux<Event> events, Function<Event, Mono<Event>> handler) {
    return events.groupBy(Event::account)
            .flatMap(group -> group.concatMap(handler));   // sequential within a key, parallel across keys
}

docs.title: 8. Hedged request (senior)
docs.text:
Call the primary; if it hasn't answered in 50 ms, also call the replica; take the first value.

Solution 
/** Ex 8: hedged request — ask the replica only if the primary hasn't answered within 50 ms. */
static <T> Mono<T> hedged(Mono<T> primary, Mono<T> replica) {
    return Mono.firstWithValue(primary, replica.delaySubscription(Duration.ofMillis(50)));
}

docs.title: 9. Rate pacing (senior)
docs.text:
Emit at most N elements per second without dropping any.

Solution 
/** Ex 9: rate-limit outgoing calls to N per second without dropping any. */
static <T> Flux<T> ratePaced(Flux<T> source, int perSecond) {
    return source.buffer(perSecond)
            .zipWith(Flux.interval(Duration.ZERO, Duration.ofSeconds(1)), (batch, tick) -> batch)
            .concatMapIterable(Function.identity());
}

docs.title: 10. Find the bug (all levels)
docs.text:
The audit log is never written. Why, and how do you fix it?

Solution 
/** Ex 10: fix the bug — the audit log was never written. */
static Mono<String> saveBuggy(Function<String, Mono<String>> save, Function<String, Mono<Void>> audit, String v) {
    return save.apply(v).doOnNext(saved -> audit.apply(saved));     // ❌ Mono created, never subscribed
}

static Mono<String> saveFixed(Function<String, Mono<String>> save, Function<String, Mono<Void>> audit, String v) {
    return save.apply(v).flatMap(saved -> audit.apply(saved).thenReturn(saved)); // ✅ part of the chain
}

audit.apply(saved) returns a Mono that nobody subscribes to. Side effects that are themselves reactive must be part of the chain (flatMap/then), never created inside doOnNext.

Twelve more, WebFlux-heavy

Functional endpoints, WebClient fan-out, blocking bridges, backpressure policies, batching, hot feeds, Context, polling, partial results, sagas, search-as-you-type and a hand-written circuit breaker are in the Coding Interview tab, each with its own test class.

docs.title: Intermediate (2–5 years)
docs.text:
1. Compare flatMap, concatMap, flatMapSequential and switchMap.

All map T -> Publisher<R>. flatMap: subscribes eagerly to inners (default concurrency 256), output in completion order — max throughput. concatMap: one inner at a time, source order — use when order matters or steps depend on each other. flatMapSequential: concurrent subscription but re-ordered output (buffers early finishers). switchMap: cancels the previous inner when a new element arrives — "latest wins" (type-ahead search).

Follow-up: How do you cap concurrency? flatMap(f, 8); concatMap has prefetch but no concurrency.

2. Explain publishOn vs subscribeOn.

publishOn(s) moves execution of downstream operators to scheduler s — position matters, it can appear several times. subscribeOn(s) moves the subscription (and therefore the source's emission if it is synchronous) to s — position doesn't matter, the one closest to the source wins. Typical: Mono.fromCallable(blocking).subscribeOn(boundedElastic()); publishOn(parallel()) before CPU-heavy steps.

3. Which scheduler for which work?

parallel() (cores-sized) for CPU work and timers; boundedElastic() (10×cores threads, 100k queued tasks, idle eviction) for unavoidable blocking I/O; single() for low-latency serial tasks; immediate() no switch; custom (fromExecutorService) e.g. virtual threads. Never run blocking code on parallel or event loops.

4. How do you implement retries correctly?

retryWhen(Retry.backoff(maxAttempts, minBackoff).maxBackoff(..).jitter(0.5).filter(isTransient) .onRetryExhaustedThrow((s, sig) -> sig.failure())). Retry only transient errors (5xx, timeouts, connection resets), only idempotent operations (or with idempotency keys), with backoff + jitter to avoid synchronized retry storms, and with a bounded count. Put timeout before it for per-attempt limits.

5. Where does timeout go relative to retryWhen?

Before retryWhen: each attempt has its own deadline (call.timeout(2s).retryWhen(...)). After it: one overall deadline for all attempts. Often both: per-attempt and overall budget.

6. What is the difference between onErrorResume and onErrorContinue?

onErrorResume replaces the failed sequence with a fallback publisher — the original sequence is terminated. onErrorContinue tries to drop the failing element and keep going, but it works only with operators that support it and affects upstream operators in surprising ways. Prefer per-element onErrorResume inside flatMap.

7. How does WebClient differ from RestTemplate/RestClient?

WebClient is non-blocking (Reactor Netty), returns Mono/Flux, supports streaming bodies (SSE, NDJSON), backpressure, and integrates with Reactor operators for timeouts/retries. RestTemplate and RestClient are blocking (fine on virtual threads in MVC apps). In Boot 4, the auto-configured WebClient.Builder comes from the spring-boot-webclient module.

8. retrieve() vs exchangeToMono()?

retrieve() is the high-level API: 4xx/5xx become WebClientResponseException (customisable with onStatus), then bodyToMono/Flux/toEntity. exchangeToMono(resp -> ...) hands you the raw response to branch on status/headers — but you must consume or release the body. Avoid the deprecated exchange() that could leak connections.

9. How do you handle errors centrally in WebFlux?

For annotated controllers: @RestControllerAdvice with @ExceptionHandler methods returning ProblemDetail (RFC 9457). For functional endpoints: RouterFunctions.route().onError(...) or recover in handlers. For everything else (filters, routing errors): a WebExceptionHandler ordered before Boot's default. Enable spring.webflux.problemdetails.enabled for framework exceptions.

10. How do you validate request bodies in WebFlux?

@Valid @RequestBody Mono<Dto> (or Dto) in annotated controllers — failures signal WebExchangeBindException (400). For functional endpoints, inject jakarta.validation.Validator and validate in the handler, mapping violations to a 400 ProblemDetail.

11. What is R2DBC and how is it different from JPA?

R2DBC is a non-blocking SPI for SQL databases. Spring Data R2DBC provides repositories, mapping and R2dbcEntityTemplate/DatabaseClient, but it is not an ORM: no lazy loading, no relationships, no dirty checking, no first-level cache. You model aggregates explicitly and load children with extra queries. Schema migration still uses Flyway/Liquibase (via JDBC).

12. Why does save() sometimes not insert with R2DBC?

Spring Data decides insert vs update from @Id: null → INSERT, non-null → UPDATE. If you assign ids yourself (UUIDs), save() issues an UPDATE affecting 0 rows. Fixes: DB-generated ids, implement Persistable#isNew, a @Version field, or R2dbcEntityTemplate.insert().

13. How do reactive transactions work?

R2dbcTransactionManager (a ReactiveTransactionManager) binds the connection/transaction to the Reactor Context. @Transactional on a method returning Mono/Flux, or TransactionalOperator (.as(tx::transactional)), commits on completion, rolls back on error and cancellation. The whole pipeline must be returned; detached subscribe()s run outside it.

14. How does Spring Security work in WebFlux?

A WebFilter (WebFilterChainProxy) applies a SecurityWebFilterChain built with ServerHttpSecurity. Authentication uses ReactiveAuthenticationManager / ReactiveUserDetailsService. The SecurityContext lives in the Reactor Context — read it with ReactiveSecurityContextHolder (the servlet SecurityContextHolder is empty). Method security via @EnableReactiveMethodSecurity.

15. How do you configure a JWT resource server?

Add the oauth2-resource-server starter, set spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri (JWKS discovered and cached), configure .oauth2ResourceServer(rs -> rs.jwt(...)). Scopes become SCOPE_x authorities; map custom role claims with a JwtAuthenticationConverter wrapped in ReactiveJwtAuthenticationConverterAdapter.

16. What are Sinks and why were Processors deprecated?

Sinks are thread-safe, spec-compliant ways to emit into a reactive stream from imperative code: Sinks.one(), Sinks.empty(), Sinks.many().unicast()/multicast()/replay(). Processors exposed both Subscriber and Publisher APIs and were easy to misuse (calling onNext concurrently, violating the spec). Sinks return an EmitResult (tryEmitNext) or take an EmitFailureHandler (emitNext).

17. cache() vs share()?

cache() subscribes upstream once and replays all past signals (optionally for a TTL) to every current and future subscriber — memoization. share() multicasts a live stream while there is at least one subscriber; late subscribers miss earlier elements; when everyone leaves, upstream is cancelled and a new subscriber triggers a new subscription.

18. How do you implement Server-Sent Events, and what operational concerns exist?

Return Flux<ServerSentEvent<T>> (or Flux<T>) with produces = TEXT_EVENT_STREAM. Concerns: heartbeats so proxies don't close idle connections, completing the stream when no longer needed, a strategy for slow clients (onBackpressureLatest), authentication (EventSource can't set headers), and multi-instance fan-out (shared broker).

19. SSE vs WebSocket?

SSE: server→client only, plain HTTP, auto-reconnect with Last-Event-ID, text only, proxy/HTTP-2 friendly. WebSocket: bidirectional, binary support, needs upgrade, you handle reconnection and protocol. Use SSE for feeds/notifications, WebSocket for interactive bidirectional apps.

20. How do you call a blocking legacy SDK from WebFlux?

Mono.fromCallable(() -> sdk.call(x)).subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()), with a timeout, and bounded concurrency at the call site (flatMap(..., n)) so you don't exhaust the pool. Consider a dedicated scheduler (or virtual-thread scheduler) to isolate it.

21. What are HTTP interface clients?

Interfaces annotated with @HttpExchange/@GetExchange... whose implementation Spring generates (HttpServiceProxyFactory + WebClientAdapter, or @ImportHttpServices in Framework 7). With reactive return types the proxy is non-blocking. Gotcha: collection query params are sent repeated (?ids=1&ids=2).

22. How do you test time-based code without waiting?

StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> publisher) replaces the default parallel timer with a virtual clock; thenAwait(Duration) advances it and expectNoEvent(d) asserts silence. The publisher must be created inside the supplier so it picks up the virtual scheduler.

23. How do you test a WebClient-based client without a server?

Inject a WebClient built with .exchangeFunction(req -> Mono.just(ClientResponse.create(...)...)), or use OkHttp MockWebServer/WireMock for full HTTP fidelity. Assert with StepVerifier.

24. What is Mono.defer used for in switchIfEmpty?

The argument of switchIfEmpty(x()) is evaluated at assembly — x() runs even if the source has a value. switchIfEmpty(Mono.defer(this::x)) constructs the fallback only when needed.

25. How do you stream a large result from R2DBC to the client?

Return the repository Flux directly from the controller with a streaming media type (NDJSON/SSE) or plain JSON array; WebFlux writes elements as they arrive and backpressure flows to the database cursor. Avoid collectList(); keep the connection checkout short; consider limitRate to batch fetches.

docs.title: Lead (8–12 years)
docs.text:
1. How would you decide between WebFlux and Spring MVC with virtual threads for a new service?

Start from workload and team: request/response CRUD with blocking libraries (JPA, JDBC, SDKs) and moderate fan-out → MVC + virtual threads (simpler code, debugging, hiring). Streaming (SSE/WS/NDJSON), heavy fan-out/aggregation, backpressure-sensitive pipelines, gateways/BFFs, or a fully non-blocking stack already in place → WebFlux. Validate with a spike and load test (p99, memory, CPU), and record an ADR. Mixed estates are fine; consistency within a service matters more than across services.

2. Explain operator fusion and why it matters for performance.

Reactor optimises chains: macro-fusion at assembly (e.g. scalar just paths, Mono.just().map() collapsed), micro-fusion at subscription where operators negotiate SYNC/ASYNC modes and share a queue or pull directly (QueueSubscription) instead of each operator buffering and signalling. Result: long synchronous chains cost about as much as a loop, and async boundaries (publishOn, flatMap) are where queues and allocations happen. Insight for design: minimise unnecessary thread hops; benchmark with JMH rather than guessing.

3. How do you structure a reactive service so business logic stays testable?

Ports & adapters: a pure domain (value objects, state machines, pricing/validation rules — plain Java, no Reactor where possible), an application layer that orchestrates with Mono/Flux against port interfaces, infrastructure adapters (R2DBC, WebClient, Kafka) and thin api controllers. Unit test the domain without Reactor, use cases with in-memory port fakes + StepVerifier, adapters with Testcontainers. Enforce with ArchUnit.

4. What are your team's non-negotiable reactive coding rules?

No block()/subscribe() in request paths; every I/O method returns Mono/Flux; timeouts on every remote call; bounded concurrency; retries only for idempotent transient failures; no ThreadLocal — Context instead; explicit empty handling; BlockHound in CI; StepVerifier with virtual time; ProblemDetail errors; named small methods over giant chains; observability tags on outbound calls.

5. How would you migrate a large MVC service to WebFlux?

Only with a measured reason. Strangler approach: introduce WebClient first; move data access to R2DBC per bounded context (keep Flyway on JDBC); convert bottom-up (repository → service → controller); port security/filters; replace MockMvc with WebTestClient; dual-run behind the gateway with traffic splitting; load-test parity; decommission. Avoid half-migrated states with blocking JPA behind WebFlux.

6. How do you implement a saga in reactive microservices?

Choreography (services react to events: OrderPlaced → PaymentCaptured → CourierAssigned, with compensations like RefundIssued) or orchestration (a saga orchestrator with persisted state machine issuing commands and handling replies/timeouts). Each step idempotent, events via outbox, timeouts as events (scheduled checks), state machine guards against out-of-order messages. Reactive code helps orchestration with non-blocking waits, but state must be durable — never only in a Mono in memory.

7. How do you version event contracts?

Additive changes are backward compatible (new optional fields; tolerant readers). Breaking changes go to a new topic/version (...v2) with dual publishing during migration, or use a schema registry with compatibility rules (BACKWARD/FULL). Keep events in a shared contracts module without framework dependencies, and add consumer-driven contract tests.

8. What is your testing strategy for a reactive platform?

Pyramid: pure domain unit tests; StepVerifier tests for use cases with fakes and virtual time; slice tests (@WebFluxTest, @DataR2dbcTest); Testcontainers ITs for adapters with @ServiceConnection; contract tests between services; a few E2E flows through the gateway; BlockHound in ITs; load tests (k6/Gatling) in a pipeline stage; chaos tests (toxiproxy) for timeouts/retries.

9. How would you add order cancellation to the capstone safely?

Model CANCELLED in the state machine with allowed transitions (before PICKED_UP); POST /orders/{id}/cancel with idempotency; persist the transition and an OrderCancelled outbox event in one transaction; payment-service refunds idempotently; delivery-service consumes the event, disposes the trip Disposable and marks the delivery cancelled; late delivery events are ignored by the state machine; notify via notification-service. Handle the race "picked up vs cancelled" with conditional updates (WHERE status IN (...)).

10. How do you handle multi-tenancy in a reactive service?

Resolve tenant at the edge (JWT claim/host), put it in the Reactor Context via a WebFilter, read it in repositories (R2DBC: schema/database routing with AbstractRoutingConnectionFactory keyed from the Context; or tenant column with enforced filters), tag metrics/logs, and propagate via headers on WebClient/Kafka. Test isolation explicitly.

11. When is Flux.create with a custom bridge the wrong solution?

When a supported reactive client exists (don't wrap a blocking SDK in create and block inside it), when demand cannot be respected and data must not be lost (you'd be choosing buffer-and-OOM), or when the source needs lifecycle management better handled by a framework (Kafka, JMS). Prefer official reactive drivers, fromCallable+boundedElastic for blocking calls, or Sinks for event bridges.

12. How do you make long-running streams survive deployments?

Clients reconnect (SSE EventSource does automatically) and resume from an id (Last-Event-ID mapped to Kafka offset or a sequence); servers complete streams on shutdown so connections drain; state lives outside instances (Kafka/Redis); readiness probes stop new connections before shutdown; avoid sticky in-memory state.

13. How do you approach Reactor upgrade or Spring Boot major upgrade (e.g. 3 → 4)?

Read release notes/migration guides (Boot 4: modular auto-config, Jackson 3, test slices moved, property renames like spring.mongodb.*, Gateway properties under server.webflux); upgrade dependencies with the BOM; run the full test suite including BlockHound and contract tests; use OpenRewrite recipes; canary deploy with metric comparison; watch deprecations.

14. How do you prevent a slow downstream from cascading failure?

Timeouts tighter than upstream budgets, bulkheads (concurrency limits/pools per dependency), circuit breakers with fallbacks, load shedding (reject early when queues grow), retry budgets (not just counts), hedging only for idempotent reads, and backpressure from consumers to producers.

15. What would you look for in a reactive code review?

Hidden blocking, unreturned publishers, nested subscribe, unbounded flatMap/buffers, cache() without TTL on data that changes, onErrorContinue, retries of non-idempotent calls, missing timeouts, swallowed errors, ThreadLocal usage, switchIfEmpty eager arguments, giant lambdas, missing tests for error and empty paths, Context-dependent code without tests.

16. How do you onboard developers new to reactive?

A golden-path template (service skeleton with standards built in), this playbook's levels, pair programming on real tickets, a review checklist, katas (the coding exercises), "what does this print" sessions, and visible production dashboards so they see the effect of their code.

17. What's the trade-off of using Kotlin coroutines on top of WebFlux?

Pros: sequential-looking code, structured concurrency, easier debugging, same non-blocking runtime. Cons: two mental models in a mixed Java/Kotlin estate, context bridging (ReactorContext), some operators have no direct equivalent (use Flow operators or interop). Good choice for Kotlin teams.

18. How do you expose a reactive API to non-reactive consumers?

It's HTTP — consumers don't care. Design pagination for large results (or NDJSON streaming with clear docs), stable error contracts (ProblemDetail), timeouts and rate limits. For in-process libraries, offer both: reactive API plus a thin blocking facade documented for non-reactive contexts only.

19. How do you implement request-level deadlines across services?

Accept a deadline header at the edge (or compute from SLO), store it in the Context, apply timeout(remainingBudget) on outbound calls and propagate a reduced deadline header downstream; abort work when the budget is spent; services reject requests with insufficient remaining budget.

20. What anti-patterns have you seen in reactive production systems and how were they fixed?

Strong answers are concrete: e.g. "JDBC call behind WebFlux exhausted event loops under load → moved to boundedElastic as a stopgap then R2DBC"; "retry storm after a 503 spike → added jitter and a circuit breaker"; "OOM from collectList of an export → switched to streaming NDJSON"; "lost errors from fire-and-forget subscribe() → moved to outbox and returned publishers".

docs.title: Senior (5–8 years)
docs.text:
1. Walk through how demand propagates in Flux.range(1,1000).map(f).flatMap(g, 8).subscribe(...).

subscribe(lambda) requests Long.MAX_VALUE from flatMap. flatMap (concurrency 8) requests 8 from map, which passes it to range. range emits 8 elements; flatMap subscribes to 8 inners, each inner requests its prefetch (32). When an inner completes, flatMap requests 1 more upstream (replenishment). So upstream sees bounded demand even though the final subscriber is unbounded — concurrency arguments are backpressure.

2. How do you design for a producer that can't be slowed down (e.g. market feed)?

Decide what may be lost: onBackpressureLatest() for state-like data (prices, positions); onBackpressureDrop(metric++) for telemetry; bounded onBackpressureBuffer(n, DROP_OLDEST) for recent history; onBackpressureBuffer(n) (errors on overflow) when nothing may be lost — then scale the consumer. Also sample/bufferTimeout to aggregate. Monitor drops. Never an unbounded buffer on an infinite source.

3. What is the Reactor Context and how does it differ from ThreadLocal?

An immutable map attached to the subscription, propagating from subscriber to upstream operators (contextWrite affects operators above it; the closest write wins). It survives thread hops, unlike ThreadLocal. Read with deferContextual/transformDeferredContextual. Spring Security, reactive transactions and Micrometer observation use it.

4. How do you get trace IDs into logs in a reactive app?

Use Micrometer Tracing + context-propagation with spring.reactor.context-propagation=auto (Hooks.enableAutomaticContextPropagation()): observation context stored in the Reactor Context is restored into ThreadLocals (MDC) around each operator. Logging pattern with %X{traceId}. WebClient and Kafka instrumentation propagate traceparent headers.

5. Explain cancellation and why it matters.

cancel() travels upstream when a client disconnects, take/timeout/switchMap/firstWithValue are satisfied, or a Disposable is disposed. Well-behaved sources release resources (HTTP connections, DB cursors, Kafka subscriptions). It saves resources (e.g. stops an LLM generation, a DB query). Pitfalls: detached subscribe() doesn't receive the cancellation; side effects already triggered aren't rolled back unless you use usingWhen/transactions (which roll back on cancel).

6. How do you integrate Kafka in a reactive service now that reactor-kafka is discontinued?

Produce with KafkaTemplate.send(...) adapted via Mono.fromFuture(() -> ...). Consume with @KafkaListener methods returning Mono<Void>: Spring Kafka (3.2+) treats them as async, releases the listener thread and commits offsets when the Mono completes (handling out-of-order completion). Errors go through DefaultErrorHandler (retries, DLT). Alternatives: Spring Cloud Stream reactive functions for stream transformations.

7. How do you keep a DB write and an event publish consistent?

The transactional outbox: insert the event into an outbox table in the same DB transaction, and relay it to Kafka asynchronously (Debezium CDC or a poller using FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED). Consumers must be idempotent because relays are at-least-once. Avoid "dual writes" and 2PC.

8. How do you make a Kafka consumer idempotent?

Natural idempotency (upserts, state-machine transitions that ignore stale events), unique constraints on business keys (DuplicateKeyException → treat as done), or a processed-events table keyed by event id inside the same transaction as the effect. Ordering per key via partitioning by aggregate id.

9. Describe circuit breaker states and configuration choices.

CLOSED (calls pass, failures recorded in a sliding window) → OPEN when failure rate or slow-call rate exceeds a threshold (calls fail fast with CallNotPermittedException) → HALF_OPEN after a wait (limited trial calls) → CLOSED or OPEN. Choose window size/type (count vs time), minimum calls, thresholds, slow-call duration aligned with timeouts, and a fallback. In Reactor use transformDeferred(CircuitBreakerOperator.of(cb)) so state is checked per subscription.

10. Bulkhead in reactive code?

Limit concurrency per dependency so one slow dependency can't consume everything: flatMap(f, n), Resilience4j BulkheadOperator, separate connection pools per downstream (ConnectionProvider), and separate schedulers for blocking adapters.

11. How do you find blocking calls in a WebFlux code base?

BlockHound in tests/CI (fails on blocking calls on non-blocking threads), thread-dump inspection of reactor-http-nio threads under load, metrics on event-loop pending tasks, code review for JDBC, RestTemplate, Files.*, .block(), synchronized/locks, and libraries with hidden I/O (UUID.randomUUID on low-entropy systems, DNS lookups, logging appenders).

12. What are the main performance knobs of a WebFlux service?

Event-loop count (CPU requests), WebClient ConnectionProvider (max connections, pending acquire, idle time), R2DBC pool size/acquire timeout, codec max in-memory size, flatMap concurrency and prefetch, HTTP/2, async logging, JSON payload size, and GC/direct memory sizing. Measure p99 latency and pool pending acquisitions under realistic load.

13. How do you debug a pipeline that hangs?

Check demand (.log() shows request(0) or none), missing completion (a Flux.create that never calls complete, Mono.never, a zip with an empty source never completing other branches), groupBy with more groups than flatMap concurrency, a sink with no subscribers buffering, a concatMap blocked on a never-ending inner. Use timeout + checkpoint to locate; thread dumps if blocking.

14. Flux.create vs Flux.generate vs Flux.push — when each?

generate: synchronous, one emission per callback, state-driven, demand-aware automatically (iterators, cursors). create: multi-threaded, many emissions, bridge callbacks/listeners, choose an overflow strategy, use onRequest for demand. push: like create but single-threaded producer (slightly cheaper).

15. How would you fan out live events to thousands of SSE clients?

One upstream subscription (Kafka/Redis) per instance feeding a Sinks.many().multicast() (or replay().limit(...) for late joiners); each client gets sink.asFlux().filter(...) with onBackpressureLatest() and heartbeats; complete streams on terminal events; scale horizontally with every instance consuming all events (unique group id or pub/sub); use HTTP/2 to reduce connection cost.

16. How do you propagate the caller's JWT to downstream services?

An ExchangeFilterFunction that reads the token from ReactiveSecurityContextHolder and sets the Authorization header; or ServerOAuth2AuthorizedClientExchangeFilterFunction for client-credentials tokens; or Spring Cloud Gateway's TokenRelay filter at the edge. Consider token exchange for least privilege.

17. What is the risk of @Transactional methods that call WebClient?

The DB connection stays checked out while waiting on the network — pool exhaustion under latency; the remote call isn't part of the transaction (no rollback); retries may duplicate side effects. Do remote calls before/after the transaction and use outbox/sagas for cross-service consistency.

18. How do you test code that depends on Reactor Context?

StepVerifier.create(publisher, StepVerifierOptions.create().withInitialContext(Context.of(...))), or .contextWrite(...) in the test; expectAccessibleContext().contains(k, v) to assert propagation. For security, @WithMockUser/mockJwt().

19. What's wrong with doOnNext(x -> repository.save(x))?

repository.save(x) returns a Mono that is never subscribed — nothing is saved. Even with .subscribe() inside, it would be detached (no backpressure, errors lost, outside transactions, no cancellation). Use flatMap(repository::save) or concatMap.

20. How do you implement rate limiting for outbound calls?

Resilience4j RateLimiterOperator, pacing with delayElements/zipWith(Flux.interval), a token-bucket (Bucket4j) check in flatMap, limitRate for demand shaping (not time-based). At the edge, Gateway RequestRateLimiter with Redis.

21. What happens with exceptions thrown inside subscribe(onNext) lambdas?

They're not routed to onError of the same subscriber (the sequence already delivered the element) — Reactor treats it as a bug: the subscription is cancelled and the error goes to Hooks.onErrorDropped/logged. Keep logic in operators; terminal lambdas should be trivial.

22. Explain usingWhen and where Spring uses it.

Reactive try-with-resources with async acquire and separate async completion, error and cancellation handlers. Spring's reactive transaction support follows the same model (commit on complete, rollback on error/cancel), and R2DBC connection handling uses it to close connections.

23. How do you size boundedElastic and when is it a smell?

Default cap 10×cores threads and 100k queued tasks per worker. Growth in active/queued tasks means blocking work is piling up — the service is effectively thread-per-request again. Isolate legacy blocking adapters in dedicated schedulers with explicit sizes, or move the service to MVC + virtual threads if most work is blocking.

24. How do you handle partial failure when aggregating N services?

Per-call timeouts and fallbacks (onErrorResume to a degraded value), Mono.zip only for mandatory parts; optional parts via .map(Optional::of).onErrorReturn(Optional.empty()) or defaultIfEmpty; firstWithValue for redundant sources; return partial responses with flags rather than failing the whole request; propagate deadlines (budget) downstream.

25. What metrics would you put on a reactive service dashboard?

RED per route (rate, errors, p95/p99 duration), WebClient client metrics per downstream, R2DBC pool acquired/pending, event-loop pending tasks, boundedElastic active/queued, Kafka consumer lag and listener latency, circuit-breaker state, JVM heap + direct memory + GC, SSE/WebSocket active connections.

docs.text: Open-ended questions for senior, lead and architect interviews. Each has a model answer outline — strong candidates go deeper on trade-offs and failure modes.

docs.title: Live tracking at scale
docs.text:
Design live courier tracking for a food delivery platform: 200k active deliveries, 1M concurrent viewers, 3 regions. Positions arrive every 2 seconds.

Model answer

Ingest: couriers' apps send positions to a regional ingest service (WebFlux, HTTP/2 or RSocket), validated and published to Kafka positions keyed by orderId (≈100k msg/s). Retain a short period.

State: a stream processor keeps the latest position per order (compacted topic or Redis), so new viewers get a snapshot instantly.

Fan-out tier: stateless WebFlux "edge" instances hold SSE (or WebSocket) connections. Each instance needs only the orders its viewers watch — options: (a) consistent hashing routes viewers of an order to the same instance, which consumes the relevant partitions; (b) Redis pub/sub channels per order; (c) every instance consumes everything (simple, but 100k msg/s × N instances).

Per-connection flow control: snapshot.concatWith(updates).onBackpressureLatest(), sample(1s) for slow clients, heartbeats, takeUntil(DELIVERED). Capacity: ~10–50k idle SSE connections per instance depending on memory; scale on connections.

Resilience: clients reconnect with Last-Event-ID → resume from latest snapshot; graceful drain on deploy; per-region isolation with global DNS routing; degrade to polling if the streaming tier is down.

Observability: connections per instance, fan-out latency (ingest → client), Kafka lag, dropped updates.

docs.title: Aggregating BFF
docs.text:
A mobile home screen needs data from 8 services. p99 must be under 300 ms even when one service is slow.

Model answer

WebFlux BFF; Mono.zip of mandatory parts, optional parts with timeout(budget) + onErrorResume(empty/default) and a response flag (partial: true); per-downstream connection pools and circuit breakers; hedged requests for idempotent reads with high tail latency; response caching (Mono.cache(ttl) or Redis) for slowly-changing parts; deadline propagation; RED metrics per downstream. Discuss why reactive is a good fit here (fan-out) and how virtual threads + StructuredTaskScope would compare.

docs.title: Payment flow with exactly-once effects
docs.text:
Orders must be charged exactly once even with retries, timeouts and redelivered messages.

Model answer

Client generates an Idempotency-Key; order-service stores it with a unique constraint and returns the original result on replay; payment calls carry the key and the provider dedupes; order + outbox event committed in one transaction; consumers idempotent (state machine, unique keys); timeouts lead to unknown state → query the provider before retrying; reconciliation job compares ledger with provider reports. "Exactly once" = at-least-once delivery + idempotent effects.

docs.title: Streaming export of 50M rows
docs.text:
Users can export their full history (up to 50M rows) as CSV.

Model answer

Never collectList. Either stream directly: R2DBC Flux<Row> → map to CSV lines → Flux<DataBuffer> response with backpressure to the DB cursor and limitRate for fetch batching; or (better for very large exports) an async job: request → job id → background pipeline writes to object storage in chunks (multipart upload) → notify via SSE/email with a signed URL. Consider read replicas, rate limits per user, cancellation (client disconnect cancels the stream), and resumability.

docs.title: Migrating a monolith's notifications to real-time
docs.text:
A monolith sends emails in a nightly batch; product wants real-time push in app and web.

Model answer

Outbox in the monolith → CDC (Debezium) → Kafka → notification service (reactive) that renders and routes (push, SSE/WebSocket, email) with per-channel rate limits and preferences; replay sink for late joiners; delivery receipts as events; idempotent sends; gradual rollout per notification type; keep the batch as fallback until parity.

docs.title: Rate-limited third-party API
docs.text:
A partner allows 50 requests/second; your service receives bursts of 2,000 requests/second.

Model answer

Decouple with a queue (Kafka) and a consumer paced to 50 rps (zipWith(interval)/token bucket), batching where the API allows; respond to callers asynchronously (202 + status endpoint/SSE); cache responses; prioritise traffic classes; circuit breaker on 429/5xx honouring Retry-After; capacity alerts on queue lag.

docs.title: What Does This Print?
docs.text: Short puzzles that reveal whether someone really understands assembly vs subscription, laziness, Context and error semantics. Every answer is asserted by playbook-examples/src/test/java/com/example/reactive/playbook/interview/TrickyQuestionsTest.java (print appends to a list).

docs.title: 1. Nothing is subscribed
docs.text:
Flux.just(1, 2, 3).map(i -> i * 10).doOnNext(this::print);
print("end");
Answer 

end
The pipeline is assembled but never subscribed, so doOnNext never runs.

docs.title: 2. Eager Mono.just
docs.text:
AtomicInteger counter = new AtomicInteger();
Mono<Integer> m = Mono.just(counter.incrementAndGet());
m.subscribe(this::print);
m.subscribe(this::print);
print(counter.get());
Answer 

1
1
1
counter.incrementAndGet() runs once, at assembly. Mono.just replays the captured value to every subscriber. Use Mono.fromCallable for per-subscription evaluation.

docs.title: 3. switchIfEmpty arguments are eager
docs.text:
Mono.just("a")
        .switchIfEmpty(fallback())
        .subscribe(this::print);
Answer 

fallback() called
a
fallback() is a normal method call evaluated while assembling — even though the source isn't empty. Use switchIfEmpty(Mono.defer(this::fallback)).

docs.title: 4. Errors terminate the sequence
docs.text:
Flux.just(1, 2, 3)
        .map(i -> 10 / (i - 2))
        .onErrorReturn(-1)
        .subscribe(this::print);
Answer 

-10
-1
1 → 10/-1 = -10; 2 → division by zero → onErrorReturn(-1) emits -1 and completes. Element 3 is never processed.

docs.title: 5. Which Context value wins?
docs.text:
Mono.deferContextual(ctx -> Mono.just(ctx.getOrDefault("user", "nobody")))
        .contextWrite(Context.of("user", "inner"))
        .contextWrite(Context.of("user", "outer"))
        .subscribe(this::print);
Answer 

inner
contextWrite is visible to operators above it; the write closest to the reader shadows outer ones.

docs.title: 6. zip with an empty source
docs.text:
Mono.zip(Mono.just("a"), Mono.<String>empty())
        .map(t -> t.getT1() + t.getT2())
        .defaultIfEmpty("zip was empty")
        .subscribe(this::print);
Answer 

zip was empty
zip needs a value from every source; if one completes empty, zip completes empty.

docs.title: 7. Demand and take
docs.text:
Flux.range(1, 5)
        .doOnNext(i -> print("emit " + i))
        .take(2)
        .subscribe(i -> print("got " + i));
Answer 

emit 1
got 1
emit 2
got 2
take(2) cancels upstream after the second element, so 3..5 are never emitted (elements flow one at a time through the chain).

docs.title: 8. cache()
docs.text:
Mono<String> m = Mono.fromSupplier(() -> { print("computing"); return "v"; }).cache();
m.subscribe(this::print);
m.subscribe(this::print);
Answer 

computing
v
v
The supplier runs once; the result is replayed to later subscribers.

docs.title: 9. Error in the middle of a concatenation
docs.text:
Flux.just("a", "b")
        .concatWith(Mono.error(new RuntimeException("boom")))
        .concatWith(Mono.just("c"))
        .onErrorResume(e -> Mono.just("recovered"))
        .subscribe(this::print);
Answer 

a
b
recovered
The error terminates the concatenation before c; onErrorResume switches to the fallback.

docs.title: 10. doOnSuccess on an empty Mono
docs.text:
Mono.<String>empty()
        .map(s -> s.toUpperCase())
        .doOnSuccess(v -> print("success with " + v))
        .doOnNext(v -> print("next " + v))
        .subscribe();
Answer 

success with null
doOnSuccess fires on completion with or without a value (null when empty); doOnNext only fires with a value. This is why Mono<Void> side effects with doOnSuccess always run.

docs.title: Streaming AI Responses (Spring AI)
docs.text:
LLM responses arrive token by token — a natural Flux<String>. Spring AI's ChatClient exposes a streaming API that plugs straight into WebFlux SSE.

implementation(platform("org.springframework.ai:spring-ai-bom:2.0.2"))
implementation("org.springframework.ai:spring-ai-starter-model-anthropic")   // or openai, ollama, …

@RestController
class AssistantController {

    private final ChatClient chat;

    AssistantController(ChatClient.Builder builder) {
        this.chat = builder.defaultSystem("You are a concise shopping assistant.").build();
    }

    @GetMapping(path = "/assistant", produces = MediaType.TEXT_EVENT_STREAM_VALUE)
    Flux<String> ask(@RequestParam String question) {
        return chat.prompt()
                .user(question)
                .stream()
                .content()                                   // Flux<String> of tokens/chunks
                .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(60))
                .onErrorResume(e -> Flux.just("[assistant unavailable]"));
    }
}

docs.title: Why reactive matters here
docs.text:
• Time to first token: the user sees text after ~hundreds of ms instead of waiting for the full answer.
  • Cancellation: if the browser closes the stream, the Flux is cancelled and the upstream model request is aborted — you stop paying for tokens nobody reads.
  • Concurrency: thousands of long-lived streaming responses on a handful of event-loop threads.

docs.title: Patterns
docs.text: Need Approach tool/function calling .tools(...) — tool methods can call reactive services (keep them non-blocking) RAG retrieve context (Mono from a vector store) → flatMapMany into the streaming prompt rate limits limitRate, a Resilience4j RateLimiter, and per-user quotas at the gateway full answer as well .stream().chatResponse() and reduce/collectList for post-processing

docs.title: Spring Cloud Stream (Reactive Functions)
docs.text:
Spring Cloud Stream binds plain java.util.function beans to brokers (Kafka, RabbitMQ, Pulsar…). With reactive signatures, a function receives the whole stream as a Flux.

implementation("org.springframework.cloud:spring-cloud-stream-binder-kafka")

@Configuration
class PricePipeline {

    /** price-in → enrich → price-out, as one reactive pipeline. */
    @Bean
    Function<Flux<PriceChanged>, Flux<EnrichedPrice>> enrich(FxRates fx) {
        return prices -> prices
                .filter(p -> p.priceMinor() > 0)
                .concatMap(p -> fx.rate(p.currency())
                        .map(r -> EnrichedPrice.of(p, r))
                        .onErrorResume(e -> {                 // per-element recovery: one bad message
                            log.warn("skipped {}", p, e);     // must not terminate the whole stream
                            return Mono.empty();
                        }));
    }

    @Bean
    Supplier<Flux<Heartbeat>> heartbeat() {               // reactive source: called once
        return () -> Flux.interval(Duration.ofSeconds(5)).map(Heartbeat::new);
    }

    @Bean
    Consumer<Flux<EnrichedPrice>> audit(AuditRepository repo) {
        return flux -> flux.concatMap(repo::save).subscribe();   // reactive consumers must subscribe
    }
}

spring:
  cloud:
    function:
      definition: enrich;heartbeat;audit
    stream:
      bindings:
        enrich-in-0:  { destination: prices.raw,      group: enricher }
        enrich-out-0: { destination: prices.enriched }
        audit-in-0:   { destination: prices.enriched, group: audit }

Trade-offs of reactive functions

With Function<Flux, Flux> the framework hands you the stream once: per-message retries, DLQ and acknowledgement are your responsibility (an error terminates the Flux). For most business consumers, imperative Function<In, Out> (or Function<In, Mono<Out>>) with the binder's retry/DLQ support is simpler and safer. Reactive functions shine for stream transformations (windowing, aggregation, sampling).

docs.title: Spring Cloud Gateway
docs.text:
Spring Cloud Gateway (server-webflux variant) is a reactive API gateway built on WebFlux + Reactor Netty: routing, security, rate limiting, retries and observability at the edge.

implementation(platform("org.springframework.cloud:spring-cloud-dependencies:2025.1.4"))
implementation("org.springframework.cloud:spring-cloud-starter-gateway-server-webflux")

docs.title: Routes in YAML
docs.text:
Property prefix

Since Gateway 4.3 the properties live under spring.cloud.gateway.server.webflux.* (the old spring.cloud.gateway.* names are deprecated).

spring:
  cloud:
    gateway:
      server:
        webflux:
          routes:
            - id: catalog
              uri: http://catalog:8080
              predicates:
                - Path=/api/products/**
                - Method=GET,POST
              filters:
                - StripPrefix=1
                - name: Retry
                  args: { retries: 2, methods: GET, statuses: BAD_GATEWAY,SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE }
                - name: CircuitBreaker
                  args: { name: catalog, fallbackUri: forward:/fallback/catalog }
                - name: RequestRateLimiter
                  args:
                    redis-rate-limiter.replenishRate: 10
                    redis-rate-limiter.burstCapacity: 20
                    key-resolver: "#{@userKeyResolver}"
            - id: live
              uri: ws://notifications:8080        # WebSocket routes just work
              predicates: [ Path=/ws/** ]

docs.title: Routes in Java
docs.text:
@Bean
RouteLocator routes(RouteLocatorBuilder builder) {
    return builder.routes()
            .route("reviews", r -> r.path("/api/reviews/**")
                    .filters(f -> f.addRequestHeader("X-Source", "gateway").circuitBreaker(c -> c.setName("reviews")))
                    .uri("http://reviews:8080"))
            .build();
}

docs.title: Global filters — your own edge logic
docs.text:
@Component
class TimingFilter implements GlobalFilter, Ordered {
    @Override
    public Mono<Void> filter(ServerWebExchange exchange, GatewayFilterChain chain) {
        long start = System.nanoTime();
        return chain.filter(exchange).doFinally(s -> log.info("{} took {} ms",
                exchange.getRequest().getPath(), (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000));
    }
    @Override public int getOrder() { return Ordered.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE; }
}

The capstone gateway uses global filters to strip spoofable identity headers and relay the authenticated user to downstream services — see API Gateway.

docs.title: Gateway responsibilities checklist
docs.text:
• TLS termination, authentication (JWT validation), coarse authorization
  • Routing and versioning, request/response header hygiene
  • Rate limiting, request size limits, timeouts (spring.cloud.gateway.server.webflux.httpclient.response-timeout)
  • Retries only for idempotent methods, circuit breakers with fallbacks
  • Correlation ids, access logs, metrics and tracing

docs.title: Kafka in Reactive Applications
docs.text:
implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-kafka")

What about reactor-kafka?

The reactor-kafka project (KafkaReceiver/KafkaSender) has been discontinued, and Spring Kafka deprecated its ReactiveKafka*Template wrappers. The approach below uses standard Spring Kafka with reactive return types — fully supported and simpler to operate.

docs.title: Producing without blocking
docs.text:
KafkaTemplate.send(...) returns a CompletableFuture<SendResult>. Adapt it lazily:

@Component
class PriceEventsPublisher {
    private final KafkaTemplate<String, String> kafka;
    private final JsonMapper json;                                  // Jackson 3

    Mono<Void> publish(PriceChanged event) {
        return Mono.fromCallable(() -> json.writeValueAsString(event))
                .flatMap(payload -> Mono.fromFuture(() -> kafka.send("catalog.price.changed.v1",
                        event.productId(), payload)))               // key → partition → per-key ordering
                .then();
    }
}
  • Mono.fromFuture(() -> ...) (supplier form) sends only on subscription.
  • The record key decides the partition; all events with the same key stay ordered.
  • Producer safety: acks=all, enable.idempotence=true (defaults in modern clients).

docs.title: Consuming asynchronously
docs.text:
Since Spring Kafka 3.2, a @KafkaListener may return Mono<?> or CompletableFuture<?>. The container treats it as async: the listener thread is released, and the offset is committed when the Mono completes (out-of-order commits are handled for you).

@KafkaListener(topics = "catalog.price.changed.v1", groupId = "search-indexer")
public Mono<Void> onPriceChanged(String payload) {
    return Mono.fromCallable(() -> json.readValue(payload, PriceChanged.class))
            .flatMap(indexer::reindex)                  // non-blocking work
            .then();
}

Errors signalled by the Mono go through the container's error handler (retry, DLT via DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer, @RetryableTopic).

docs.title: Delivery semantics checklist
docs.text: Concern Practice At-least-once delivery → duplicates make consumers idempotent (unique keys, upserts, processed-event table) DB write + publish atomically transactional outbox (+ Debezium CDC or poller) Ordering same key → same partition; process one key sequentially (concatMap) Poison messages bounded retries, then a dead-letter topic Schema evolution versioned topics (…v1) or Schema Registry (Avro/Protobuf)

docs.title: Kafka → browser
docs.text: A very common reactive pattern: consume a topic, push into a Sinks.Many, expose it as SSE or WebSocket. Each service instance should use its own consumer group (or unique group id) for this broadcast, so every instance sees every event. The capstone's notification-service does exactly this.

docs.title: RSocket
docs.text:
RSocket is a binary, multiplexed application protocol (over TCP or WebSocket) with Reactive Streams semantics on the wire — request(n) crosses the network.

Interaction Shape Example request-response 1 → 1 get a product fire-and-forget 1 → 0 log/metric event request-stream 1 → N price feed request-channel N → N bidirectional chat, telemetry 
implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-rsocket")

spring.rsocket.server.port: 7000

docs.title: Server
docs.text:
@Controller
class PriceRSocketController {

    @MessageMapping("product.{id}")
    Mono<Product> product(@DestinationVariable String id) { return repository.findById(id); }

    @MessageMapping("prices")
    Flux<PriceTick> prices(String productId) {
        return Flux.interval(Duration.ofSeconds(1)).map(i -> new PriceTick(productId, 1_000 + i, i));
    }

    @MessageMapping("audit")
    Mono<Void> audit(AuditEvent event) { return auditLog.save(event).then(); }  // fire-and-forget

    @MessageMapping("chat")
    Flux<String> chat(Flux<String> inbound) { return inbound.map(m -> "echo: " + m); }
}

docs.title: Client
docs.text:
RSocketRequester requester = builder.tcp("localhost", 7000);

Flux<PriceTick> ticks = requester.route("prices").data("p1").retrieveFlux(PriceTick.class);
Mono<Void> sent = requester.route("audit").data(event).send();

RSocket also supports @RSocketExchange interface clients (like HTTP interface clients), resumption after disconnects, and lease-based load control. It is a strong fit for service-to-service streaming inside a platform; for browser-facing APIs, SSE/WebSocket over HTTP are easier to operate.

docs.title: ❌ → ✅
docs.text: Anti-pattern Why it hurts Do this instead block() in a handler freezes an event-loop thread (and throws on Netty threads) return the publisher; compose with operators subscribe() inside map/flatMap/a handler detached work: no backpressure, no cancellation, errors lost, transactions/context lost flatMap it into the chain; if it must be fire-and-forget, then()-chain it or hand it to a managed component Blocking I/O in operators (JDBC, RestTemplate, file I/O) stalls the loop non-blocking driver, or fromCallable(...).subscribeOn(boundedElastic()) Mono.just(sideEffect()) runs eagerly, even if never subscribed Mono.fromCallable / Mono.defer Ignoring a returned Mono the operation never happens return / chain it ThreadLocal / MDC / SecurityContextHolder values vanish across thread hops Reactor Context, ReactiveSecurityContextHolder, context-propagation Unbounded flatMap over large inputs hundreds of concurrent calls, pool exhaustion flatMap(f, concurrency) collectList() on unbounded streams OOM stream the Flux; buffer(n) for batches onErrorContinue everywhere surprising semantics per-element onErrorResume inside flatMap retry() without backoff/filter retry storms, duplicate side effects retryWhen(Retry.backoff(...).jitter(...).filter(...)) + idempotency switchIfEmpty(expensiveCall()) expensiveCall() executes eagerly switchIfEmpty(Mono.defer(this::expensiveCall)) Huge operator chains in one method unreadable, untestable extract named methods returning Mono/Flux, use transform Flux<Void>/Mono<Optional<T>> awkward semantics Mono<Void>, empty Mono<T> Mixing @Transactional with remote calls holds DB connections while waiting do remote calls outside the transaction; outbox for events

docs.title: Habits of healthy reactive code
docs.text:
1. Every public method returns Mono/Flux (or a plain value if it does no I/O).
  2. Name things: small methods (loadUser, priceCart) composed with flatMap read like a story.
  3. Decide what "empty" means at each step (switchIfEmpty(Mono.error(...)), defaultIfEmpty).
  4. Put timeouts on every remote call and know your error budget.
  5. Test with StepVerifier and virtual time; run BlockHound in CI.
  6. Keep the domain pure — business rules as plain Java functions, reactive code as the glue (see the capstone's Pricing and OrderStatus classes).

docs.title: Kotlin Coroutines
docs.text:
Spring WebFlux has first-class Kotlin coroutine support: suspend functions instead of Mono, Flow instead of Flux — same non-blocking engine, imperative-looking code.

implementation("org.jetbrains.kotlinx:kotlinx-coroutines-reactor")

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/products")
class ProductController(private val repository: ProductCoroutineRepository,
                        private val client: WebClient) {

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    suspend fun get(@PathVariable id: String): Product =
        repository.findById(id) ?: throw ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)

    @GetMapping
    fun all(): Flow<Product> = repository.findAll()

    @GetMapping("/{id}/view")
    suspend fun view(@PathVariable id: String): ProductView = coroutineScope {
        val product = async { repository.findById(id)!! }                       // concurrent
        val stock = async { client.get().uri("/stock/{id}", id).retrieve().awaitBody<Stock>() }
        ProductView(product.await(), stock.await())
    }
}

interface ProductCoroutineRepository : CoroutineCrudRepository<Product, String>
Reactor Coroutines Mono<T> suspend fun(): T? Flux<T> Flow<T> Mono.zip(a, b) async { } + await() in coroutineScope .block() never — runBlocking only in main/tests Context ReactorContext coroutine element mono.awaitSingle() / flux.asFlow() bridges in kotlinx-coroutines-reactor

Coroutines and Reactor interoperate freely, so a team can mix Java services written with Reactor and Kotlin services written with coroutines on the same platform.

docs.title: Should you?
docs.text: Revisit Reactive vs Virtual Threads first. Migrate a service when it is I/O-bound with high concurrency, streams data, or fans out to many dependencies — not because reactive is fashionable.
