docs.title: Step by step
docs.text:
1. Edge first: introduce WebClient for outbound calls inside the MVC app (it works there too).
  2. Data access: replace JDBC/JPA with R2DBC in one bounded context; keep Flyway on JDBC for migrations.
  3. Switch the web stack: swap the starter, convert controllers bottom-up (repository → service → controller).
  4. Security & filters: port to the reactive equivalents above.
  5. Tests: MockMvc → WebTestClient, add StepVerifier tests for services, run BlockHound.
  6. Load test and compare with the baseline before decommissioning the old version.

Half-migrated services are the worst of both worlds

A WebFlux controller calling a blocking JPA repository through boundedElastic gives you reactive complexity and thread-pool limits. Finish the data layer or stay on MVC.

docs.title: Measure first
docs.text: Load test with realistic concurrency (Gatling, k6, wrk2) and watch: p99 latency, error rate, CPU, event-loop pending tasks, pool pending acquisitions and GC. Reactive apps usually saturate CPU or a pool — rarely threads.

docs.title: Event loops
docs.text:
• Default reactor.netty.ioWorkerCount = available processors (min 4). In containers, set CPU requests/limits so the JVM sees the right core count.
  • Anything slow on the event loop (big JSON, regex, crypto, logging to a blocking appender) delays all connections on it. Offload CPU-heavy steps with publishOn(Schedulers.parallel()).
  • Use async logging (Logback AsyncAppender / Log4j2 async loggers).

docs.title: Connection pools
docs.text:
Pool Settings WebClient (Reactor Netty ConnectionProvider) maxConnections (default 2 × cores, min 16), pendingAcquireMaxCount, pendingAcquireTimeout, maxIdleTime, evictInBackground R2DBC (r2dbc-pool) spring.r2dbc.pool.max-size, max-acquire-time, max-idle-time, validation-query Redis (Lettuce) one multiplexed connection is usually enough; pool only for blocking/transactional commands

Make maxIdleTime shorter than any load balancer idle timeout to avoid "connection reset" on reuse.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
• Bound everything: limitRate, bounded onBackpressureBuffer, flatMap concurrency, bufferTimeout.
  • spring.codec.max-in-memory-size caps aggregated bodies; stream large payloads (Flux<DataBuffer>) instead of bodyToMono(String.class).
  • Leaked DataBuffers show up as Netty LEAK: logs — run tests with -Dio.netty.leakDetection.level=paranoid.

docs.title: Latency
docs.text:
• Fan out with Mono.zip/flatMap instead of sequential flatMap chains.
  • cache() hot reference data; use Mono.fromCallable(...).cache(ttl) for config-like lookups.
  • Enable HTTP/2 (server.http2.enabled=true) for many concurrent requests per client.
  • Set timeouts at every hop, shortest at the edge-most caller minus downstream budgets.

docs.title: Startup & footprint
docs.text:
• Functional endpoints + fewer auto-configurations start faster.
  • GraalVM native images (org.graalvm.buildtools.native plugin + nativeCompile) shrink memory and startup dramatically; test reflection-heavy libraries carefully.
  • CDS/AOT cache (JDK 24+ -XX:AOTCache) speeds JVM startup with no code changes.

docs.title: @Scheduled with reactive methods
docs.text:
Since Spring Framework 6.1, @Scheduled methods may return a Publisher: Spring subscribes on every trigger — no subscribe()/block() needed.

@Scheduled(fixedDelay = 30, timeUnit = TimeUnit.SECONDS)
Mono<Void> expireCarts() {
    return carts.findExpired(Instant.now())
            .flatMap(carts::delete, 8)
            .then();
}

With fixedDelay, the next run starts after the returned Mono completes. In a cluster, guard jobs with a distributed lock (ShedLock supports R2DBC/Mongo/Redis) so only one instance runs them.

docs.title: Reactive streams as background jobs
docs.text:
For continuous processing (e.g. consuming a change stream), start the pipeline on ApplicationReadyEvent, keep its Disposable, add retryWhen for resilience, and dispose it on shutdown:

@Component
class ChangeStreamProjector implements SmartLifecycle {
    private Disposable subscription;

    @Override public void start() {
        subscription = changes.listen()
                .concatMap(projection::apply)
                .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(Long.MAX_VALUE, Duration.ofSeconds(1)).maxBackoff(Duration.ofMinutes(1)))
                .subscribe();
    }
    @Override public void stop() { subscription.dispose(); }
    @Override public boolean isRunning() { return subscription != null && !subscription.isDisposed(); }
}

docs.title: Graceful shutdown
docs.text:
server:
  shutdown: graceful                     # stop accepting, finish in-flight requests
spring:
  lifecycle:
    timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 25s     # < Kubernetes terminationGracePeriodSeconds

Long-lived SSE/WebSocket streams don't "finish" — complete them on shutdown (e.g. takeUntilOther a shutdown signal) so clients reconnect to another instance.

docs.title: Startup checks
docs.text: Use reactive health indicators and readiness probes; don't block() in @PostConstruct to warm caches — run warm-up in an ApplicationRunner that returns once the Mono completes (blocking in a runner on the main thread is acceptable at startup).

docs.title: Project Reactor
docs.text:
Project Reactor is the Reactive Streams library underneath Spring WebFlux, Spring Data reactive repositories, Spring Security's reactive stack and Spring Cloud Gateway. Mastering it is 80% of mastering reactive Spring.

docs.title: Reading marble diagrams
docs.text:
Reactor's Javadoc explains operators with marble diagrams: a timeline per sequence, circles for onNext, | for onComplete, X for onError. This playbook uses small tables and tests instead, but the official diagrams are worth opening for any operator you meet for the first time.

All examples on these pages are tests

Source: playbook-examples/src/test/java/com/example/reactive/playbook/reactor/. Run them with ./gradlew :playbook-examples:test.

docs.title: Assembly, subscription, execution
docs.text:
Each operator call creates a new Publisher wrapping the previous one (assembly). subscribe() walks the chain upwards, creating one Subscriber per operator (subscription); then request(n) travels up and onNext signals flow down (execution).

flowchart RL SUB[subscriber] -- "subscribe ↑" --> F[filter] -- "subscribe ↑" --> M[map] -- "subscribe ↑" --> R[range] R -. "onNext ↓" .-> M -. "onNext ↓" .-> F -. "onNext ↓" .-> SUB

docs.title: Operator fusion
docs.text:
Reactor negotiates fusion between adjacent operators: macro-fusion replaces operators at assembly (e.g. Flux.just(x) → scalar Mono), micro-fusion lets operators share a queue or iterate directly (SYNC/ASYNC modes). A long synchronous chain therefore costs about as much as a loop.

// range → map → filter are "fuseable": Reactor collapses them into one loop with no queues,
// so a long synchronous chain costs roughly what a hand-written for-loop costs.
StepVerifier.create(Flux.range(1, 5).map(i -> i * 2).filter(i -> i > 4))
        .expectFusion()                                    // assert the chain negotiated fusion
        .expectNext(6, 8, 10)
        .verifyComplete();

docs.title: Prefetch and queues
docs.text: Asynchronous boundaries (publishOn, flatMap, concatMap, zip) hold queues with a prefetch (Queues.SMALL_BUFFER_SIZE = 256 by default, XS = 32). They request prefetch upstream and replenish at 75% (limitRate semantics). Tune with operator overloads (publishOn(s, 32), flatMap(f, 16, 8)).

docs.title: Introspection with Scannable
docs.text:
Flux<Integer> pipeline = Flux.range(1, 10).name("numbers").filter(i -> i % 2 == 0).publishOn(
        reactor.core.scheduler.Schedulers.parallel(), 32);
Scannable s = Scannable.from(pipeline);
assertThat(s.scan(Scannable.Attr.PREFETCH)).isEqualTo(32);       // publishOn's queue size
assertThat(s.parents().map(Scannable::name).toList()).contains("numbers");

docs.title: Writing your own operator
docs.text:
Prefer composition over implementing Publisher/Subscriber:

/** A reusable "operator": per-subscriber state, built with transformDeferred. */
static <T> Function<Flux<T>, Flux<String>> numbered() {
    return flux -> {
        int[] counter = {0};                       // fresh state for EVERY subscriber (deferred)
        return flux.map(v -> (++counter[0]) + ". " + v);
    };
}

@Test
void customOperatorWithTransformDeferred() {
    Flux<String> lines = Flux.just("alpha", "beta").transformDeferred(numbered());
    StepVerifier.create(lines).expectNext("1. alpha", "2. beta").verifyComplete();
    StepVerifier.create(lines).expectNext("1. alpha", "2. beta").verifyComplete(); // not "3. alpha"
}
Tool Use transform(fn) reusable chain, applied once at assembly transformDeferred(fn) per-subscriber chain (state, Context-dependent logic) transformDeferredContextual((flux, ctx) -> …) chain that reads the Context Operators.lift(...) / Operators.liftPublisher(...) decorate every subscriber (metrics, tracing hooks) — rarely needed Hooks.onEachOperator(key, fn) apply a lift to every operator globally (instrumentation libraries)

Reactor add-ons worth knowing
docs.text: Library What reactor-pool generic reactive object pool (it powers r2dbc-pool) reactor-extra MathFlux (sum/average/min/max), BooleanUtils, extra retry helpers reactor-core-micrometer tap(Micrometer.metrics(...)), Micrometer.observation(...) reactor-tools ReactorDebugAgent blockhound blocking-call detector Reactive Streams TCK verify a custom Publisher against the spec rules

docs.title: Demand, explicitly
docs.text:
List<Long> requests = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();
List<Integer> received = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();

Flux.range(1, 10)
        .doOnRequest(requests::add)                       // observe demand flowing upstream
        .subscribe(new BaseSubscriber<Integer>() {
            @Override
            protected void hookOnSubscribe(Subscription s) {
                request(2);                               // "I can handle 2 for now"
            }

            @Override
            protected void hookOnNext(Integer value) {
                received.add(value);
                if (received.size() % 2 == 0) {
                    request(2);                           // processed a batch → ask for more
                }
            }
        });

assertThat(received).hasSize(10);
assertThat(requests).containsOnly(2L);

docs.title: limitRate — protect a source from unbounded requests
docs.text:
block(), subscribe(lambda) and many terminal consumers request Long.MAX_VALUE. limitRate(n) re-shapes that into batches: request n, then replenish 75%.

List<Long> requests = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();
Flux.range(1, 100)
        .doOnRequest(requests::add)
        .limitRate(10)        // request 10 upfront, then replenish 75% (8) at a time
        .blockLast();         // block() requests unbounded — limitRate protects the source
assertThat(requests.getFirst()).isEqualTo(10L);
assertThat(requests).contains(8L);

docs.title: Overflow strategies
docs.text:
When the source can't slow down, pick what to lose:

// A fast producer (1..100, emitted without looking at demand) meets a slow subscriber that
// requests 1 element, and only later requests more. What survives depends on the strategy:
assertThat(slowConsumer(fastProducer().onBackpressureDrop()))
        .containsExactly("1", "C", "|later");   // 2..100 dropped on arrival; completion needs no demand

assertThat(slowConsumer(fastProducer().onBackpressureLatest()))
        .containsExactly("1", "|later", "100", "C");                // only the newest is kept

assertThat(slowConsumer(fastProducer().onBackpressureBuffer(5, dropped -> { }, BufferOverflowStrategy.DROP_OLDEST)))
        .containsExactly("1", "|later", "96", "97", "98", "99", "100", "C"); // newest 5

assertThat(slowConsumer(fastProducer().onBackpressureBuffer(5)))     // default: ERROR on overflow
        .containsExactly("1", "|later", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6", "error:OverflowException");
// the overflow error is delayed until the buffered elements have been drained
Strategy Keeps Loses Good for onBackpressureDrop() what fits current demand everything else metrics, telemetry onBackpressureLatest() the newest value intermediate values UI state, prices, positions onBackpressureBuffer(n, DROP_OLDEST) newest n oldest recent-history views onBackpressureBuffer(n) up to n nothing — errors when full must-not-lose, bounded onBackpressureBuffer() everything memory 💥 avoid on infinite sources

docs.title: Batching: buffer, bufferTimeout, window, groupBy
docs.text:
StepVerifier.create(Flux.range(1, 7).buffer(3))
        .expectNext(List.of(1, 2, 3), List.of(4, 5, 6), List.of(7))
        .verifyComplete();

// size OR time, whichever comes first — ideal for bulk inserts / batched Kafka sends
StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> Flux.interval(Duration.ofMillis(300)).take(5)
                .bufferTimeout(10, Duration.ofSeconds(1)))
        .thenAwait(Duration.ofSeconds(2))
        .expectNext(List.of(0L, 1L, 2L, 3L))  // timer starts at the first element (t=300ms) → flush at 1.3s
        .expectNext(List.of(4L))              // flushed on completion
        .verifyComplete();

StepVerifier.create(Flux.range(1, 6).window(2).flatMap(w -> w.reduce(Integer::sum)))
        .expectNext(3, 7, 11)                 // window = buffer of Fluxes (streamed, not collected)
        .verifyComplete();

StepVerifier.create(Flux.just("apple", "bean", "avocado", "beet")
                .groupBy(s -> s.charAt(0))
                .flatMap(g -> g.count().map(c -> g.key() + "=" + c)))
        .expectNextMatches(s -> s.equals("a=2") || s.equals("b=2"))
        .expectNextMatches(s -> s.equals("a=2") || s.equals("b=2"))
        .verifyComplete();

groupBy needs enough concurrency

Each group is a Flux that must be consumed. With more distinct keys than flatMap concurrency (default 256), groupBy can hang. Keep cardinality low or raise concurrency.

docs.title: zip — wait for all, combine
docs.text:
The classic parallel fan-out / fan-in: call independent services concurrently, combine results.

// three independent calls, executed concurrently, combined when ALL have a value
Mono<String> name = Mono.just("Asha").delayElement(Duration.ofMillis(30));
Mono<Integer> orders = Mono.just(12).delayElement(Duration.ofMillis(20));
Mono<String> tier = Mono.just("GOLD").delayElement(Duration.ofMillis(10));

Mono<Profile> profile = Mono.zip(name, orders, tier)
        .map(t -> new Profile(t.getT1(), t.getT2(), t.getT3()));

StepVerifier.create(profile).expectNext(new Profile("Asha", 12, "GOLD")).verifyComplete();
// if ANY source is empty, zip completes empty; if any errors, zip errors
gantt dateFormat X axisFormat %L ms section sequential (flatMap chain) name :0, 30 orders :30, 50 tier :50, 60 section Mono.zip name :0, 30 orders :0, 20 tier :0, 10

Flux.zip/zipWith pairs elements by index and stops at the shortest source.

docs.title: merge vs concat
docs.text:
StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> {
            Flux<String> slow = Flux.just("s1", "s2").delayElements(Duration.ofMillis(30));
            Flux<String> fast = Flux.just("f1", "f2").delayElements(Duration.ofMillis(20));
            return Flux.merge(slow, fast);          // subscribe to both now; interleave by time
        })
        .thenAwait(Duration.ofSeconds(1))
        .expectNext("f1", "s1", "f2", "s2")
        .verifyComplete();

StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> {
            Flux<String> slow = Flux.just("s1", "s2").delayElements(Duration.ofMillis(30));
            Flux<String> fast = Flux.just("f1", "f2").delayElements(Duration.ofMillis(20));
            return Flux.concat(slow, fast);         // subscribe to `fast` only after `slow` completes
        })
        .thenAwait(Duration.ofSeconds(1))
        .expectNext("s1", "s2", "f1", "f2")
        .verifyComplete();
merge concat mergeSequential Subscribes all at once one after another all at once Order by arrival time source by source source by source (buffers)

docs.title: combineLatest — recompute when any input changes
docs.text:
// recompute whenever EITHER input changes (e.g. price × fx-rate)
StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> Flux.combineLatest(
                Flux.just(100, 200).delayElements(Duration.ofMillis(10)),     // price at t=10, 20
                Flux.just(2, 3).delayElements(Duration.ofMillis(15)),         // rate at t=15, 30
                (price, rate) -> price * rate))
        .thenAwait(Duration.ofSeconds(1))
        .expectNext(200, 400, 600)   // t=15: 100×2, t=20: 200×2, t=30: 200×3
        .verifyComplete();

docs.title: firstWithValue — race (hedged requests)
docs.text:
StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> Mono.firstWithValue(
                Mono.just("primary").delayElement(Duration.ofMillis(50)),
                Mono.just("replica").delayElement(Duration.ofMillis(10))))  // hedged request
        .thenAwait(Duration.ofSeconds(1))
        .expectNext("replica")                                              // fastest wins, other cancelled
        .verifyComplete();

Mono.firstWithSignal takes the first signal of any kind (including errors and empty completion).

docs.title: Sequencing: then, thenMany, when, startWith
docs.text:
StringBuilder log = new StringBuilder();
Mono<Void> audit = Mono.fromRunnable(() -> log.append("audit;"));
Mono<Void> save = Mono.fromRunnable(() -> log.append("save;"));

Mono<String> pipeline = save
        .then(audit)                              // run after save completes, ignore its value
        .then(Mono.just("done"));                 // then switch to another publisher
StepVerifier.create(pipeline).expectNext("done").verifyComplete();
StepVerifier.create(Mono.when(save, audit)).verifyComplete();  // wait for both, no values
StepVerifier.create(Flux.just(2, 3).startWith(1)).expectNext(1, 2, 3).verifyComplete();

Choosing quickly

  • Need all results together → zip
  • Need all results as they come → merge / flatMap
  • Need them in order → concat / concatMap
  • Need the fastest → firstWithValue
  • Need the latest of each → combineLatest
  • Only need completion → then / when

docs.title: Context
docs.text: In reactive code one request hops across many threads, so ThreadLocal (MDC, security context, tenant id, transaction) does not work. Reactor's Context is an immutable key/value map attached to the subscription instead of the thread.

docs.title: Writing and reading
docs.text:
/** Reads a value that was written further DOWN the chain (closer to the subscriber). */
static Mono<String> greet(String name) {
    return Mono.deferContextual(ctx -> Mono.just(
            "[" + ctx.getOrDefault("tenant", "default") + "] hello " + name));
}

@Test
void contextFlowsFromSubscriberUpwards() {
    Mono<String> result = greet("asha")
            .contextWrite(Context.of("tenant", "acme"));   // e.g. set by a WebFilter

    StepVerifier.create(result).expectNext("[acme] hello asha").verifyComplete();
}

docs.title: It flows from the subscriber upwards
docs.text:
contextWrite is visible to operators above it (closer to the source). The write nearest to the reader wins:

Mono<String> m = Mono.just("x")
        .flatMap(x -> Mono.deferContextual(ctx -> Mono.just(ctx.get("key").toString())))
        .contextWrite(Context.of("key", "inner"))   // visible to the flatMap above
        .contextWrite(Context.of("key", "outer"));  // shadowed: the closer write wins
StepVerifier.create(m).expectNext("inner").verifyComplete();
flowchart BT SUB[subscriber] --> W2["contextWrite(key=outer)"] --> W1["contextWrite(key=inner)"] --> FM["flatMap reads key → inner"] --> SRC[source]

docs.title: Where Spring uses Context
docs.text:
Feature Key / API Spring Security ReactiveSecurityContextHolder.getContext() Reactive transactions TransactionContext (managed by @Transactional / TransactionalOperator) Micrometer tracing / observation automatic context propagation (see Observability) Your own WebFilter chain.filter(exchange).contextWrite(ctx -> ctx.put(...)) — see Filters

Testing with Context

StepVerifier.create(mono, StepVerifierOptions.create().withInitialContext(Context.of(...))) — see StepVerifier.

docs.title: Static factories
docs.text: Factory Behaviour Mono.just(v) / Flux.just(a, b) emit known values (evaluated eagerly, at assembly) Mono.empty() / Flux.empty() complete immediately Mono.error(e) / Mono.error(() -> e) fail immediately (supplier form is lazy) Mono.never() never signals — useful in tests and timeouts Flux.range(start, count) integer sequence Flux.fromIterable / fromArray / fromStream from collections (fromStream is single-use!) Mono.justOrEmpty(optional) Optional → Mono Mono.fromCallable / fromSupplier / fromRunnable lazy, per subscription Mono.fromFuture(() -> cf) CompletableFuture → Mono (supplier form defers the call) Mono.defer(() -> mono) / Flux.defer build the publisher lazily, per subscriber Flux.interval(d) / Mono.delay(d) time-based (runs on Schedulers.parallel())

docs.title: Eager just vs lazy defer
docs.text:
AtomicInteger counter = new AtomicInteger();
Mono<Integer> eager = Mono.just(counter.incrementAndGet());            // evaluated NOW, once
Mono<Integer> lazy = Mono.defer(() -> Mono.just(counter.incrementAndGet())); // per subscription

StepVerifier.create(eager).expectNext(1).verifyComplete();
StepVerifier.create(eager).expectNext(1).verifyComplete();             // same captured value
StepVerifier.create(lazy).expectNext(2).verifyComplete();
StepVerifier.create(lazy).expectNext(3).verifyComplete();

Tip

Mono.just(expensiveCall()) calls expensiveCall() immediately, even if nobody subscribes. Use Mono.fromCallable(this::expensiveCall) or Mono.defer(...) for anything with side effects.

docs.title: generate: synchronous, stateful, one element per round
docs.text:
Demand-aware by construction — Reactor calls your generator only when downstream requests more.

// Fibonacci: one sink.next per round, state carried between rounds
Flux<Long> fibonacci = Flux.generate(
        () -> new long[] {0, 1},
        (state, sink) -> {
            sink.next(state[0]);
            return new long[] {state[1], state[0] + state[1]};
        });

StepVerifier.create(fibonacci.take(7))
        .expectNext(0L, 1L, 1L, 2L, 3L, 5L, 8L)
        .verifyComplete();

docs.title: create: bridge callback/listener APIs
docs.text:
Flux.create gives you a FluxSink you can call from any thread, any number of times. Choose an OverflowStrategy for when the source ignores demand (BUFFER default, DROP, LATEST, ERROR, IGNORE). Register onDispose/onCancel to release the underlying resource.

// Flux.create adapts listener/callback APIs; it may emit from any thread, many at once
Flux<String> events = Flux.create(sink -> {
    PriceTicker ticker = new PriceTicker();
    ticker.onPrice(sink::next);
    ticker.onClose(sink::complete);
    sink.onDispose(ticker::stop);         // cleanup when the subscriber cancels
    ticker.start();
}, FluxSink.OverflowStrategy.BUFFER);

StepVerifier.create(events).expectNext("AAPL 190", "AAPL 191").verifyComplete();
generate create push Threads single, synchronous any, concurrent single producer thread Emissions per call exactly one unlimited unlimited Respects demand yes, automatically only via sink.requestedFromDownstream() / onRequest same as create

docs.title: Time-based sources
docs.text:
StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> Flux.interval(Duration.ofSeconds(1)).take(3))
        .expectSubscription()
        .thenAwait(Duration.ofSeconds(3))
        .expectNext(0L, 1L, 2L)
        .verifyComplete();

docs.title: Debugging
docs.text: Reactive stack traces show where the operator executed (deep inside Reactor), not where you assembled the pipeline. Reactor offers three tools, from cheapest to most expensive.

docs.title: 1. log() — see every signal
docs.text:
Flux.range(1, 2).map(i -> i * 10).log("calc").subscribe();
// [calc] onSubscribe(FluxMap.MapSubscriber)
// [calc] request(unbounded)
// [calc] onNext(10)
// [calc] onNext(20)
// [calc] onComplete()

Place log() right after the operator you are suspicious of; it shows demand (request), cancellation and the thread each signal runs on.

docs.title: 2. checkpoint() — mark assembly points
docs.text:
Flux<Integer> f = Flux.just(1, 2, 0)
        .map(i -> 10 / i)
        .checkpoint("after-division")    // adds this description to the error's stack trace
        .log("calc");                    // logs every signal: onSubscribe, request, onNext, onError
StepVerifier.create(f)
        .expectNext(10, 5)
        .verifyErrorSatisfies(e -> org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat(e.getSuppressed()[0])
                .hasMessageContaining("after-division"));

checkpoint("description") is cheap (no stack capture); checkpoint() without args captures a stack trace at assembly time (more expensive).

docs.title: 3. Global assembly tracing
docs.text:
Option Cost When Hooks.onOperatorDebug() high — captures a stack for every operator local debugging only ReactorDebugAgent.init() (reactor-tools) low — bytecode instrumentation at load time safe for production Spring Boot: spring.reactor.debug-agent.enabled=true same as agent default true when reactor-tools is on the classpath 
runtimeOnly("io.projectreactor:reactor-tools")   // enables the debug agent in Spring Boot apps

docs.title: Other useful hooks
docs.text:
• Hooks.onErrorDropped(e -> ...) — errors that had nowhere to go (after termination, bare subscribe()).
  • Hooks.onNextDropped(v -> ...) — values emitted after cancellation.
  • Hooks.enableAutomaticContextPropagation() — copy ThreadLocals (e.g. MDC, tracing) across thread hops; Spring Boot turns it on with spring.reactor.context-propagation=auto.

docs.title: A debugging checklist
docs.text:
1. Nothing happens? Somebody forgot to subscribe / return the publisher.
  2. Hangs? A Mono never completes (missing sink.complete(), groupBy starvation, Mono.never()), or demand is 0.
  3. Runs twice? Cold publisher subscribed twice — cache() or restructure.
  4. Wrong thread? Add .doOnNext(v -> log.info("{}", Thread.currentThread())) around publishOn/subscribeOn.
  5. Event loop blocked? Run tests with BlockHound.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
In Reactor an exception becomes an onError signal that travels downstream and terminates the sequence. There is no try/catch around a pipeline — you place error operators in the pipeline.

Flux<Integer> f = Flux.just(1, 2, 0, 4).map(i -> 10 / i);
StepVerifier.create(f)
        .expectNext(10, 5)
        .verifyError(ArithmeticException.class);   // 4 is never processed

docs.title: Recovery operators
Recover per element, not per stream
docs.text:
Put the recovery inside flatMap so one bad element doesn't terminate the whole stream:

// handle errors on the INNER publisher so one bad element doesn't kill the whole stream
Flux<String> results = Flux.just("1", "two", "3")
        .flatMap(s -> Mono.fromCallable(() -> Integer.parseInt(s))
                .map(i -> "ok:" + i)
                .onErrorResume(NumberFormatException.class, e -> Mono.just("bad:" + s)));
StepVerifier.create(results).expectNext("ok:1", "bad:two", "ok:3").verifyComplete();

Avoid onErrorContinue

onErrorContinue changes the behaviour of upstream operators in non-obvious ways and only works with operators that explicitly support it. The inner-onErrorResume pattern above is explicit and predictable.

docs.title: Retries
docs.text:
retry(n) resubscribes immediately — that hammers a struggling dependency. Use retryWhen with exponential backoff, jitter and a filter for transient errors only:

AtomicInteger attempts = new AtomicInteger();
Mono<String> flaky = Mono.defer(() -> attempts.incrementAndGet() < 3
        ? Mono.error(new IOException("transient"))
        : Mono.just("success on attempt " + attempts.get()));

StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> flaky.retryWhen(Retry.backoff(5, Duration.ofMillis(100))
                .maxBackoff(Duration.ofSeconds(2))
                .jitter(0.5)
                .filter(IOException.class::isInstance)          // only retry what is retryable
                .onRetryExhaustedThrow((spec, signal) -> signal.failure())))
        .thenAwait(Duration.ofSeconds(10))
        .expectNext("success on attempt 3")
        .verifyComplete();

Only retry what is safe to retry

Retrying a POST /payments can charge twice unless the call is idempotent (e.g. carries an Idempotency-Key). The capstone's order-service does exactly that.

docs.title: Timeouts
docs.text:
StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> Mono.just("slow").delayElement(Duration.ofSeconds(5))
                .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(1), Mono.just("fallback")))
        .thenAwait(Duration.ofSeconds(1))
        .expectNext("fallback")
        .verifyComplete();

StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> Mono.never().timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(1)))
        .thenAwait(Duration.ofSeconds(1))
        .verifyError(TimeoutException.class);

Put timeout before retryWhen for a per-attempt limit, after it for an overall limit.

docs.title: Checked exceptions inside lambdas
docs.text:
Flux<String> lines = Flux.just("a", "b").map(s -> {
    try {
        return readFile(s);
    } catch (IOException e) {
        throw Exceptions.propagate(e);   // wraps; Reactor unwraps it again for onError
    }
});
StepVerifier.create(lines).verifyErrorSatisfies(e -> assertThat(e).isInstanceOf(IOException.class));

docs.title: Observing signals without changing them
docs.text:
StringBuilder trace = new StringBuilder();
Mono<Integer> m = Mono.just(1)
        .doOnSubscribe(s -> trace.append("subscribe;"))
        .doOnNext(v -> trace.append("next:").append(v).append(';'))
        .doOnError(e -> trace.append("error;"))
        .doOnSuccess(v -> trace.append("success;"))
        .doFinally(signal -> trace.append("finally:").append(signal));
m.block();
assertThat(trace).hasToString("subscribe;next:1;success;finally:onComplete");

docs.title: Errors you should not swallow
docs.text:
• Exceptions.isOverflow(e) — backpressure bug, fix the design.
  • Exceptions.isBubbling(e) / Error subclasses — fatal, let them propagate.
  • "Unhandled" errors from a bare subscribe() go to Hooks.onErrorDropped and are just logged — always pass an error consumer.

docs.title: Filtering
docs.text:
Flux<Integer> n = Flux.just(1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 1);
StepVerifier.create(n.filter(i -> i % 2 == 0)).expectNext(2, 2, 4).verifyComplete();
StepVerifier.create(n.distinct()).expectNext(1, 2, 3, 4).verifyComplete();
StepVerifier.create(n.distinctUntilChanged()).expectNext(1, 2, 3, 4, 1).verifyComplete();
StepVerifier.create(n.take(3)).expectNext(1, 2, 2).verifyComplete();          // then cancels upstream
StepVerifier.create(n.skip(6)).expectNext(4, 1).verifyComplete();
StepVerifier.create(n.takeWhile(i -> i < 3)).expectNext(1, 2, 2).verifyComplete();
StepVerifier.create(n.skipUntil(i -> i == 4)).expectNext(4, 1).verifyComplete();
StepVerifier.create(n.next()).expectNext(1).verifyComplete();                   // Flux → Mono (first)
StepVerifier.create(n.last()).expectNext(1).verifyComplete();
StepVerifier.create(n.elementAt(6)).expectNext(4).verifyComplete();
Operator Notes filter(predicate) synchronous predicate filterWhen(t -> Mono<Boolean>) asynchronous predicate (e.g. a lookup) distinct() / distinctUntilChanged() distinct keeps a set of everything seen — unbounded on infinite streams! take(n) / takeWhile / takeUntil / take(Duration) cancels upstream once satisfied skip(n) / skipWhile / skipUntil next() / last() / elementAt(i) / single() Flux → Mono ignoreElements() / then() keep only the completion signal

docs.title: Asynchronous predicates
docs.text:
// keep only usernames that are NOT taken — the check itself is asynchronous
Flux<String> candidates = Flux.just("ann", "bob", "cy");
Flux<String> available = candidates.filterWhen(name -> isTaken(name).map(taken -> !taken));
StepVerifier.create(available).expectNext("ann", "cy").verifyComplete();

docs.title: Dealing with empty
docs.text:
An empty Mono is not an error — it is absence. Decide explicitly what absence means:

Mono<String> missing = Mono.empty();
StepVerifier.create(missing.defaultIfEmpty("guest")).expectNext("guest").verifyComplete();
StepVerifier.create(missing.switchIfEmpty(Mono.fromSupplier(() -> "loaded lazily")))
        .expectNext("loaded lazily").verifyComplete();
StepVerifier.create(missing.switchIfEmpty(Mono.error(new IllegalArgumentException("not found"))))
        .verifyError(IllegalArgumentException.class);
StepVerifier.create(Flux.empty().hasElements()).expectNext(false).verifyComplete();

switchIfEmpty argument is evaluated eagerly

switchIfEmpty(loadFromDb()) calls loadFromDb() at assembly time even when the source is not empty (the returned publisher just isn't subscribed). Wrap expensive construction in Mono.defer(() -> loadFromDb()).

docs.title: Hot vs Cold & Sinks
Turning cold into hot
Sinks — emitting from imperative code
docs.text:
Sinks are the safe, spec-compliant way to push values into a reactive stream from callbacks, controllers, listeners or schedulers (they replace the deprecated Processors).

Factory Subscribers Late subscriber gets Sinks.one() many the single value Sinks.empty() many completion only Sinks.many().unicast() exactly one buffered elements Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer() many elements after it joined (buffers until the first subscriber) Sinks.many().multicast().directBestEffort() many elements after it joined; slow subscribers miss items Sinks.many().replay().all() / limit(n) / limit(Duration) many history multicastreplayone 
// Programmatic hot source: emit from imperative code (listeners, controllers, schedulers)
Sinks.Many<String> sink = Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer();
Flux<String> events = sink.asFlux();

StepVerifier.create(events.take(2))
        .then(() -> sink.tryEmitNext("price-changed"))
        .expectNext("price-changed")
        .then(() -> sink.tryEmitNext("stock-low"))
        .expectNext("stock-low")
        .verifyComplete();

Sinks.Many<Integer> sink = Sinks.many().replay().limit(2);  // late subscribers get the last 2
sink.tryEmitNext(1);
sink.tryEmitNext(2);
sink.tryEmitNext(3);
StepVerifier.create(sink.asFlux().take(2)).expectNext(2, 3).verifyComplete();

Sinks.One<String> reply = Sinks.one();   // a promise you complete later, e.g. from a callback
Mono<String> response = reply.asMono();
reply.tryEmitValue("pong");
StepVerifier.create(response).expectNext("pong").verifyComplete();

docs.title: Emission results are not exceptions
docs.text:
Sinks.Many<String> unicast = Sinks.many().unicast().onBackpressureBuffer();
assertThat(unicast.tryEmitNext("a")).isEqualTo(Sinks.EmitResult.OK);
unicast.tryEmitComplete();
assertThat(unicast.tryEmitNext("b")).isEqualTo(Sinks.EmitResult.FAIL_TERMINATED);  // not thrown!

Concurrent emitters

Sinks reject concurrent tryEmitNext calls with FAIL_NON_SERIALIZED. If several threads emit, use emitNext(value, Sinks.EmitFailureHandler.busyLooping(Duration.ofMillis(50))), or serialise the emitters.

docs.title: Mono & Flux
Assembly time vs subscription time
docs.text:
Writing Flux.just(1,2,3).map(...) assembles a pipeline — a description. Nothing executes until something subscribes. In WebFlux, the framework subscribes for you when it writes the response.

AtomicInteger calls = new AtomicInteger();
Mono<Integer> lazy = Mono.fromCallable(calls::incrementAndGet); // assembly: just a recipe

assertThat(calls).hasValue(0);           // nothing ran yet
lazy.block();                            // subscription triggers execution
lazy.block();                            // ...every time (cold publisher)
assertThat(calls).hasValue(2);

The #1 beginner bug: nobody subscribed

public Mono<Void> delete(String id) {
    repository.deleteById(id);          // ❌ returned Mono is dropped → nothing is deleted
    return Mono.empty();
}
public Mono<Void> delete(String id) {
    return repository.deleteById(id);   // ✅ framework subscribes to what you return
}

docs.title: Cold by default
docs.text: Each subscription re-executes the pipeline from the source (a new HTTP call, a new query). That is usually what you want; when it is not, see Hot vs Cold & Sinks.

docs.title: Converting between them
docs.text: From → To Operator Flux → Mono<List> collectList(), collectMap(), collectMultimap() Flux → Mono (one element) next(), last(), elementAt(i), single() Flux → Mono (aggregate) reduce(), count(), hasElements(), all(), any() Flux → Mono<Void> then() Mono → Flux flux(), flatMapMany(), thenMany()

docs.title: Subscribing
docs.text:
flux.subscribe();                                       // fire and forget (rarely correct in a server)
flux.subscribe(v -> log.info("{}", v));                 // onNext
flux.subscribe(v -> {}, err -> log.error("", err));     // + onError — ALWAYS handle errors
flux.subscribe(v -> {}, err -> {}, () -> log.info("done"));
Disposable d = flux.subscribe(); d.dispose();           // cancel

block() belongs in tests, main methods and batch jobs — never on an event loop

Calling block()/blockFirst()/blockLast() inside a WebFlux handler freezes a Netty thread and Reactor throws IllegalStateException: block()/blockFirst()/blockLast() are blocking, which is not supported in thread reactor-http-nio-*.

docs.title: Operator Cheat Sheet
docs.text: "I have … and I want …" — pick the operator.

docs.title: Create
docs.text: I want to … Use emit values I already have just, fromIterable, range call something lazily, per subscriber fromCallable, defer adapt a CompletableFuture Mono.fromFuture(() -> cf) adapt a callback/listener API Flux.create, Flux.push generate from state Flux.generate emit from imperative code Sinks.one(), Sinks.many() tick periodically Flux.interval, Mono.delay

docs.title: Transform
docs.text: I want to … Use change each value synchronously map call an async API per value (fast, unordered) flatMap(f, concurrency) … preserving order, one at a time concatMap … preserving order, concurrently flatMapSequential … keeping only the latest switchMap map and filter at once handle get a List / Map collectList, collectMap, collectMultimap fold / running total reduce / scan walk a tree / pagination expand, expandDeep reuse a chain transform, transformDeferred

docs.title: Filter
docs.text: I want to … Use keep matching filter, filterWhen the first N / until a condition take, takeWhile, takeUntil, takeUntilOther skip skip, skipWhile, skipUntil unique distinct, distinctUntilChanged a default when empty defaultIfEmpty, switchIfEmpty(Mono.defer(...))

docs.title: Combine
docs.text: I want to … Use all results together Mono.zip, zipWith, zipWhen everything as it arrives merge, flatMap sources one after another concat, concatWith the fastest firstWithValue latest of each on any change combineLatest wait for completion of several Mono.when, then

docs.title: Errors & time
docs.text: I want to … Use default value / fallback publisher onErrorReturn / onErrorResume translate an exception onErrorMap retry transient failures retryWhen(Retry.backoff(n, d).jitter(0.5).filter(...)) a deadline timeout(d) / timeout(d, fallback) delay / pace delayElements, delaySubscription, sample, limitRate measure latency elapsed, timed

docs.title: Threads, sharing, side effects
docs.text: I want to … Use run blocking code fromCallable(...).subscribeOn(boundedElastic()) continue on another thread publishOn compute once, share result cache multicast a live stream share, publish().autoConnect() log / metrics / side effects doOnNext, doOnError, doFinally, log, tap pass request-scoped data contextWrite, deferContextual

docs.title: Cancellation is a first-class signal
docs.text:
When a client disconnects, take(n) is satisfied, a timeout fires or switchMap moves on, Reactor sends cancel upstream. Well-behaved sources stop work and release resources.

List<String> log = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();
Disposable subscription = Flux.interval(java.time.Duration.ofMillis(5))
        .doOnCancel(() -> log.add("cancelled"))
        .subscribe();
subscription.dispose();       // e.g. client disconnected → stop the upstream work
assertThat(log).containsExactly("cancelled");
assertThat(subscription.isDisposed()).isTrue();

docs.title: using and usingWhen
docs.text:
The reactive try-with-resources. usingWhen supports asynchronous acquire and cleanup with separate commit/rollback/cancel paths — exactly how reactive transactions are implemented.

List<String> log = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();
Flux<String> rows = Flux.usingWhen(
        Mono.fromSupplier(() -> { log.add("open"); return "conn"; }),          // acquire
        conn -> Flux.just("row1", "row2"),                                        // use
        conn -> Mono.fromRunnable(() -> log.add("commit")),                       // on complete
        (conn, err) -> Mono.fromRunnable(() -> log.add("rollback")),              // on error
        conn -> Mono.fromRunnable(() -> log.add("rollback-cancel")));             // on cancel

StepVerifier.create(rows).expectNext("row1", "row2").verifyComplete();
assertThat(log).containsExactly("open", "commit");

docs.title: Cleanup hooks
docs.text:
Hook Runs on doFinally(signalType -> ...) complete, error or cancel — after the signal propagated doOnCancel(...) cancel only doOnTerminate(...) / doAfterTerminate(...) complete or error FluxSink.onDispose(...) in Flux.create any termination of the sink

Server-side effect of cancellation

In WebFlux, an SSE client closing its browser tab cancels the response Flux, which cancels the Flux.interval, the database tailable cursor, the Kafka-backed sink subscription… all the way up. Long-running work started with a detached subscribe() does not get that cancellation — track its Disposable and dispose it yourself (the capstone's delivery-service does this on shutdown).

docs.title: Schedulers & Threading
docs.text: Reactor is concurrency-agnostic: by default everything runs on the thread that called subscribe (or the thread that emitted the signal — e.g. a Netty event loop). Schedulers let you move work.

docs.title: Built-in schedulers
docs.text: Scheduler Threads Use for Schedulers.immediate() current thread no-op Schedulers.single() 1 reusable thread low-latency one-off tasks Schedulers.parallel() N = CPU cores CPU-bound work, timers (interval, delay) Schedulers.boundedElastic() grows to 10 × cores, queues 100k tasks, idle threads evicted blocking I/O you cannot avoid Schedulers.fromExecutorService(e) yours custom pools, virtual threads

docs.title: publishOn vs subscribeOn
Wrapping blocking calls
docs.text:
The single most important scheduler pattern:

/** The canonical way to call a blocking API (JDBC, legacy SDK, file I/O) from reactive code. */
static Mono<String> legacyLookup(String key) {
    return Mono.fromCallable(() -> BlockingLegacyClient.get(key))   // lazy: runs on subscribe
            .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic());              // never on the event loop
}

Never block an event-loop thread

Thread.sleep, JDBC, InputStream.read, future.get(), block() on a reactor-http-nio-* thread stalls every connection on that loop. Detect it in tests with BlockHound.

docs.title: Virtual threads
docs.text:
// Java 21+: a scheduler backed by virtual threads — cheap to block on, unbounded in count
try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    Scheduler virtual = Schedulers.fromExecutorService(executor, "virtual");
    String thread = Mono.fromCallable(() -> Thread.currentThread().isVirtual() ? "virtual" : "platform")
            .subscribeOn(virtual)
            .block();
    assertThat(thread).isEqualTo("virtual");
}
// -Dreactor.schedulers.defaultBoundedElasticOnVirtualThreads=true makes boundedElastic() virtual too

docs.title: Parallel processing of CPU work
docs.text:
// CPU-bound work split across 'rails' (one per core by default)
Mono<Long> sumOfSquares = Flux.range(1, 1_000)
        .parallel()
        .runOn(Schedulers.parallel())
        .map(i -> (long) i * i)
        .reduce(Long::sum);
StepVerifier.create(sumOfSquares).expectNext(333_833_500L).verifyComplete();

flatMap gives concurrency (many async calls in flight); parallel().runOn() gives parallelism (CPU work on several cores). For I/O, you almost always want flatMap.

docs.title: Time Operators
docs.text: Time-based operators schedule work on Schedulers.parallel() by default, so they are fully non-blocking — and testable instantly with virtual time.

docs.title: Delaying
docs.text:
StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> Flux.just("a", "b", "c").delayElements(Duration.ofSeconds(1)))
        .expectSubscription()
        .expectNoEvent(Duration.ofSeconds(1)).expectNext("a")   // one element per second
        .expectNoEvent(Duration.ofSeconds(1)).expectNext("b")
        .thenAwait(Duration.ofSeconds(1)).expectNext("c")
        .verifyComplete();

StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> Mono.just("x").delaySubscription(Duration.ofSeconds(5)))
        .expectSubscription()
        .expectNoEvent(Duration.ofSeconds(5))                   // the source isn't even subscribed yet
        .expectNext("x")
        .verifyComplete();
Operator Delays delayElements(d) every element (and spaces them out) Mono.delayElement(d) the single value delaySubscription(d) / delaySubscription(publisher) the subscription itself — the source starts later delaySequence(d) shifts the whole sequence, keeping the gaps between elements Mono.delay(d) emits 0L after d — a non-blocking sleep

docs.title: Sampling and throttling
docs.text:
// a value every 150ms; keep only the latest one per second (e.g. a UI update rate)
StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> Flux.interval(Duration.ofMillis(150)).take(18)
                .sample(Duration.ofSeconds(1)))
        .thenAwait(Duration.ofSeconds(3))
        .expectNext(5L, 12L, 17L)          // latest value at t=1s, t=2s, then the final value
        .verifyComplete();

// sampleFirst: take the first value, then ignore the rest of the window (throttle / debounce-click)
StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> Flux.interval(Duration.ofMillis(150)).take(18)
                .sampleFirst(Duration.ofSeconds(1)))
        .thenAwait(Duration.ofSeconds(3))
        .expectNext(0L, 7L, 14L)           // emitted at 150ms, 1200ms, 2250ms
        .verifyComplete();
Operator Keeps sample(d) the latest value per period sampleFirst(d) the first value, then ignores the rest of the period (click throttling) sampleTimeout(v -> Mono.delay(d)) a value only if no newer value arrives within d (debounce, type-ahead)

docs.title: Measuring
docs.text:
StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> Mono.just("result").delayElement(Duration.ofMillis(250)).elapsed())
        .thenAwait(Duration.ofSeconds(1))
        .assertNext(t -> {
            assertThat(t.getT1()).isEqualTo(250L);              // milliseconds since subscription
            assertThat(t.getT2()).isEqualTo("result");
        })
        .verifyComplete();

timed() gives richer info (elapsed(), elapsedSinceSubscription(), timestamp()) per element.

docs.title: Polling and repeating
docs.text:
// poll a job status every 2s until it is DONE (max 10 polls)
java.util.Iterator<String> statuses = java.util.List.of("PENDING", "RUNNING", "DONE").iterator();
Mono<String> poll = Mono.fromSupplier(statuses::next);

StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> poll
                .repeatWhen(done -> done.delayElements(Duration.ofSeconds(2)).take(10))
                .takeUntil("DONE"::equals)
                .last())
        .thenAwait(Duration.ofSeconds(10))
        .expectNext("DONE")
        .verifyComplete();

repeat resubscribes after completion; retry resubscribes after error. repeatWhenEmpty keeps polling until a value arrives.

docs.title: Time windows
docs.text:
// events per second (a rolling counter)
StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> Flux.interval(Duration.ofMillis(300)).take(8)
                .window(Duration.ofSeconds(1))
                .concatMap(Flux::count))
        .thenAwait(Duration.ofSeconds(3))
        .expectNext(3L, 3L, 2L)            // events at 300..900 | 1200..1800 | 2100..2400
        .verifyComplete();

docs.title: Timeouts
docs.text: See Error Handling → Timeouts. Remember: timeout cancels the upstream when it fires, so make sure cancellation actually releases the resource.

docs.title: map — synchronous 1:1
docs.text:
StepVerifier.create(Flux.just("a", "b").map(String::toUpperCase))
        .expectNext("A", "B")
        .verifyComplete();

Use map for pure, fast, non-blocking functions. If the function returns a Mono/Flux, you want one of the flatMap family.

docs.title: The async family: flatMap, concatMap, flatMapSequential, switchMap
docs.text:
All four take T -> Publisher<R>. They differ in concurrency and ordering:

Operator Inner subscriptions Output order Use when flatMap concurrent (default 256) completion order (interleaved) independent async calls, max throughput concatMap one at a time source order order matters, or each step depends on the previous flatMapSequential concurrent source order (buffers early results) throughput and order switchMap only the latest; previous cancelled latest only type-ahead search, "latest value wins"

Each example below looks up users with simulated latency (id 1 = 30 ms, 2 = 20 ms, 3 = 10 ms):

flatMapconcatMapflatMapSequentialswitchMap 
// ids 1..3 have latencies 30ms, 20ms, 10ms: flatMap subscribes to all at once → completion order
StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> Flux.just(1, 2, 3).flatMap(TransformingOperatorsTest::fetchUser))
        .thenAwait(Duration.ofSeconds(1))
        .expectNext("user-3", "user-2", "user-1")
        .verifyComplete();

StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> Flux.just(1, 2, 3).concatMap(TransformingOperatorsTest::fetchUser))
        .thenAwait(Duration.ofSeconds(1))
        .expectNext("user-1", "user-2", "user-3")   // sequential: total ≈ 60ms
        .verifyComplete();

StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> Flux.just(1, 2, 3).flatMapSequential(TransformingOperatorsTest::fetchUser))
        .thenAwait(Duration.ofSeconds(1))
        .expectNext("user-1", "user-2", "user-3")   // concurrent: total ≈ 30ms, results re-ordered
        .verifyComplete();

// type-ahead search: each new query cancels the in-flight search for the previous one
Flux<String> queries = Flux.just("r", "re", "rea")
        .delayElements(Duration.ofMillis(100));          // a keystroke every 100ms
Flux<String> results = queries.switchMap(q ->
        Mono.just("results for " + q).delayElement(Duration.ofMillis(250))); // search takes 250ms

StepVerifier.create(results).expectNext("results for rea").verifyComplete();
// (tests that depend on timing should use StepVerifier.withVirtualTime — see Testing chapter)

Bound your concurrency

flatMap subscribes to up to 256 inner publishers at once. Calling a downstream service for every element of a 10,000-element Flux can open hundreds of connections. Pass a concurrency argument:

Flux<String> bounded = Flux.range(1, 100)
        .flatMap(TransformingOperatorsTest::callSlowService, 8); // at most 8 in flight
StepVerifier.create(bounded.count()).expectNext(100L).verifyComplete();

docs.title: handle — map + filter in one step
docs.text:
Flux<Integer> parsed = Flux.just("1", "x", "3").handle((s, sink) -> {
    try {
        sink.next(Integer.parseInt(s));
    } catch (NumberFormatException ignored) {
        // emit nothing → element dropped
    }
});
StepVerifier.create(parsed).expectNext(1, 3).verifyComplete();

docs.title: Aggregation: collectList, reduce, scan, count, collectMultimap
docs.text:
Flux<Integer> numbers = Flux.range(1, 5);
StepVerifier.create(numbers.collectList()).expectNext(List.of(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)).verifyComplete();
StepVerifier.create(numbers.reduce(0, Integer::sum)).expectNext(15).verifyComplete();
StepVerifier.create(numbers.scan(0, Integer::sum)).expectNext(0, 1, 3, 6, 10, 15).verifyComplete();
StepVerifier.create(numbers.count()).expectNext(5L).verifyComplete();
StepVerifier.create(Flux.just("apple", "avocado", "banana").collectMultimap(s -> s.charAt(0)))
        .expectNext(Map.of('a', List.of("apple", "avocado"), 'b', List.of("banana")))
        .verifyComplete();

Caution

collectList() holds the whole stream in memory. Fine for a page of results, dangerous for an unbounded stream. Prefer streaming the Flux to the client.

docs.title: expand — recursive traversal
docs.text:
// breadth-first walk of a tree, e.g. following "next page" links or category children
Map<String, List<String>> tree = Map.of("root", List.of("a", "b"), "a", List.of("a1"), "b", List.of());
Flux<String> all = Mono.just("root")
        .expand(node -> Flux.fromIterable(tree.getOrDefault(node, List.of())));
StepVerifier.create(all).expectNext("root", "a", "b", "a1").verifyComplete();

docs.title: transform — reuse operator chains
docs.text:
java.util.function.Function<Flux<String>, Flux<String>> sanitize =
        f -> f.map(String::trim).filter(s -> !s.isEmpty()).map(String::toLowerCase);

StepVerifier.create(Flux.just(" Foo ", "  ", "BAR").transform(sanitize))
        .expectNext("foo", "bar")
        .verifyComplete();

transform applies at assembly time; transformDeferred re-applies per subscriber (useful when the chain depends on Context).

docs.title: Resilience & Observability
docs.text:
Distributed reactive systems fail partially: a dependency gets slow, a broker rebalances, a pod is evicted. These pages cover how to contain failures and how to see what is happening.

Page Topics Resilience Patterns timeouts, retries with jitter, circuit breaker, bulkhead, rate limiter, fallbacks, hedging Observability Micrometer metrics & observations, tracing, context propagation, logging/MDC, Actuator

docs.text:

implementation("io.micrometer:micrometer-registry-prometheus")

docs.text:
Mono<Quote> quote = pricingClient.quote(id)
        .name("pricing.quote")              // metric/observation name
        .tag("source", "pricing-service")
        .tap(Micrometer.observation(observationRegistry));   // timer + span for this Mono

docs.title: Tracing and context propagation
docs.text:
Each request hops threads, so ThreadLocal-based tracing and MDC need help. Boot wires Micrometer's context-propagation library into Reactor:

spring:
  reactor:
    context-propagation: auto       # Hooks.enableAutomaticContextPropagation()
management:
  tracing:
    sampling:
      probability: 1.0              # sample everything in dev; lower in production
  otlp:
    tracing:
      endpoint: http://otel-collector:4318/v1/traces

With that, traceId/spanId are restored into the MDC around every operator, so plain log.info(...) inside map/flatMap prints the right trace id, and WebClient/Kafka calls carry the traceparent header automatically.

logging:
  pattern:
    correlation: "[${spring.application.name:},%X{traceId:-},%X{spanId:-}] "

docs.title: Health
docs.text:
management:
  endpoint:
    health:
      probes:
        enabled: true          # /actuator/health/liveness and /readiness for Kubernetes
      show-details: when-authorized

Reactive health indicators (ReactiveHealthIndicator) exist for R2DBC, Mongo, Redis — they never block the event loop.

docs.title: What to put on the dashboard
docs.text:
• request rate, error rate, p95/p99 latency per route (RED)
  • event-loop saturation: pending tasks, reactor.netty.eventloop.pending.tasks
  • pool usage: R2DBC pending acquisitions, WebClient connection pool pending
  • boundedElastic active/queued tasks — growth means blocking work piling up
  • Kafka consumer lag, circuit breaker states

docs.title: The layered defence
docs.text:
flowchart LR C[call] --> T[timeout<br/>per attempt] --> R[retry<br/>backoff + jitter] --> CB[circuit breaker] --> B[bulkhead<br/>max concurrency] --> F[fallback] Pattern Reactor / library Prevents Timeout timeout(Duration) threads/connections waiting forever Retry retryWhen(Retry.backoff(...).jitter(0.5).filter(...)) failing on transient blips Circuit breaker Resilience4j CircuitBreakerOperator / Spring Cloud ReactiveCircuitBreaker hammering a dead dependency Bulkhead flatMap(f, maxConcurrency), Resilience4j BulkheadOperator one dependency exhausting all capacity Rate limiter Resilience4j RateLimiterOperator, gateway RequestRateLimiter overload Fallback onErrorResume, timeout(d, fallback) user-visible failure Hedging Mono.firstWithValue(primary, delayedSecondary) tail latency

Timeouts and retries are covered in Error Handling.

docs.title: Circuit breaker with Resilience4j (plain library)
docs.text:
implementation("io.github.resilience4j:resilience4j-reactor:2.4.0")
implementation("io.github.resilience4j:resilience4j-circuitbreaker:2.4.0")

CircuitBreaker breaker = CircuitBreaker.of("inventory", CircuitBreakerConfig.custom()
        .slidingWindowSize(20)
        .failureRateThreshold(50)                       // open at ≥ 50% failures…
        .slowCallDurationThreshold(Duration.ofSeconds(1))
        .slowCallRateThreshold(80)                      // …or ≥ 80% slow calls
        .waitDurationInOpenState(Duration.ofSeconds(10))
        .permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState(3)
        .build());

Mono<Stock> stock = inventoryClient.stock(id)
        .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2))
        .transformDeferred(CircuitBreakerOperator.of(breaker))   // per-subscription state check
        .onErrorResume(CallNotPermittedException.class, e -> Mono.just(Stock.unknown(id)));
stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> Closed Closed --> Open: failure rate ≥ threshold Open --> HalfOpen: wait duration elapsed HalfOpen --> Closed: trial calls succeed HalfOpen --> Open: trial calls fail

    return factory -> factory.configureDefault(id -> new Resilience4JConfigBuilder(id)
            .circuitBreakerConfig(CircuitBreakerConfig.ofDefaults())

// usage
ReactiveCircuitBreaker cb = factory.create("inventory");
Mono<Stock> guarded = cb.run(inventoryClient.stock(id), error -> Mono.just(Stock.unknown(id)));

docs.title: Idempotency makes retries safe
docs.text:
Retries and at-least-once messaging produce duplicates. Make writes idempotent:

  • client sends an Idempotency-Key; the server stores it with a unique constraint and returns the original result on replay;
  • consumers upsert by business key or record processed event ids.

docs.title: Checklist per downstream dependency
docs.text:
• connect + response timeouts at the HTTP client, plus an operator timeout
  • retries only for transient errors and idempotent operations, with backoff + jitter, bounded
  • circuit breaker with a sensible fallback (cached value, degraded response, clear 503)
  • concurrency limit (flatMap concurrency or bulkhead)
  • metrics: latency, error rate, breaker state

docs.title: Career Roadmap: 0 → 15+ Years
docs.text:
A five-level roadmap for growing from your first Mono to architecting reactive platforms. Each level lists what to master, which pages to study, hands-on exercises, a checkpoint, and the matching interview questions.

timeline title Spring Reactive mastery 0–2 years : Level 1 Foundation : Mono/Flux, core operators, WebFlux CRUD, StepVerifier 2–5 years : Level 2 Practitioner : schedulers, error handling, WebClient, R2DBC, security, SSE 5–8 years : Level 3 Senior : backpressure, Context, Kafka, resilience, observability, performance 8–12 years : Level 4 Lead : service design, migration strategy, internals, platform standards 12–15+ years: Level 5 Architect : reactive systems, trade-offs, org-wide strategy, mentoring Level Experience You can… Roadmap Interview set 1 · Foundation 0–2 years build and test a reactive CRUD API Level 1 Beginner 2 · Practitioner 2–5 years integrate databases, services and security without blocking Level 2 Intermediate 3 · Senior 5–8 years run event-driven reactive services in production Level 3 Senior 4 · Lead 8–12 years design multi-service reactive solutions and lead teams through them Level 4 Lead 5 · Architect 12–15+ years set platform-wide direction: when (not) to go reactive, and how Level 5 Architect

Years are a guide, not a gate

Experience bands describe typical scope and depth. Someone with 3 years who has run reactive services in production may be at Level 3; a 10-year veteran new to reactive should start at Level 1 — and will move fast.

There is also a compact quick learning path if you only want the reading order.

docs.title: Level 1 · Foundation (0–2 years)
docs.text: Goal: think in streams, and write and test simple reactive endpoints without blocking.

docs.title: Master these
docs.text:
• Why reactive exists; event loop vs thread-per-request — Why Reactive?
  • Reactive Streams signals: onSubscribe, onNext, onError, onComplete, request(n) — Spec
  • Mono vs Flux; nothing happens until subscribe — Mono & Flux
  • Creating: just, empty, error, fromIterable, range, fromCallable, defer — Creating
  • map vs flatMap; filter; defaultIfEmpty/switchIfEmpty — Transforming, Filtering
  • zip, then, collectList — Combining
  • Basic errors: onErrorReturn, onErrorResume, onErrorMap — Error Handling
  • Annotated controllers returning Mono/Flux — Annotated Controllers
  • StepVerifier basics and WebTestClient — StepVerifier, WebTestClient

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. Run ./gradlew :playbook-examples:test. Break one expectation in TransformingOperatorsTest and read the failure.
  2. Build a /books CRUD API with an in-memory reactive repository (copy the shape of ProductController). Return 404 via switchIfEmpty(Mono.error(...)) + @RestControllerAdvice.
  3. Write StepVerifier tests for every endpoint method and WebTestClient tests for the HTTP layer.
  4. Add .log() to a pipeline and explain each line of output to a colleague.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text: You can explain, without notes: why Mono.just(callDb()) is a bug, why the returned Mono must be returned, and when to use flatMap instead of map.

docs.title: Typical mistakes at this level
docs.text: • calling block() inside a controller · forgetting to return a Mono · subscribe() inside map · testing with Thread.sleep instead of virtual time.

docs.title: Level 2 · Practitioner (2–5 years)
docs.text: Goal: build complete services: data access, downstream calls, security, streaming — all non-blocking.

docs.title: Master these
docs.text:
• flatMap vs concatMap vs flatMapSequential vs switchMap; bounded concurrency — Transforming
  • Schedulers: publishOn vs subscribeOn; wrapping blocking calls on boundedElastic — Schedulers
  • Retries with backoff and filters; timeouts — Error Handling, Time Operators
  • Functional endpoints and WebFilter — Functional Endpoints, Filters
  • ProblemDetail error design — Error Handling
  • WebClient and HTTP interface clients — WebClient, HTTP Interface Clients
  • R2DBC repositories, DatabaseClient, reactive transactions — R2DBC, Transactions
  • Reactive MongoDB or Redis — MongoDB, Redis
  • Spring Security for WebFlux, JWT resource server — WebFlux Security, OAuth2 & JWT
  • SSE and WebSocket — Streaming, WebSocket
  • Hot vs cold, cache(), share(), Sinks — Hot vs Cold
  • Integration tests with Testcontainers — Integration Tests

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. Back the /books API with R2DBC/PostgreSQL; add a Testcontainers @ServiceConnection IT.
  2. Add /books/{id}/reviews that aggregates a second service via WebClient with timeout + retry; test with an ExchangeFunction stub.
  3. Secure writes with JWT scopes; test with mockJwt().
  4. Stream new books over SSE using a Sinks.Many; consume it with WebClient in a test.
  5. Solve coding exercises 1–6.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text: You can review a pull request and spot: hidden blocking calls, unbounded flatMap, retried non-idempotent calls, lost errors in detached subscribe()s, and ThreadLocal usage.

docs.title: Level 3 · Senior (5–8 years)
docs.text: Goal: own reactive services in production: event-driven integration, resilience, observability, performance.

docs.title: Master these
docs.text:
• Backpressure strategies and batching; designing for slow consumers — Backpressure & Batching
  • Reactor Context, context propagation, MDC/tracing — Context, Observability
  • Resources and cancellation semantics (usingWhen, Disposable) — Resources
  • Kafka with async listeners, idempotent consumers, outbox — Kafka
  • Spring Cloud Gateway, rate limiting — Gateway
  • Circuit breakers, bulkheads, hedging — Resilience Patterns
  • Performance tuning: event loops, pools, memory, codecs — Performance
  • BlockHound in CI; debugging with checkpoints and the debug agent — BlockHound, Debugging
  • Method security, OAuth2 client token relay — Method Security
  • Scheduling and lifecycle of background streams — Scheduling & Lifecycle
  • Streaming AI responses, GraphQL subscriptions — AI Streaming, GraphQL

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. Trace one order through the Food Delivery App; set PAYMENT_FAILURE_RATE=0.8 and explain every log line until the breaker opens.
  2. Add an outbox table to order-service and relay it with a poller (@Scheduled returning Mono).
  3. Make SSE fan-out work across two instances (Kafka group per instance or Redis pub/sub).
  4. Load test an endpoint with k6; find the bottleneck using metrics only.
  5. Solve coding exercises 7–10.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text: You can explain a production incident in reactive terms (who requested what, where the signal stopped, which pool was exhausted) and design the fix.

docs.title: Level 4 · Lead (8–12 years)
docs.text: Goal: design multi-service reactive solutions, set team standards, and lead migrations.

docs.title: Master these
docs.text:
• Reactor internals: assembly/subscription/execution, fusion, prefetch, custom operators — Advanced Internals
  • Choosing models per service: WebFlux vs MVC + virtual threads vs coroutines — Reactive vs Virtual Threads, Kotlin
  • Migration strategy from MVC — Migrating from MVC
  • Event-driven design: contracts, versioning, ordering, idempotency, sagas — Kafka, Cloud Stream
  • Ports & adapters to keep domain logic free of Reactor — Order Service
  • Testing strategy across levels (unit, slice, IT, contract) — Testing
  • Deployment: Kubernetes sizing for Netty, native images — Deployment
  • Interop: RxJava/Mutiny/Flow, ReactiveAdapterRegistry
  • Code-review checklists and coding standards — Best Practices

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. Write your team's reactive coding standard (one page) based on Best Practices.
  2. Produce an ADR: "WebFlux or MVC + virtual threads for service X", with measurements.
  3. Design order cancellation for the capstone: cancel the courier simulation (Disposable), refund the payment (idempotent), publish OrderCancelled, and handle races with delivery events.
  4. Run a brown-bag session teaching flatMap vs concatMap using the tested examples.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text: You can design a reactive service end to end, defend its trade-offs to non-reactive peers, and grow Level 1–3 engineers.

docs.title: Level 5 · Architect (12–15+ years)
docs.text: Goal: shape platform-wide architecture: reactive systems (not just reactive code), organisational adoption, and long-term cost of ownership.

docs.title: Master these
docs.text:
• Reactive Manifesto as an architecture review lens — Reactive Manifesto
  • Where reactive belongs in a platform: edge, BFF, streaming, event processing — and where it doesn't
  • End-to-end flow control: TCP, HTTP/2, RSocket, Kafka consumer pacing, client backpressure — Backpressure, RSocket
  • Consistency across services: outbox, CDC, sagas, idempotency keys, exactly-once myths
  • Multi-region / failure-domain design: timeouts budgets, hedging, load shedding, graceful degradation
  • Observability as architecture: SLOs, tracing across async boundaries, cardinality budgets
  • Cost: CPU vs memory efficiency, native images, scale-to-zero, team cognitive load
  • Technology radar: virtual threads, structured concurrency, Reactor and Spring release roadmaps, Kotlin coroutines

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. Review the Food Delivery App as an architect: list the top 5 risks and the hardening plan in priority order with effort estimates.
  2. Design live courier tracking for 1M concurrent viewers across 3 regions (see System Design questions).
  3. Write the organisation's "reactive adoption guide": decision tree, golden paths, templates, training plan.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text: You can state, with evidence, when reactive is the right tool for a platform — and when it is an expensive mistake — and you can make teams successful with either choice.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Spring Security has a complete reactive implementation: a WebFilter chain, reactive authentication managers, and a security context stored in the Reactor Context (no ThreadLocal).

Page Topics WebFlux Security SecurityWebFilterChain, users, password encoding, reading the principal OAuth2 & JWT resource server, JWT validation, scopes → authorities, token relay with WebClient Method Security @EnableReactiveMethodSecurity, @PreAuthorize on Mono/Flux methods

docs.title: Method Security
docs.text:
@Configuration
@EnableReactiveMethodSecurity
class MethodSecurityConfig { }

@Service
class ProductAdminService {

    @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")
    public Mono<Void> delete(String id) { ... }

    @PreAuthorize("#ownerId == authentication.name")
    public Flux<Product> myProducts(String ownerId) { ... }

    @PostAuthorize("returnObject.ownerId == authentication.name")
    public Mono<Product> get(String id) { ... }
}

Methods must return a Publisher (Mono/Flux) or be Kotlin suspend functions: the check is evaluated when the result is subscribed, using the security context from the Reactor Context. A denied call produces an AccessDeniedException signal → 403.

@PreFilter/@PostFilter work on Flux arguments/results element by element.

Tip

Keep URL rules for coarse access (authenticated? which scope?) and method security for domain rules (ownership, tenant). Both can coexist.

docs.title: Resource server
docs.text:
implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server")

spring:
  security:
    oauth2:
      resourceserver:
        jwt:
          issuer-uri: https://auth.example.com/realms/shop   # Keycloak, Cognito, Auth0, Okta…
          audiences: [catalog-api]

@Bean
SecurityWebFilterChain api(ServerHttpSecurity http) {
    return http
            .authorizeExchange(a -> a
                    .pathMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/products/**").hasAuthority("SCOPE_catalog.read")
                    .anyExchange().authenticated())
            .oauth2ResourceServer(rs -> rs.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()))
            .csrf(ServerHttpSecurity.CsrfSpec::disable)
            .build();
}

Boot builds a NimbusReactiveJwtDecoder that fetches the issuer's JWKS (cached), validates signature, exp/nbf, issuer and audience. Scopes become SCOPE_* authorities.

docs.title: Mapping roles from custom claims
docs.text:
@Bean
ReactiveJwtAuthenticationConverterAdapter jwtConverter() {
    JwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter roles = new JwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter();
    roles.setAuthoritiesClaimName("roles");
    roles.setAuthorityPrefix("ROLE_");
    JwtAuthenticationConverter converter = new JwtAuthenticationConverter();
    converter.setJwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter(roles);
    return new ReactiveJwtAuthenticationConverterAdapter(converter);
}
// .oauth2ResourceServer(rs -> rs.jwt(jwt -> jwt.jwtAuthenticationConverter(jwtConverter())))

docs.title: Symmetric keys (local development)
docs.text:
@Bean
ReactiveJwtDecoder jwtDecoder(@Value("${app.jwt.secret}") String secret) {
    SecretKey key = new SecretKeySpec(secret.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8), "HmacSHA256");
    return NimbusReactiveJwtDecoder.withSecretKey(key).macAlgorithm(MacAlgorithm.HS256).build();
}

docs.title: Tokens in query strings
docs.text:
Browsers can't send headers with EventSource or WebSocket. Allow ?access_token= explicitly — and only on those routes if possible (query strings end up in logs):

var bearer = new ServerBearerTokenAuthenticationConverter();
bearer.setAllowUriQueryParameter(true);
http.oauth2ResourceServer(rs -> rs.bearerTokenConverter(bearer).jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()));

docs.title: OAuth2 client: calling other services with a token
docs.text:
implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-oauth2-client")

spring:
  security:
    oauth2:
      client:
        registration:
          inventory:
            provider: keycloak
            client-id: catalog-service
            client-secret: ${CLIENT_SECRET}
            authorization-grant-type: client_credentials
        provider:
          keycloak:
            issuer-uri: https://auth.example.com/realms/shop

@Bean
WebClient inventoryClient(WebClient.Builder builder, ReactiveOAuth2AuthorizedClientManager manager) {
    var oauth = new ServerOAuth2AuthorizedClientExchangeFilterFunction(manager);
    oauth.setDefaultClientRegistrationId("inventory");           // fetch + cache + refresh tokens
    return builder.clone().baseUrl("http://inventory:8080").filter(oauth).build();
}

To relay the caller's token instead (token propagation), read it from ReactiveSecurityContextHolder in an ExchangeFilterFunction and set the Authorization header — or let Spring Cloud Gateway's TokenRelay filter do it at the edge.

docs.title: WebFlux Security
docs.text: implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-security")

docs.title: The filter chain
docs.text:
@Configuration
@EnableWebFluxSecurity
class SecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    SecurityWebFilterChain security(ServerHttpSecurity http) {
        return http
                .authorizeExchange(auth -> auth
                        .pathMatchers("/actuator/health/**", "/public/**").permitAll()
                        .pathMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/products/**").permitAll()
                        .pathMatchers("/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")
                        .anyExchange().authenticated())
                .httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults())
                .csrf(ServerHttpSecurity.CsrfSpec::disable)     // only for stateless token APIs!
                .build();
    }

    @Bean
    MapReactiveUserDetailsService users(PasswordEncoder encoder) {
        UserDetails user = User.withUsername("ana").password(encoder.encode("pw")).roles("USER").build();
        UserDetails admin = User.withUsername("root").password(encoder.encode("pw")).roles("ADMIN").build();
        return new MapReactiveUserDetailsService(user, admin);
    }

    @Bean
    PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() {
        return PasswordEncoderFactories.createDelegatingPasswordEncoder();
    }
}

For users in a database, implement ReactiveUserDetailsService with a reactive repository.
