docs.text: Level Tool Needs Docker? Page Publisher logic StepVerifier, TestPublisher, PublisherProbe, virtual time no StepVerifier HTTP layer WebTestClient bound to controllers/routers, @WebFluxTest no WebTestClient Data/messaging @DataR2dbcTest, @DataMongoTest, Testcontainers yes Integration Tests Non-blocking guarantee BlockHound no BlockHound

docs.title: BlockHound
docs.text:
BlockHound is a Java agent that fails fast when blocking calls (Thread.sleep, socket/file I/O, Object.wait, LockSupport.park) run on threads marked non-blocking — Reactor's parallel/single schedulers and Netty event loops.

testImplementation("io.projectreactor.tools:blockhound:1.0.18.RELEASE")

class NoBlockingTest {

    @BeforeAll
    static void install() {
        BlockHound.install();                // once per JVM
    }

    @Test
    void detectsBlockingOnParallelScheduler() {
        Mono<String> bad = Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(1))           // runs on parallel-*
                .map(i -> { sleepQuietly(10); return "x"; });         // ❌ blocking
        StepVerifier.create(bad)
                .expectErrorMatches(e -> e.getMessage().contains("Blocking call!"))
                .verify();
    }
}

On JDK 13+ add -XX:+AllowRedefinitionToAddDeleteMethods to the test JVM:

tasks.test { jvmArgs("-XX:+AllowRedefinitionToAddDeleteMethods") }

docs.title: Allow-listing
docs.text:
Some libraries block briefly and harmlessly during initialisation (class loading, SecureRandom seeding). Allow specific methods instead of disabling the agent:

BlockHound.install(builder -> builder
        .allowBlockingCallsInside("java.util.UUID", "randomUUID"));

Tip

Run BlockHound in CI for your WebFlux integration tests. It turns "the app is mysteriously slow under load" into "this test fails on line 42".

docs.title: Integration Tests
docs.text:
Use real infrastructure in containers for anything involving SQL dialects, Mongo queries, Kafka semantics or serialization across process boundaries.

testImplementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-testcontainers")
testImplementation("org.testcontainers:testcontainers-postgresql")
testImplementation("org.testcontainers:testcontainers-kafka")
testImplementation("org.testcontainers:testcontainers-mongodb")
testImplementation("org.testcontainers:testcontainers-junit-jupiter")

docs.title: @ServiceConnection — zero-config wiring
docs.text:
@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT)
@Testcontainers
class OrderFlowIT {

    @Container @ServiceConnection
    static PostgreSQLContainer postgres = new PostgreSQLContainer("postgres:17-alpine");

    @Container @ServiceConnection
    static KafkaContainer kafka = new KafkaContainer("apache/kafka:4.1.0");

    @Autowired WebTestClient client;   // bound to the running server

    @Test
    void placesOrder() {
        client.post().uri("/api/orders").header("X-User-Id", "it-user")
                .bodyValue(Map.of("restaurantId", 1, "deliveryAddress", "x",
                                  "items", List.of(Map.of("menuItemId", 1, "quantity", 1))))
                .exchange()
                .expectStatus().isCreated();
    }
}

@ServiceConnection produces the matching ConnectionDetails beans, so Boot builds an R2DBC ConnectionFactory (and Kafka/Mongo clients) pointing at the container — no @DynamicPropertySource needed.

docs.title: Data slices
docs.text:
@DataR2dbcTest          // org.springframework.boot.data.r2dbc.test.autoconfigure
@Testcontainers
class ProductRowRepositoryTest {
    @Container @ServiceConnection
    static PostgreSQLContainer postgres = new PostgreSQLContainer("postgres:17-alpine");

    @Autowired ProductRowRepository repository;

    @Test
    void derivedQuery() {
        StepVerifier.create(repository.save(new ProductRow(null, "Pen", "office", 199, Instant.now()))
                        .thenMany(repository.findByCategoryOrderByName("office")))
                .expectNextMatches(p -> p.name().equals("Pen"))
                .verifyComplete();
    }
}

docs.title: Waiting for asynchronous outcomes
docs.text:
Kafka-driven effects happen eventually. Poll reactively instead of sleeping:

StepVerifier.create(Mono.defer(() -> deliveries.findByOrderId(orderId))
                .repeatWhenEmpty(r -> r.delayElements(Duration.ofMillis(200)).take(50)))
        .expectNextMatches(d -> d.courierId() != null)
        .verifyComplete();

(Awaitility works too.)

docs.title: Contract tests
docs.text: For service boundaries, add consumer-driven contracts (Pact, Spring Cloud Contract) so a provider change that breaks a consumer fails the provider's build.

docs.title: StepVerifier
docs.text:
StepVerifier subscribes to a publisher and asserts the exact sequence of signals.

StepVerifier.create(Flux.range(1, 5).map(i -> i * 10))
        .expectNext(10)
        .expectNextMatches(v -> v > 15)
        .assertNext(v -> org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat(v).isEqualTo(30))
        .expectNextCount(2)
        .expectComplete()
        .verify(Duration.ofSeconds(1));     // ALWAYS terminate with verify*() — or nothing runs

Forgetting verify()

StepVerifier.create(flux).expectNext(1) alone does nothing — no subscription happens until a verify*() method is called. A test that "passes" without verify asserts nothing.

docs.title: Virtual time
docs.text:
Replace the clock for operators that use Schedulers.parallel() timers (delay, interval, timeout, delayElements). The publisher must be created inside the supplier:

// a daily report that would take 3 days of wall-clock time to test
StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> Flux.interval(Duration.ofDays(1)).map(d -> "report-" + d).take(3))
        .expectSubscription()
        .expectNoEvent(Duration.ofDays(1))
        .expectNext("report-0")
        .thenAwait(Duration.ofDays(2))
        .expectNext("report-1", "report-2")
        .verifyComplete();

docs.title: TestPublisher — drive signals by hand
docs.text:
TestPublisher<String> source = TestPublisher.create();
Flux<String> upper = source.flux().map(String::toUpperCase).onErrorReturn("RECOVERED");

StepVerifier.create(upper)
        .then(() -> source.emit("a", "b"))       // emit + complete
        .expectNext("A", "B")
        .verifyComplete();

TestPublisher<String> failing = TestPublisher.create();
StepVerifier.create(failing.flux().map(String::toUpperCase).onErrorReturn("RECOVERED"))
        .then(() -> failing.next("x").error(new RuntimeException()))
        .expectNext("X", "RECOVERED")
        .verifyComplete();

TestPublisher.createNoncompliant(...) lets you test how your operators cope with misbehaving sources.

docs.title: PublisherProbe — which branch ran?
docs.text:
PublisherProbe<String> fallback = PublisherProbe.of(Mono.just("fallback"));
Mono<String> result = Mono.<String>empty().switchIfEmpty(fallback.mono());

StepVerifier.create(result).expectNext("fallback").verifyComplete();
fallback.assertWasSubscribed();

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Mono<String> user = Mono.deferContextual(ctx -> Mono.just(ctx.<String>get("user")));
StepVerifier.create(user, StepVerifierOptions.create().withInitialContext(Context.of("user", "asha")))
        .expectNext("asha")
        .verifyComplete();

docs.title: Cheat sheet
docs.text: Method Asserts expectNext(a, b) / expectNextCount(n) values / number of values expectNextMatches(pred) / assertNext(consumer) value with a predicate / AssertJ thenConsumeWhile(pred) skip matching values expectNoEvent(d) silence for a duration (virtual time) thenRequest(n) / StepVerifier.create(p, 0) manual demand thenCancel() cancel and verify cancellation path verifyComplete() / verifyError(Type) / verifyErrorMessage(m) terminal signal verify(Duration) fail if it takes too long (real time) expectAccessibleContext() inspect Context

docs.title: WebTestClient
docs.text:
WebTestClient tests HTTP endpoints. It can bind to a controller, a router function, an ApplicationContext, or a real running server.

Binding Starts Use bindToController(...) nothing — controller instances you pass fast unit-style tests bindToRouterFunction(...) nothing functional endpoints bindToApplicationContext(ctx) / @WebFluxTest + @Autowired Spring context (web slice) annotated + config + security bindToServer().baseUrl(...) / @SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT) the real server end-to-end over a socket

docs.text:
client = WebTestClient
        .bindToController(new ProductController(repository), new PriceStreamController())
        .controllerAdvice(new GlobalErrorHandler())
        .webFilter(new RequestIdWebFilter())
        .validator(validator)

        .exchange()

        .expectHeader().exists(RequestIdWebFilter.HEADER)
        .expectBody(Product.class)
        .returnResult().getResponseBody();

client.get().uri("/products/{id}", created.id())
        .exchange()
        .expectStatus().isOk()
        .expectBody()
        .jsonPath("$.name").isEqualTo("Keyboard")
        .jsonPath("$.priceMinor").isEqualTo(4999);

routes.post().uri("/v2/products").bodyValue(new Product(null, "Mouse", "electronics", 1_999))

routes.post().uri("/v2/products").header("X-Api-Key", "secret")

docs.text:
import org.springframework.boot.webflux.test.autoconfigure.WebFluxTest;   // Boot 4 package
import org.springframework.test.context.bean.override.mockito.MockitoBean;

@WebFluxTest(ProductController.class)
class ProductControllerSliceTest {

docs.title: Streaming responses
docs.text:
Flux<ServerSentEvent<PriceTick>> events = client.get().uri("/products/p1/prices")
        .accept(MediaType.TEXT_EVENT_STREAM)
        .exchange()
        .expectStatus().isOk()
        .returnResult(new ParameterizedTypeReference<ServerSentEvent<PriceTick>>() { })
        .getResponseBody();

StepVerifier.create(events.take(2))      // take(2) cancels the infinite stream
        .assertNext(e -> assertThat(e.event()).isEqualTo("price"))
        .assertNext(e -> assertThat(e.data().sequence()).isEqualTo(1))
        .verifyComplete();

docs.title: Spring WebFlux
docs.text:
Spring WebFlux is Spring's non-blocking web stack, running on Reactor Netty by default. It offers two programming models over the same engine:

Model Style Page Annotated controllers @RestController, @GetMapping — familiar from Spring MVC Annotated Controllers Functional endpoints RouterFunction + HandlerFunction — routes as code Functional Endpoints

On the client side, WebClient and HTTP interface clients make non-blocking calls. Beyond REST: GraphQL (queries, batch loading, subscriptions), Reactor Netty directly (HTTP/TCP), and file streaming with DataBuffers.

The examples use a small, generic product catalog (playbook-examples/src/main/java/.../web), tested in WebFluxExamplesTest.

docs.title: Annotated Controllers
docs.text:
Annotated controllers look almost exactly like Spring MVC — the difference is the return types (and that nothing may block).

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/products")
public class ProductController {

    private final ProductRepository repository;

    public ProductController(ProductRepository repository) {   // constructor injection
        this.repository = repository;
    }

    /** Flux return type → streamed JSON array (or NDJSON/SSE if the client asks for it). */
    @GetMapping
    public Flux<Product> list(@RequestParam(required = false) String category) {
        return category == null ? repository.findAll() : repository.findByCategory(category);
    }

    /** Empty Mono → error → mapped to 404 by the @RestControllerAdvice. */
    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public Mono<Product> get(@PathVariable String id) {
        return repository.findById(id)
                .switchIfEmpty(Mono.error(() -> new ProductNotFoundException(id)));
    }

    /** @Valid on a reactive body: validation runs when the body is decoded. */
    @PostMapping
    public Mono<ResponseEntity<Product>> create(@Valid @RequestBody Mono<Product> body) {
        return body.flatMap(repository::save)
                .map(saved -> ResponseEntity.created(URI.create("/products/" + saved.id())).body(saved));
    }

    @DeleteMapping("/{id}")
    public Mono<ResponseEntity<Void>> delete(@PathVariable String id) {
        return repository.deleteById(id)
                .map(deleted -> deleted
                        ? ResponseEntity.noContent().<Void>build()
                        : ResponseEntity.notFound().<Void>build());
    }
}

docs.title: Return types
docs.text: Return Meaning Mono<T> single body, written when the Mono emits Flux<T> streamed — JSON array, or NDJSON/SSE depending on produces/Accept Mono<ResponseEntity<T>> control status and headers reactively ResponseEntity<Mono<T>> / ResponseEntity<Flux<T>> status/headers known up front, body streamed Mono<Void> empty body after completion plain T allowed, but computed on the event loop — fine only if trivial

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text:
All the MVC arguments work (@PathVariable, @RequestParam, @RequestHeader, @CookieValue, @RequestBody, @ModelAttribute, Principal), plus reactive variants:

@PostMapping("/bulk")
Flux<Product> bulk(@RequestBody Flux<Product> products) {        // stream the request body
    return products.flatMap(repository::save, 8);
}

@GetMapping("/me")
Mono<String> me(Mono<Principal> principal) {                     // resolved lazily
    return principal.map(Principal::getName);
}

@GetMapping("/raw")
Mono<String> raw(ServerWebExchange exchange) {                   // full request/response access
    return Mono.just(exchange.getRequest().getPath().value());
}

docs.title: Validation
docs.text: @Valid @RequestBody Mono<Product> validates during decoding and signals WebExchangeBindException (→ 400). Handle it once, in an advice — see Error Handling.

docs.title: OpenAPI documentation
docs.text:
implementation("org.springdoc:springdoc-openapi-starter-webflux-ui:3.2.0")   // springdoc 3.x = Boot 4

Swagger UI is served at /swagger-ui.html and the spec at /v3/api-docs. Mono<T>/Flux<T> are documented as T / array of T; annotate streaming endpoints (text/event-stream) explicitly with @Operation and @ApiResponse(content = @Content(mediaType = "text/event-stream")).

docs.title: Server-side views (Thymeleaf)
docs.text:
WebFlux supports view rendering. With spring-boot-starter-thymeleaf, a controller can return a view name, and a data-driven context variable streams a large Flux into the page in chunks:

@GetMapping("/catalog")
String catalog(Model model) {
    model.addAttribute("products", new ReactiveDataDriverContextVariable(repository.findAll(), 50));
    return "catalog";   // templates/catalog.html renders rows as each batch of 50 arrives
}

docs.title: The request path
docs.text:
flowchart LR N[Reactor Netty<br/>event loop] --> H[HttpHandler adapter] H --> WF[WebFilter chain<br/>security, CORS, your filters] WF --> D[DispatcherHandler] D --> HM{HandlerMapping} HM -->|"@RequestMapping"| AC[Annotated controller] HM -->|RouterFunction| FE[Handler function] HM -->|URL map| WS[WebSocketHandler] AC & FE --> RH[HandlerResultHandler<br/>encodes Mono/Flux to response] RH --> N
  • Reactor Netty owns sockets; a few reactor-http-nio-N threads (default: CPU cores) run all request processing.
  • HttpHandler is the lowest-level contract (Mono<Void> handle(request, response)) — servers other than Netty (Tomcat, Jetty, Undertow via Servlet 6.1 non-blocking I/O) adapt to it.
  • WebFilter — cross-cutting interception (Spring Security is a WebFilter).
  • DispatcherHandler — the reactive counterpart of MVC's DispatcherServlet.
  • HandlerResultHandler — subscribes to your returned Mono/Flux and streams it out through codecs (Jackson 3 JSON, SSE, NDJSON, protobuf…).

docs.title: Who subscribes?
docs.text: You return a publisher; WebFlux subscribes to it when writing the response, and cancels it if the client disconnects. That's why handlers must return the full pipeline — work started with a detached subscribe() is invisible to the framework (no backpressure, no cancellation, no error mapping).

docs.title: Threading model in practice
docs.text:
Work Runs on Request decoding, your controller code, operators Netty event loop (reactor-http-nio-*) R2DBC / WebClient callbacks their own Netty event loops Mono.delay, interval, timeout timers parallel-* Blocking code you wrapped boundedElastic-*

Spring MVC and WebFlux on the classpath

If both spring-boot-starter-web and spring-boot-starter-webflux are present, Boot starts Spring MVC (servlet). Adding WebFlux to an MVC app just to use WebClient is fine; force the reactive stack with spring.main.web-application-type=reactive only if you mean it.

docs.title: Codecs
docs.text:
Codecs turn DataBuffers into objects and back. Boot configures Jackson 3 JSON, SSE, NDJSON, strings, resources, form data and multipart.

@Configuration
class CodecConfig implements WebFluxConfigurer {
    @Override
    public void configureHttpMessageCodecs(ServerCodecConfigurer configurer) {
        configurer.defaultCodecs().maxInMemorySize(2 * 1024 * 1024);   // DataBufferLimitException above this
        configurer.defaultCodecs().enableLoggingRequestDetails(false);
    }
}

Or simply spring.codec.max-in-memory-size=2MB. Customise Jackson through JsonMapperBuilderCustomizer beans (Jackson 3) rather than replacing the mapper.

docs.title: CORS
docs.text:
@Configuration
class CorsConfig implements WebFluxConfigurer {
    @Override
    public void addCorsMappings(CorsRegistry registry) {
        registry.addMapping("/api/**")
                .allowedOrigins("https://shop.example.com")
                .allowedMethods("GET", "POST", "PUT", "DELETE")
                .allowCredentials(true)
                .maxAge(3600);
    }
}

With Spring Security, also enable http.cors(Customizer.withDefaults()) so preflight requests are not rejected before reaching the mapping. For functional endpoints use a CorsWebFilter bean.

docs.title: Multipart uploads (streaming)
docs.text:
@PostMapping(path = "/upload", consumes = MediaType.MULTIPART_FORM_DATA_VALUE)
Mono<String> upload(@RequestPart("file") FilePart file) {
    Path target = Path.of("/tmp/uploads", file.filename());
    return file.transferTo(target).thenReturn("stored " + file.filename());  // non-blocking write
}

docs.title: Static resources
docs.text: Files under src/main/resources/static are served at /. Configure caching with spring.web.resources.cache.cachecontrol.max-age.

docs.title: Server tuning (Reactor Netty)
docs.text:
server:
  netty:
    connection-timeout: 5s
    idle-timeout: 60s
    max-keep-alive-requests: 1000
  http2:
    enabled: true

For deeper control register a NettyServerCustomizer. Event-loop thread count defaults to the number of CPUs (-Dreactor.netty.ioWorkerCount=N to override). See Performance Tuning.

docs.title: Problem Details (RFC 9457)
docs.text:
Spring Framework returns application/problem+json bodies when you return a ProblemDetail or throw an ErrorResponse exception (e.g. ResponseStatusException). Enable it for framework exceptions with spring.webflux.problemdetails.enabled=true.

{
  "type": "about:blank",
  "title": "Product not found",
  "status": 404,
  "detail": "product 42 not found",
  "instance": "/products/42"
}

docs.title: @RestControllerAdvice for annotated controllers
docs.text:
/** RFC 9457 problem details for every annotated controller. */
@RestControllerAdvice
public class GlobalErrorHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(ProductNotFoundException.class)
    ProblemDetail notFound(ProductNotFoundException e) {
        ProblemDetail problem = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, e.getMessage());
        problem.setTitle("Product not found");
        return problem;
    }

    /** Thrown by @Valid on reactive bodies. */
    @ExceptionHandler(WebExchangeBindException.class)
    ProblemDetail invalid(WebExchangeBindException e) {
        ProblemDetail problem = ProblemDetail.forStatus(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST);
        problem.setTitle("Validation failed");
        problem.setProperty("errors", e.getFieldErrors().stream()
                .map(f -> f.getField() + ": " + f.getDefaultMessage())
                .sorted()
                .toList());
        return problem;
    }
}

Throw domain exceptions inside the pipeline (Mono.error(...), switchIfEmpty(Mono.error(...))) and map them centrally.

docs.title: Functional endpoints
docs.text:
Advice does not apply to RouterFunctions. Use onError on the router builder, or recover in the handler:

RouterFunctions.route()
        .GET("/v2/products/{id}", handler::get)
        .onError(ProductNotFoundException.class, (e, req) ->
                ServerResponse.status(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)
                        .bodyValue(ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, e.getMessage())))
        .build();

docs.title: Global: WebExceptionHandler
docs.text: For errors raised outside handlers (filters, routing), implement WebExceptionHandler or extend Boot's AbstractErrorWebExceptionHandler, ordered before Boot's default (@Order(-2)).

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• Map expected errors (not found, validation, conflict) to 4xx with a precise detail.
  • Never leak stack traces or internal messages in 5xx bodies.
  • Add a type URI per problem kind if clients branch on it.
  • Log 5xx once, at the edge, with the request/trace id.

docs.title: Files, DataBuffers & Large Payloads
docs.text: At the lowest level, request and response bodies are Flux<DataBuffer> — chunks of bytes, often pooled Netty memory. Working with them directly lets you stream gigabytes in constant memory.

docs.title: Streaming a file download
docs.text:
@GetMapping(path = "/reports/{name}", produces = MediaType.APPLICATION_OCTET_STREAM_VALUE)
Flux<DataBuffer> download(@PathVariable String name) {
    Path file = reportsDir.resolve(name).normalize();
    return DataBufferUtils.read(file, DefaultDataBufferFactory.sharedInstance, 64 * 1024);  // 64 KB chunks
}

Or return a Resource (new FileSystemResource(file)) and WebFlux uses zero-copy file transfer where the transport supports it.

docs.title: Streaming an upload to disk
docs.text:
@PostMapping(path = "/uploads", consumes = MediaType.APPLICATION_OCTET_STREAM_VALUE)
Mono<Void> upload(@RequestBody Flux<DataBuffer> body) {
    return DataBufferUtils.write(body, uploadsDir.resolve(UUID.randomUUID().toString()),
            StandardOpenOption.CREATE_NEW);
}

docs.title: Proxying a body without loading it
docs.text:
Mono<Void> proxy(ServerHttpRequest request, ServerHttpResponse response) {
    Flux<DataBuffer> upstream = webClient.get().uri("/big").retrieve().bodyToFlux(DataBuffer.class);
    return response.writeWith(upstream);       // backpressure end to end, constant memory
}

docs.title: Memory rules
docs.text:
• Pooled buffers must be released: if you consume DataBuffers yourself, call DataBufferUtils.release(buffer) (or use DataBufferUtils.join and release the result).
  • bodyToMono(String.class) aggregates the whole body — bounded by spring.codec.max-in-memory-size.
  • Detect leaks in tests: -Dio.netty.leakDetection.level=paranoid.

docs.title: Reading files without blocking
docs.text: java.nio file APIs are blocking. DataBufferUtils.read(Path, …) uses AsynchronousFileChannel internally; for other file operations (listing, metadata, Files.readString) wrap them: Mono.fromCallable(() -> Files.size(p)).subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()).

docs.title: WebFilter — every request
docs.text:
/**
 * Runs for every request (annotated AND functional endpoints). Adds a request id to the response and
 * to the Reactor Context so any downstream operator can read it — the reactive replacement for MDC/ThreadLocal.
 */
@Component
@Order(-200)  // before Spring Security (-100) so even rejected requests get an id
public class RequestIdWebFilter implements WebFilter {

    public static final String HEADER = "X-Request-Id";
    public static final String CONTEXT_KEY = "requestId";

    @Override
    public Mono<Void> filter(ServerWebExchange exchange, WebFilterChain chain) {
        String incoming = exchange.getRequest().getHeaders().getFirst(HEADER);
        String requestId = incoming != null ? incoming : UUID.randomUUID().toString();
        exchange.getResponse().getHeaders().set(HEADER, requestId);
        return chain.filter(exchange)
                .contextWrite(ctx -> ctx.put(CONTEXT_KEY, requestId));
    }
}

Any operator downstream of the controller can now read the request id:

Mono.deferContextual(ctx -> Mono.just("request " + ctx.get(RequestIdWebFilter.CONTEXT_KEY)))

Order

Spring Security's filter chain runs at order -100 (WebFilterChainProxy). Use a lower number to run before security (e.g. request ids), a higher one to run after authentication.

docs.title: HandlerFilterFunction — functional routes only
docs.text: See the apiKeyRequiredForWrites() filter in Functional Endpoints.

docs.title: Typical uses
docs.text:
Concern Hook request id / correlation id WebFilter + contextWrite authentication, authorization Spring Security (SecurityWebFilterChain) CORS CorsWebFilter or WebFluxConfigurer#addCorsMappings request/response logging, timing WebFilter with doFinally tenant resolution WebFilter → Context rate limiting gateway RequestRateLimiter, or a WebFilter with Redis/Bucket4j

Don't read the body in a filter

The request body is a one-shot Flux<DataBuffer>. Consuming it in a filter leaves nothing for the handler (use ServerWebExchangeDecorator with caching only if you really must).

docs.title: Functional Endpoints
docs.text: Routes are plain values (RouterFunction<ServerResponse>) built with a DSL, and handlers are functions ServerRequest -> Mono<ServerResponse>. No annotations, no reflection — easy to compose, test and even build dynamically.

docs.title: Handler
docs.text:
static final class ProductHandler {
    private final ProductRepository repository;

    ProductHandler(ProductRepository repository) {
        this.repository = repository;
    }

    Mono<ServerResponse> list(ServerRequest request) {
        return ServerResponse.ok().body(repository.findAll(), Product.class);
    }

    Mono<ServerResponse> get(ServerRequest request) {
        return repository.findById(request.pathVariable("id"))
                .flatMap(p -> ServerResponse.ok().bodyValue(p))
                .switchIfEmpty(ServerResponse.status(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)
                        .bodyValue(ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, "no such product")));
    }

    Mono<ServerResponse> create(ServerRequest request) {
        return request.bodyToMono(Product.class)
                .flatMap(repository::save)
                .flatMap(p -> ServerResponse.created(URI.create("/v2/products/" + p.id())).bodyValue(p));
    }
}

docs.title: Router + filter
docs.text:
@Bean
public RouterFunction<ServerResponse> productRoutes(ProductRepository repository) {
    ProductHandler handler = new ProductHandler(repository);
    return RouterFunctions.route()
            .path("/v2/products", builder -> builder
                    .GET("", accept(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON), handler::list)
                    .GET("/{id}", handler::get)
                    .POST("", handler::create))
            .filter(apiKeyRequiredForWrites())
            .build();
}

/** HandlerFilterFunction: like a WebFilter, but scoped to these routes only. */
static HandlerFilterFunction<ServerResponse, ServerResponse> apiKeyRequiredForWrites() {
    return (request, next) -> request.method().name().equals("GET")
            || "secret".equals(request.headers().firstHeader("X-Api-Key"))
            ? next.handle(request)
            : ServerResponse.status(HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED).build();
}

docs.title: Building blocks
docs.text: API Purpose RouterFunctions.route() builder: GET, POST, path, nest, filter, before, after, onError RequestPredicates accept(...), contentType(...), queryParam(...), headers(...) — compose with and/or ServerRequest pathVariable, queryParam, bodyToMono, bodyToFlux, principal(), exchange() ServerResponse ok(), created(uri), status(...), .bodyValue(obj), .body(publisher, Type.class) HandlerFilterFunction per-route interception (auth, logging, timing)

docs.title: Annotated vs functional — which one?
docs.text:
Prefer annotated when … Prefer functional when … the team knows Spring MVC you want explicit, testable routing you want OpenAPI generation with zero config routes are built conditionally / dynamically you use rich argument resolution (@ModelAttribute, validation) you want minimal reflection (fast startup, GraalVM native)

Both can live in the same application.

docs.text:
WebTestClient routes = WebTestClient.bindToRouterFunction(new ProductRouter().productRoutes(repository)).build();

routes.post().uri("/v2/products").bodyValue(new Product(null, "Mouse", "electronics", 1_999))
        .exchange().expectStatus().isUnauthorized();               // filter rejects writes without key

routes.post().uri("/v2/products").header("X-Api-Key", "secret")
        .bodyValue(new Product(null, "Mouse", "electronics", 1_999))
        .exchange().expectStatus().isCreated();

routes.get().uri("/v2/products").accept(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
        .exchange().expectStatus().isOk()
        .expectBodyList(Product.class).hasSize(1);

docs.title: GraphQL (Spring for GraphQL)
docs.text:
Spring for GraphQL runs on WebFlux transparently: controller methods may return Mono/Flux, batch loaders are reactive, and subscriptions stream over WebSocket (or SSE).

implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-graphql")
implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-webflux")
src/main/resources/graphql/schema.graphqls
type Query        { product(id: ID!): Product, products(category: String): [Product] }
type Product      { id: ID!, name: String!, priceMinor: Int!, reviews: [Review] }
type Review       { stars: Int!, text: String }
type Subscription { priceChanged(productId: ID!): PriceTick }
type PriceTick    { productId: ID!, priceMinor: Int!, sequence: Int! }

@Controller
class ProductGraphqlController {

    @QueryMapping
    Mono<Product> product(@Argument String id) { return products.findById(id); }

    @QueryMapping
    Flux<Product> products(@Argument String category) { return products.findByCategory(category); }

    /** Solves N+1: one call for all products in the response. */
    @BatchMapping
    Mono<Map<Product, List<Review>>> reviews(List<Product> products) {
        return reviews.findByProductIds(products.stream().map(Product::id).toList())
                .collectMultimap(Review::productId)
                .map(byId -> products.stream().collect(Collectors.toMap(p -> p,
                        p -> List.copyOf(byId.getOrDefault(p.id(), List.of())))));
    }

    @SubscriptionMapping
    Flux<PriceTick> priceChanged(@Argument String productId) { return prices.stream(productId); }
}

docs.title: HTTP Interface Clients
docs.text:
Declare an interface; Spring generates the implementation on top of WebClient (or RestClient). Return reactive types and the proxy is fully non-blocking.

@HttpExchange("/api/products")
public interface ProductApi {

    @GetExchange
    Flux<Product> list(@RequestParam(required = false) String category);

    @GetExchange("/{id}")
    Mono<Product> get(@PathVariable String id);

    @PostExchange
    Mono<ResponseEntity<Product>> create(@RequestBody Product product);

    @DeleteExchange("/{id}")
    Mono<Void> delete(@PathVariable String id);
}

@Bean
ProductApi productApi(WebClient.Builder builder) {
    WebClient client = builder.clone().baseUrl("http://catalog:8080").build();
    return HttpServiceProxyFactory.builderFor(WebClientAdapter.create(client))
            .build()
            .createClient(ProductApi.class);

docs.title: Resilience stays explicit
docs.text:
The proxy returns plain Mono/Flux, so you compose timeouts, retries and circuit breakers exactly as with WebClient:

productApi.get(id)
        .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2))
        .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(2, Duration.ofMillis(100)));

Collections as query parameters

A Collection argument for @RequestParam("ids") is sent as repeated parameters (?ids=1&ids=2), not comma-separated. Servers must read all values (queryParams().get("ids")). The capstone hit exactly this — see Restaurant Service.

docs.title: Streaming & Server-Sent Events
docs.text:
Returning a Flux with a streaming media type writes each element as soon as it is emitted — no buffering of the whole result.

Media type Format Consumer text/event-stream (SSE) id:/event:/data: frames browsers (EventSource), WebClient application/x-ndjson one JSON per line services, CLI tools, WebClient application/json a JSON array (still streamed on the wire) any client, but parsed at the end 
/** Server-Sent Events: an infinite stream; cancelled automatically when the client disconnects. */
@GetMapping(path = "/products/{id}/prices", produces = MediaType.TEXT_EVENT_STREAM_VALUE)
public Flux<ServerSentEvent<PriceTick>> prices(@PathVariable String id) {
    return Flux.interval(Duration.ofSeconds(1))
            .map(seq -> new PriceTick(id, 1_000 + (seq % 5) * 10, seq))
            .map(tick -> ServerSentEvent.builder(tick)
                    .id(String.valueOf(tick.sequence()))
                    .event("price")
                    .build());
}

/** NDJSON: one JSON document per line — great for service-to-service streaming. */
@GetMapping(path = "/products/{id}/prices.ndjson", produces = MediaType.APPLICATION_NDJSON_VALUE)
public Flux<PriceTick> pricesNdjson(@PathVariable String id) {
    return Flux.interval(Duration.ofMillis(100)).take(3).map(seq -> new PriceTick(id, 1_000, seq));
}

docs.title: Operating streams in production
docs.text:
• Heartbeats: proxies close idle connections (often after 60 s). Merge a comment event every 15 s: Flux.merge(updates, Flux.interval(ofSeconds(15)).map(i -> ServerSentEvent.builder().comment("ping").build())).
  • Termination: complete the stream when the client no longer needs it (takeUntil(...)), so it doesn't hold a connection forever.
  • Slow clients: decide on a backpressure strategy for hot sources (onBackpressureLatest()).
  • Scale-out: an in-memory Sinks.Many only knows events from this instance. Feed each instance from Kafka (one consumer group per instance) or Redis pub/sub.

docs.title: WebClient
docs.text:
WebClient is the non-blocking, streaming HTTP client (Reactor Netty underneath). In Boot, inject the auto-configured WebClient.Builder (from spring-boot-webclient) — it carries codecs, observation/tracing and customizers — and build one client per downstream service.

@Configuration
class ClientsConfig {
    @Bean
    WebClient inventoryWebClient(WebClient.Builder builder) {
        return builder.clone()                         // don't mutate the shared builder
                .baseUrl("http://inventory:8080")
                .defaultHeader(HttpHeaders.ACCEPT, MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE)
                .build();
    }

    @Bean
    InventoryClient inventoryClient(WebClient inventoryWebClient) {
        return new InventoryClient(inventoryWebClient);
    }
}

docs.title: A production-shaped call
docs.text:
/** A resilient downstream call with WebClient: status mapping, timeout, retry, fallback. */
public class InventoryClient {

    public record Stock(String productId, int available) {
    }

    public static class InventoryUnavailableException extends RuntimeException {
        public InventoryUnavailableException(String message) {
            super(message);
        }
    }

    private final WebClient webClient;

    public InventoryClient(WebClient webClient) {     // built from the auto-configured WebClient.Builder
        this.webClient = webClient;
    }

    public Mono<Stock> stock(String productId) {
        return webClient.get()
                .uri("/inventory/{id}", productId)
                .retrieve()
                .onStatus(status -> status.value() == 404, resp -> Mono.empty())   // 404 → empty Mono
                .onStatus(HttpStatusCode::is4xxClientError, resp -> resp.createException())
                .bodyToMono(Stock.class)
                .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2))                                    // per attempt
                .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(100))
                        .filter(InventoryClient::isTransient)
                        .onRetryExhaustedThrow((spec, signal) -> signal.failure())) // surface the real cause
                .onErrorMap(InventoryClient::isTransient,
                        e -> new InventoryUnavailableException("inventory down: " + e.getMessage()));
    }

    private static boolean isTransient(Throwable e) {
        return e instanceof WebClientResponseException w && w.getStatusCode().is5xxServerError()
                || e instanceof java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException;
    }
}

docs.text:
Stub the transport with an ExchangeFunction:

// Stub the transport with an ExchangeFunction: no server, no mock-server library needed
AtomicInteger calls = new AtomicInteger();
ExchangeFunction flakyThenOk = request -> Mono.just(calls.incrementAndGet() < 3
        ? ClientResponse.create(HttpStatus.SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE).build()
        : ClientResponse.create(HttpStatus.OK)
                .header(HttpHeaders.CONTENT_TYPE, MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE)
                .body("{\"productId\":\"p1\",\"available\":7}")
                .build());
var inventory = new InventoryClient(WebClient.builder().exchangeFunction(flakyThenOk).build());

StepVerifier.create(inventory.stock("p1"))
        .expectNext(new Stock("p1", 7))
        .verifyComplete();
assertThat(calls).hasValue(3);   // two 503s retried, third call succeeded

docs.title: WebSocket
docs.text:
A reactive WebSocketHandler gets an inbound Flux<WebSocketMessage> and returns a Mono<Void> that represents the whole session. Generic example — a chat room broadcasting to everyone:

@Component
class ChatHandler implements WebSocketHandler {

    private final Sinks.Many<String> room = Sinks.many().multicast().directBestEffort();

    @Override
    public Mono<Void> handle(WebSocketSession session) {
        Mono<Void> inbound = session.receive()
                .map(WebSocketMessage::getPayloadAsText)
                .doOnNext(text -> room.emitNext(text, Sinks.EmitFailureHandler.busyLooping(Duration.ofMillis(50))))
                .then();

        Mono<Void> outbound = session.send(room.asFlux().map(session::textMessage));

        return Mono.zip(inbound, outbound).then();   // session lives until both complete
    }
}

@Configuration
class WebSocketConfig {
    @Bean
    HandlerMapping chatMapping(ChatHandler handler) {
        return new SimpleUrlHandlerMapping(Map.of("/ws/chat", handler), -1);  // before controllers
    }
}
